In cases where heavy neutral leptons are significantly heavier, we expand upon existing research to create complete standard model amplitude representations for electron-heavy neutral lepton pair production, with precise calculations for both tree-level and virtual corrections. Furthermore, we develop and record the corresponding sub-processes at the tree-level and virtual level with helicity amplitudes, with loop corrections occurring at the order of $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_Z^2 m_e^2/(4m_H^2))$. Future direct neutrino mass measurement devices, such as the KATRIN experiment, aim to detect masses in the range of a few meV, which corresponds to production rates of the relevant process we are analyzing that we find to be on the order of a few femtobarns for masses in this range and relevant Z boson masses.

Permutation decoding has become more prominent lately, allowing it to take advantage of codes' symmetries in parallel. Furthermore, research has found that by treating permuted polar codes as polar subcodes, the number of applicable permutations in permutation decoding can be enlarged. We have taken this concept a step further to pre-transformed polar codes, including those augmented with cyclic redundancy check (CRC) codes, which could previously not be decoded through permutations due to their limited symmetrical properties. We utilize BP-based subdecoders to demonstrate a level of performance that approaches CRC-aided SCL decoding, ultimately achieving better error-rate and lower latency compared to previously best-performing iterative CRC-aided belief propagation list (CA-BPL) decoders.

We investigate the link between the choice of image co-adding method and point spread function (PSF) characteristics. A set of rigorous mathematical conditions is established to ensure that a linear co-adding process yields a co-added image with a defined and unaltered point source profile. A novel set of linear operators that maintain the PSF is introduced and characterized. A co-adding method that preserves the PSF without restricting the image data fails to meet the criteria defined by the set of linear operators that preserve the PSF without restricting the image data, except in cases where specified subspaces coincide naturally. Several co-adding methods, that maintain the PSF, are identified and evaluated, with their effectiveness tested using the Hubble Space Telescope's F160BWF (160 nanometers) FOCAS camera images. A co-adding method that incorporates prior knowledge to optimize image processing is introduced, allowing for image improvements based on prior observations and high-resolution input images. This new technique improves image resolution and accurately maintains the PSF, successfully applied to FOCAS data and producing images with a defined and unaltered point source profile. By using a combination of observations taken under different seeing conditions, it's possible to produce images with a well-defined point spread function. Applying prior knowledge enables the creation of images with a well-defined point spread function, except in cases where a given image segment corresponds to a prior observation, a situation that occurs in images taken under extreme observation conditions, a common occurrence with a

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of solid crystals at their most basic level. Founded on the thermodynamic dislocation theory, it begins by postulating that the behavior of dislocations in these solids must comply with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics. A critical premise is that the fracture of a solid initiates when the apex of a pre-existing notch reaches a critical instability point, beyond which it begins to sharpen uncontrollably. The resulting predictions derived from this analysis were tested and validated against the meticulous measurements conducted by Gumbsch and associates, who examined the notch toughness of predeformed and non-deformed tungsten crystals under various conditions, spanning a wide range of temperatures, loading rates, and initial states. Notably, the theoretical framework's quantitative predictions consistently aligned with the experimental findings, covering both types of fracture and encompassing different thermal conditions and initial dislocation densities.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of a Gaussian free field and an elliptic curve over the non-commutative analogue of the complex numbers, which are represented by central elements of a finite-dimensional commutative algebra. Specifically, they showed that the Dyson model can be interpreted as a Gaussian free field on an imaginary surface with a specific action of the free group. In this work, multiple Dyson models associated with different groupings are combined into a single field on an imaginary surface, which corresponds to a specific compactified version of the space that contains all possible one-dimensional arrangements of the eigenvalues.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm.

The verification problem for quantum computation is crucial and challenging, where a quantum server attempts to convince a less computationally powerful classical client that a quantum circuit has produced a specific output. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has a time complexity of O(poly(κ)) compared to the classical protocol, specifically O(L^3). A new, more efficient protocol has been developed to counteract this complexity disadvantage. The new protocol reduces the computational burden of the classical client by a significant factor, from O(poly(κ)) to O(L), mirroring the classical standard. The new protocol relies on a special type of quantum computation called a random oracle, distinguishing it from other protocols that utilize oracular structures in a fundamentally different way. Additionally, the construction satisfies constant levels of statistical security, ensuring the classical client receives the correct computation result with virtually no uncertainty.

A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, making it a prime candidate for establishing trust within the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem, where its applications extend beyond digital currencies. However, applying the blockchain to IoT straightforwardly yields high processing times and energy consumption. To address these limitations in supply chain management, where various IoT devices operate in parallel, a new blockchain architecture has been developed, specifically designed to incorporate a lightweight consensus protocol, known as LC4IoT. Simulations were conducted to test the performance of LC4IoT and revealed that the proposed approach consumes minimal computational power, storage space, and processing delay.

Generating synthetic cell shapes for training cell image segmentation from diverse cell types remains underdeveloped. Current methods primarily rely on voxel-based representations or polygon meshes, which are inefficient and impractical for training due to their coarse or fragmented nature. Our approach utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to model cells, which offer a balanced, detailed, and efficient representation. Our contributions include a novel synthetic cell data generation framework utilizing neural fields to create cell shapes. This framework extends to synthesis of cell membranes and included substructures. Our method also extends to synthesis of proxy labels from a standard histology image. Our approach enables rapid generation of numerous diverse cell shapes and proxy labels, which can be utilized to simulate real-world segmentation scenarios with high quality. Our results demonstrate superior performance in comparison to existing synthetic data methods on actual cell segmentation tasks. Our code and synthetic data can be accessed at https://github.com/amoitov/synthetic-cell-data.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals still struggle with printed documents. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as references, footnotes, and glossaries. Unlike existing solutions, we present a new approach involving document fingerprinting, which enables the identification of referenced content across different documents, even when the target document is unknown. Similar to a search engine, our system helps look up content based on a brief description, but unlike traditional searching, the description is extracted automatically from the reference itself. The efficacy of our method was tested through two studies conducted via the internet, which revealed very accurate results, outperforming existing technologies in the process.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning by leveraging permutations of factorization order, and naturally captures both global and local positional dependencies. Moreover, XLNet incorporates the capabilities of BERT, transformer-based architectures, and autoregressive language modeling, resulting in superior performance across a range of benchmark tests as demonstrated in recent findings.

We've developed computational models aimed at assessing the visibility of planetary water signs in the spectra of transiting exoplanets, taking into account the active star effects as described in recent research. By simulating the effects of stellar activity on the O$_2$ and H$_2$O absorption features in the frame of a one-dimensional model, we calculated the impact of these effects on the combined light of the star and planet as it passes through the telescope's aperture. Using observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, we obtained the necessary input data on stellar activity indicators, applied models to the data, and then simulated the resulting spectra of transit events. Our approach enables the estimation of errors in measuring planetary parameters, including those related to the detection of atmospheric signals, which are influenced by stellar activity. Moreover, our models include a second method for directly quantifying the ratio of planetary to stellar water features ($f_{\rm planet}/f_{\rm star}$) and examine its potential in reducing uncertainty regarding water content in the host star. According to our findings, water signals in host stars can obscure planetary water features in the visible spectrum, which in turn increases the planetary radius discrepancy in relation to models of planets' internal structure and mass, which in certain situations can be as large as 6.5% of the planetary radius. Our study indicates that detecting water in host stars can help minimize this phenomenon, which in some cases can be as large as 0.04 $R_\odot$.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-forms. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially established by Troyanov.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by creating waves along the body, this species moves using waves in the opposite direction, from tail to head. Its low mass and the presence of fluids against its body cause movement dynamics where drag forces overcome inertia, which are difficult to analyze mathematically. To resolve this, scientists used a combination of long series expansions and asymptotic analysis to study two fluid flow models, the lubrication model and the free-surface greenberg model, which both apply to the centipede's movement, although the greenberg model is more accurate and helps to explain why the centipede's tail is typically more agile than its head pair of legs.

The ultimate aim of this project is the creation of highly detailed simulation tools that can accurately model tsunami behavior that is affected by their dispersion, and we begin by examining the ideal scenario where the water's depth remains uniform. By simplifying the complex equations governing tsunami motion, we derive a mathematical equation that is well-suited for numerical simulation in terms of uniform depth. Following significant advancements in the numerical methods used for such scenarios, we turn our attention to the more practical case where the water's depth varies, and once again reduce the complex equations at play. Similar to the uniform depth case, this enables highly accurate computer simulations of a wide range of situations, including the impact of various models that describe how tsunami behavior changes over time.

Recent observations from ALMA and Spitzer have uncovered a population of large galaxies that lack detectable rest-ultraviolet or far-ultraviolet radiation, and emit intense dust-corrected far-infrared radiation. The data suggest these galaxies are predominantly large, massive, and highly star-forming systems located at least 1 billion light-years away. To better understand their characteristics, we aimed to find counterparts for these galaxies in ultra-deep UltraVista UltraVista imaging data. The study focused on 102 galaxies with specific far-infrared, radio, and UV properties, and was conducted across multiple filters in the near-infrared and ultraviolet spectrums. The analysis revealed 67% of FISDSS-faint FUV emitters had near-infrared and UV luminosities below specific sets, and were either extremely diffuse or highly dust-obscured. The study also found that less than a quarter of the sample could be detected by HST, and those detected had surface brightnesses similar to extremely diffuse galaxy candidates. The data further suggests these galaxies have short star-forming timescales, extremely low escape fractions for ultraviolet photons, and highly dust-observed star-forming regions. The study aims to contribute to a greater understanding of extremely diffuse galaxy candidates by including those undetected in ultraviolet spectra. The study's findings will also be compared to future data from James Webb Space Telescope, and the Simulating Star formation and Assembly of Galaxies model.

By incorporating two topological terms into the Einstein-Hilbert action, we form a novel seven-dimensional theory of gravity. Depending on specific constant values, these terms may be equivalent to a 3-form field equation correction in eleven-dimensional supergravity. The complete equations of motion are subsequently determined. Interestingly, the addition of these terms leaves static, spherically-symmetric black holes unchanged. The new theory also yields AdS_7 spaces, squashed seven-dimensional spheres, and Q^{111} spaces in a Euclidean signature.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure all the disks come into contact with one of the container's walls when it reaches equilibrium, resulting in a confined volume. By viewing this system as a mixture of particles in contact with heat and momentum sources, we find that the volume is restricted to a narrow range and explore how different parameters, such as disk size and speed, affect the system's equilibrium state, revealing diverse jammed configurations that can be probed experimentally.

Research into El Ni\~no's two main flavors - East Pacific and Central Pacific types - has become a significant focus in climate variability studies. Recent investigations heavily rely on statistical techniques such as multivariate analysis, often combining multiple atmospheric and oceanic indicators. However, a crucial question remains without a clear answer: Which initial Pacific Oscillation phase influences each flavor of El Ni\~no, and how do these phases correlate with distinct climate impacts? We employ advanced data analysis methods using a comprehensive climate reanalysis to thoroughly investigate the dynamics of East Pacific and Central Pacific types of El Ni\~no. Our findings indicate that variations in East Pacific-type El Ni\~no are closely associated with East Pacific Oscillation fluctuations, whereas Central Pacific-type El Ni\~no is linked to Central Pacific Oscillation changes. We utilize comprehensive multivariate statistical techniques to derive two main components of atmospheric anomalies, one corresponding with East Pacific-type El Ni\~no and the other with Central Pacific-type El Ni\~no. These components exhibit differing responses to opposite phases of Pacific Oscillation, resulting in contrasting climate effects. Our investigation highlights the distinct effects of each flavor of El Ni\~no on the climate system, leading to significant, varied impacts based on their differing atmospheric and oceanic anomalies, ultimately causing distinct weather patterns to emerge.

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to mechanical pressure, the distortion within the material doesn't primarily result from the external force; instead, nearby particles are also pulled in random ways, causing internal stress. We've investigated how rearrangements of particles occur under certain conditions using tests on 2D and 3D foams. In the initial stages, smaller groups of particles cluster together and rearrange. The time it takes for these clusters to rearrange increases as the external force decreases. The clusters eventually combine into larger units, with the distance between them growing over time. The distance between these domains increases as the external force decreases. The rate of growth is the same as the rate of movement in a random walk and depends on the strength of the external force and the size of the domains, not on how tightly packed the material is. Our findings can help in the development of models that accurately account for how the body of the material responds to external forces.

This research investigates the dynamics of insect populations, factoring in the effects of environmental toxins and inter-specific competition, through a non-linear mathematical model that accounts for the adult insects' psychological impact on mortality rates. By combining theoretical analysis with computational simulations, we examine the complex interactions between these components, which influence the population's adult and juvenile phases. Specifically, we evaluate the influence of psychological effects, inter-specific competition, and environmental toxicity on the population's multi-faceted dynamics, as characterized by the emergence, extinction, and coexistence of the adult stages with their respective predator-prey dynamics.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with certain weakening and contraction properties. This achievement builds on a previous result regarding the contraction counterparts of these extensions, while the computational complexity was not determined for them. In this study, we introduce just the necessary concepts related to well-quasi-orderings and fast-growing complexity classes, enabling us to provide upper bounds on complexity for the extensions in question.

Hierarchical taxonomies have immense value in numerous applications, but their applicability is restricted by the costly and time-consuming process of manual maintenance. Current research seeks to automatically enhance taxonomies by leveraging external knowledge sources, but fails to leverage the inherent structure of the taxonomy itself. Considering taxonomies as entities within hyperbolic space, where relationships are preserved, enables the development of a novel framework that enhances existing hyperbolic approaches. This results in improved semantic similarity between concepts and accelerated learning. The proposed method was tested using two minimal and two comprehensive open-source concept datasets, with results indicating a substantial enhancement in accuracy over state-of-the-art approaches and outperforming all existing hyperbolic approaches. The developed framework efficiently integrates external knowledge to enhance semantic similarity, particularly between distant concepts, and achieves optimal performance in concept similarity prediction.

A comprehensive study has analyzed the interaction dipole moments of molecular pairs in 407 unique gas-phase complexes involving nitrogen base analogues. The research utilized a highly accurate method, which combines coupled-cluster theory with a large basis set. The investigation found that the interaction dipole moment plays a crucial role in understanding complex formations through various chemical interactions. In cases where molecules interact via hydrogen bonding, $\pi$-ring stacking, or aryl-aryl interactions, the intermolecular dipole moment is significantly high, approaching 20 debye or more. The research revealed that dipole moments are influenced by spatial orientation but also demonstrated that averaging effects can lead to reduced variation. The study provides data on the absolute and relaxed interaction dipole moments of these complexes, allowing for a direct comparison with experimental data that has not been previously corrected for structural relaxation. The difference between the total and relaxed dipole moments has been quantified and shown to be relatively small. The research offers the complete set of absolute and relaxed dipole moments for all analyzed complexes, along with their relevant structural coordinates, to facilitate comparison with experimental data that has not been previously corrected for structural relaxation. The data show that, on average, the difference between the total and relaxed dipole moments amounts to about 1.6 debye, which is relatively small.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved industrial productivity and efficiency, incorporating data analytics and cyber-physical systems for enhanced planning and scheduling. Nonetheless, uncertainties inherent in real-world environments, particularly time vagaries and budget estimation inaccuracies, impede the smooth operation of industrial consignment systems. Compounding these issues, feedback-induced nonlinearities only exacerbate the problem. This study proposes a novel feedback control approach for the consignment system, integrating the principles of event-triggered scheduling to minimize monitoring frequencies and thereby reducing computational burdens. Although this integrated method offers numerous benefits, implementing it in the consignment system is complicated due to the presence of time delays and nonlinearities, requiring a comprehensive stability analysis framework. This research provides a theoretical foundation for the combined event-triggering and feedback control approach, demonstrating its superiority in terms of performance and efficiency. However, due to the presence of time delays and nonlinearities, solving the related Lyapunov equation remains computationally expensive, necessitating a zealous reduction in the number of grid points in the ZE solution by adopting a novel ZE formulation with ZE constraints. This research presents two distinct methods for determining the optimal number of grid points in the ZE solution: (i) a parameter-dependent method using LMIs with LEX and (ii) a minimization problem with ZE constraints. Notably, both methods can significantly reduce the number of grid points in the ZE solution without compromising system stability while minimizing computational complexities.

Cyber-Physical Systems require robust resilience properties to withstand disruptions, yet a standardized approach remains lacking. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency, which involves measuring the time and effort required for recovery from disturbance. This framework divides resiliency into two interconnected components: swift recovery from adverse conditions, and cost-effective recovery that minimizes operational expenses. To assess these factors, we employ three key indicators: performance duration, damage severity, and financial cost. This resiliency evaluation method is applied to a real-world smart building application, specifically a modern energy-efficient lighting system.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally affects luminous matter, this interaction makes accelerometer-based searches particularly intriguing. This article details ongoing and future searches for dark matter particles such as feebly interacting matter trapped on Earth, scalar domain walls, and axion quark nuggets, employing accelerometers in a network configuration and discussing how atomic interferometry-based networks might enhance these searches.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension m, equipped with the metric g, whose Bakry-\'{E}mery Ricci curvature is bounded below by zero. We derive a localized version of Hamilton's gradient estimate for the solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation, which have a positive, smooth, and bounded u. The equation u_t is given by \[ \Delta u - \nabla \phi \cdot \nabla u = (au + b) \log u. \] In our analysis, \phi is a twice continuously differentiable function and a and b are non-zero constants. Our findings extend existing work from Souplet and Zhang (2006) and Wu (2008) by introducing a localized Hamilton's estimate.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, this study calculates the median fractional polarization in relation to angular size. It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible internal state, which can still cause probabilities to change over time. When describing such processes, it's necessary to consider three elements: a finite set of internal states (Q), a finite set of observable symbols (O), and a transition probability matrix (A) that dictates how probabilities change over time. Additionally, there's a matrix (B) that maps internal states to observable symbols, and a matrix (P) that dictates how probabilities converge over time. However, this standard form can become cumbersome when working with models where the number of possible states or symbols increases over time. To address this, we've developed an approach called Adaptive HMMs (AHMMs), which builds on existing models by increasing the size of the internal state and observation spaces over time. AHMMs use initial transition and emission probabilities for the initial states, with transition and emission probabilities for new states derived from the probability distributions of the previous states. We've shown that AHMMs can be represented as a type of continuous HMM with increasing dimensions, which makes them amenable to standard estimation techniques. To estimate AHMMs, we simply apply standard HMM estimation techniques to the extended model, which simplifies the process. We've shown the effectiveness of AHMMs on real-world data from a health monitoring system and an activity recognition dataset, which suggests that AHMM

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's essence, characterized by the shift from one coherent structure to another. Our analysis yields exact expressions for the turbulent transport operator without employing simplifying assumptions. In the limit where spatial and temporal locality prevail, our operator reduces to the conventional estimate of turbulent transport as a diffusivity tensor, with its components being the integrated velocity field auto-correlation.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a complete understanding of the dynamics behind nucleon-nucleus and
nucleus-nucleus scattering. When phenomenological models are too limited,
vital information about the processes that occur during collisions on both
macro and micro scales are lost. In particular, we express concern that the
folding model, widely used in both phenomenology and theory to understand
scattering processes, may not fully utilize the wealth of experimental
data at play. By employing an unconventional approach to describe the
scattering of one neutron against deuterium, we test the assumption that
phenomenological parameters have universal meanings, ultimately paving the
way for a more comprehensive and unified understanding of nuclear elastic
scattering processes, whether involving large or small nuclei.

We examine electromagnetic radiation confined within a thin wall-separated space with perfectly conductive walls, focusing on its thermodynamic behavior and electromagnetic properties. At ordinary temperatures, the confined radiation follows the predictions of the ideal gas theory, with an added twist of zero chemical potential. However, at extremely low temperatures, the confined radiation displays distinct non-quasi particle characteristics, where the energy and density have a linear relationship. The low-temperature behavior results in the free energy and various thermodynamic parameters having a low temperature power law dependence. Furthermore, the low-temperature behavior implies the presence of a finite specific heat that diverges at a low temperature, contradicting the standard blackbody radiation theory. We also investigate the electromagnetic properties, including the low-temperature magnetic permeability and electric permittivity derivatives. The low temperature behavior of these derivatives implies the presence of magnetization and dielectric polarization within the confined radiation. The low-temperature behavior of the electric permittivity derivative can be understood within the framework of dipole interaction, whereas the low-temperature behavior of the magnetic permeability derivative suggests the presence of magnetization originating from dipoles.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to protecting such data, with an application in our case study protecting a manufacturing company's routes from being exposed.

A highly sought-after component in autonomous driving, 3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in locations where GPS signals are unreliable. The incorporation of multi-scale information in topological networks has yielded superior outcomes. Despite the potential of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in processing multi-scale data, applying GCNs to 3D point clouds necessitates data reduction due to their large size. Our proposed research introduces a novel approach, the Deep Topological Feature Network (DTFN), which utilizes a multi-scale GCN to extract topological features from reduced point clouds, and then utilizes these features along with multi-scale information from pyramidal convolutions to learn descriptive features. These features are then fed into a classifier to determine the place category. Our results demonstrate that DTFN achieves high accuracy with a 90.6% ratio of recall, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods in 3D point cloud-based place recognition. Additionally, our network's multi-scale capabilities allow it to withstand noise and data augmentation attacks. The source code of our model will be made available to the public.

Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we investigated how site-specific factors might affect our ability to detect significant differences in connectivity when analyzing data from two different groups across multiple research centers. Focusing on N-back tasks, we utilized functional connectivity data from the dorsal medial prefrontal parietal network and assigned it to distinct classes based on known task-related connectivity patterns. When analyzing data from two groups of subjects scanned at different sites, we found that multisite studies significantly reduced our ability to detect significant differences in connectivity when compared to within-site analyses. Additionally, we observed a higher likelihood of incorrectly identifying significant differences in connectivity when analyzing data from multiple sites. Our findings highlight potential pitfalls to be considered in the design of future multisite resting-state connectivity studies.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to form a distributed communication system. We explore the distributed computing domain's two core challenges, naming and counting issues, and our objective is to refine existing algorithms to reduce their energy usage and processing speed. Our key contribution is the development of efficient, randomized algorithms that achieve optimal O(n log n) processing efficiency and O(log n) energy usage for n-station beeping networks, addressing both the naming and counting problems.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
particularly among speakers of mixed languages, but data availability and 
multilingual considerations pose significant challenges. One critical issue is 
the lack of adequate word embeddings for code-mixed languages. This paper presents 
an innovative, generative method for building word embeddings specifically tailored 
for code-mixed languages, leveraging the power of GANs. This approach circumvents 
issues related to data scarcity and allows for the integration of linguistic rules 
when constructing the embeddings. We conducted exhaustive experiments on datasets 
from Hindi-English and Hindi-Spanish code-mixed languages, comparing our method with 
conventional word embeddings and state-of-the-art GAN-based techniques. We evaluated 
the quality of the generated embeddings using six standardized metrics and found 
them to surpass embeddings produced by other methods in five out of six measurements.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S as a function of pressure between 162 and 250 GPa. Our results show that accounting for the variable density of states significantly improves the match with experimental data for the critical temperature. Additionally, we found that considering two key components - the electron-phonon interaction near the Fermi level and the density of states at the Fermi level - is sufficient to explain the known characteristics of H3S under high pressure.

This paper presents an innovative technique to create spatial boundaries for navigation in dynamic environments. In the field of autonomous driving and robotics, motion planning often relies on map-based constraints provided by a global planner. However, existing methods are susceptible to poor performance in dynamic environments. To overcome this limitation, we propose an end-to-end learning approach for motion planning that utilizes a graph-based space and an encoder-decoder network for collision avoidance. Our method does not require a predefined map or global planner, instead, it uses the observed dynamics to create a graph-based space and learns the optimal navigation strategy. Furthermore, we employ a reinforcement learning framework that integrates an actor-critic model and a graph-based LSTM to investigate the relationship between the space and time domains. Our method demonstrates superior performance in dynamic environments, as evident from both simulation and real-world testing with a mobile robot.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric entities via global indices obtained through mapping rendering. By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes key pose parameters, ultimately facilitating fast and independent keyframe localization using a sparse, globally mapped network. Moreover, this technique incorporates both geometric and photometric information to enhance accuracy and robustness. Evaluations on diverse datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this 3D surfel-based approach.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for finite harmonic mappings between tropical curves, the rational function semifield of the first curve can be expressed as a finite set of elements over the pull-back of the rational function semifield of the second curve.

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles through integration produces a specific Vassiliev invariant, having a precise order of three. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, stating that such integrations yield Vassiliev invariants of order two. Notably, the resulting invariant exhibits its roots in combinatorial mathematics, specifically in relation to the spaces described through Barry Meschkowski's representation, and we have successfully translated the problem into an equivalent form that makes its connection to this space's properties clear.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still the subject of controversy. While in most FeSCs superconductivity arises close to a nematic and magnetic state, the iron-based compound LiFeAs exhibits unique characteristics, becoming superconducting below 18 K without undergoing a magnetic or structural phase transition. Some studies have hinted at the existence of nematic fluctuations and a nematic superconducting state in LiFeAs, but recent findings indicate that these earlier results were likely due to data analysis errors. To correct this, we have re-evaluate a set of neutron scattering data from LiFeAs and find that, upon correction for accidental coincidences, there is no substantial peak appearing in the (Q,ω) space, which indicates there are no long-lived quasiparticle excitations at low energy. Consequently, our data does not support the presence of magnetic domains or nematic fluctuations and, instead, suggests that the superconducting state in LiFeAs is likely isotropic in nature.

Upcoming measurements of the Higgs boson and other particles will significantly influence the parameters of Type-II two Higgs doublet models, especially those related to dark matter and electroweak symmetry breaking. This study examines whether these future measurements can uncover Type-II 2HDM models, even when considering interactions with third-generation fermions and accounting for theoretical constraints. It appears that even with increased precision, future measurements will only slightly restrict the potential parameter space, leaving a considerable area compatible with a Type-II 2HDM model. Furthermore, in most scenarios, the Higgs boson will exhibit standard coupling behaviour, although there will be a range of possibilities for the interactions of top and bottom quarks with the Higgs boson. Additionally, in some scenarios, the second scalar can be primarily responsible for electroweak symmetry breaking, and this may still be within reach of future measurements. Finally, while split supersymmetry can partially avoid constraints from LHC searches, even with increased precision, future measurements will still have limited restrictions. This study shows that even with enhanced precision, future measurements will have difficulty distinguishing between the Higgs boson in standard models and various Type-II 2HDM models.

We demonstrate through simulated molecular surface experiments that neuroevolutionary learning can independently design particles and temporal strategies for enhancing spontaneous assembly processes, based solely on the desired end properties and specified structural characteristics, and not relying on static structures or potential energy landscapes. By applying this method, we successfully evolved a simple, homogeneous particle that assembles a highly symmetric, hollow structure with high efficiency, and another particle that produces a less efficient but more complex arrangement within a specific time frame, both of which surpass the efficiency of particles designed using alternative, trailblazing techniques based on genetic algorithms.

Our research appears to suggest a dynamical-Higgs-phase outcome in a broad range of chiral gauge theories, particularly those that are strongly-coupled. In contrast, a different scenario featuring flavor symmetric vacuums with massless baryonlike composite fermions does not seem as likely. The possibility of formulating a strong-anomaly effective action, similar to one applied to QCD, using the infrared theory's low-energy degrees of freedom serves as a key criterion in our argument. Additionally, our findings also relate to other theories, such as the concepts of complementarity and the large $N$ planar dominance in chiral gauge theories, leading to significant implications in both theory and practice.

This study contributes towards addressing a critical question in mathematical fluid dynamics research posed by Tsurumi in 2019: Are solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations and their nonlinear convergence sequence in a bounded area uniformly bounded when initial and boundary conditions are specified? Specifically, for the 3-dimensional space, if the density of the fluid is constant or if it undergoes a unique mathematical transformation, it becomes possible to establish that certain types of fluid equations will remain uniformly bounded. In a more general context, if the dimension of the space is greater than 1 and a specific fraction of the dimension is part of a different type of mathematical transformation, it becomes possible to establish that certain types of fluid equations will remain uniformly bounded. To achieve this, the ideas of a different mathematical method will be successfully applied to control a diverse set of equations that include but are not limited to linear fluid equations, linear transport equations, linear vector analysis equations, and linear vector logarithmic equations. Furthermore, the study also demonstrates that the most complex of these equations can be derived from the basic linear fluid equations by employing certain mathematical principles.

We are studying how the interactions between magnons impact the dispersion and
polarization of these magnons in specific types of antiferromagnetic materials.
By utilizing both classical and quantum methods, we have identified the
high-frequency limit of the magnon dispersion and established the
high-frequency approximation for a specific Heisenberg model. In materials
where the exchange interaction is the primary influence, we have determined the
polarization of magnon modes and developed a set of equations that governs how
these magnons interact with each other. In particular, we have shown how the
interactions between magnons at different levels affect the polarization of these
magnons. By combining our findings with previous research on magnon dispersion,
we have created a comprehensive picture of magnon polarization in specific
types of antiferromagnetic materials and have proposed methods for measuring and
studying magnon polarization in these materials.

This research introduces two modifications to enhance the security of Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, specifically against linear algebra attacks. The first modification replaces the matrix GL$n(Fq)$ with a matrix obtained from a random, finite field-oriented matrix. The second substitution involves using a random, subspace-oriented matrix derived from a unitary transformation within the matrix GL$n(Fq)$. The proposed systems maintain an identical message capacity as the original Loidreau system and retain its signature and signature-based security advantages.

To improve pre-trained language models (PLMs), which are trained on large
datasets and generate general word meanings, researchers are exploring new ways
to enhance model performance. The quality of these word meanings depends on how
often the words appear in the data, leading to underoptimized representations of
infrequent words. This paper investigates a novel method to address this issue by
leveraging dictionaries with rich lexical information to guide PLMs during
training. The goal is to encourage the model to represent words based on their
semantic contexts rather than solely relying on statistical frequency. The
dictionary provides explicit guidelines for the model, effectively implementing
interpolation to combine the two sources of information. The proposed
approach is evaluated on multiple tasks and demonstrates significant
improvements, averaging a 3.1% increase in accuracy across the tasks.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalent, the minimum spanning acycle in simplicial complexes, were previously linked to a particular value by the zeta function. A recent study of these structures focused on the expected weight convergence. In this work, we investigate the distribution of weights of a minimum spanning acycle when only partial data is available. We use a new method to derive the empirical distribution and demonstrate the convergence to a probability measure. Importantly, this measure does not rely on the structure of the supporting acycle, making it applicable in cases where the structure is not clearly defined.

This paper explores the key concepts and challenges associated with horizontal and vertical federated learning. We begin with an overview of the key research topics in this field. The first section provides a comprehensive analysis of horizontal federated learning, focusing on the communication dynamics and data distribution. The second section delves into vertical federated learning, highlighting the data fusion and utility maximization elements. The final section discusses the comparative studies of both approaches, including a detailed examination of the application of privacy-enhancing technologies in both. This paper also includes an extensive review of existing studies in both horizontal and vertical federated learning, encompassing a broad range of topics such as motivating scenarios, mathematical formulations, and applications.

A theoretical framework called B-Mesogenesis, which involves hypothetical dark matter components, forecasts specific decays of B mesons. Researchers propose a new method for determining the amplitude of the primary type of such decay: B+ particles breaking down into a proton and an antiparticle composed of dark matter, known as the Psi particle. By using data from QCD light-cone sum rules, they analyzed how B Mesons interact with a quark and a gluon, ultimately providing the formula to calculate the amplitude of this particular decay and showing its relationship to the wave function of the B Meson at a specific spatial location in its internal structure, as well as certain features of the dark matter antiparticle.

In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interconnected cyber and social layers, safeguarding public safety is increasingly complex. Agencies must now contend with potential threats from both conventional and cyber-based terrorist attacks. This study develops a unified approach to modeling and analyzing these threats within Smart City networks, incorporating the interconnections between agencies' cyber, social, and operational layers. It introduces a game-theoretic framework that enables learning and interaction between agents, allowing them to adapt and respond to changing situations. An attacker agent, characterized as a ruthless perfect hacker, utilizes a Markov decision process to maximize damage and profitability. On the other hand, the city agency seeks to minimize losses and protect itself. An artificial neural network is employed to solve the state and action space curse of dimensionality, enabling both agents to make informed decisions. Performance evaluation confirms that the city agency can develop effective defense strategies, outperforming the hacker, and that learning and social interactions play crucial roles in their interaction and adaptation.

Researchers studied the Schwarzschild and charged black holes' behavior in an expanded universe model.  They considered these black holes within a large empty sphere of radius $R$, where the area of this sphere, $A$, and the pressure, $P$, on its surface influence the black hole's phase transition.  From thermodynamic parameters such as entropy and temperature, they determined the Schwarzschild black hole undergoes no phase transition and the charged black hole undergoes a phase transition at specific temperatures, which they compared to previous outcomes.  They further explored how changes in confinement, as represented by $R$, impact the stability of these black holes in an expanded universe model.

Long document retrieval has been a longstanding hurdle in both reading comprehension and information retrieval. Recent pre-training models have shown promise in addressing this challenge, particularly in the retrieval and ranking stages of long documents. Nonetheless, issues persist in the realm of long document ranking, such as the presence of noisy labels and the challenges posed by unbalanced sampling of long documents. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach comprising a bag sampling method, robust model training, and bag-level post-ranking, which collectively enhance long document retrieval and ranking. Our method, dubbed LDRNet, boasts exceptional long document retrieval and ranking performance, achieving an ROUGE-L score of 16.14 in MSDMAR and an average recall of 87% and average precision of 87.5% in subtopic-level retrieval, outperforming state-of-the-art models.

Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often used to mitigate this issue, which aims to label unlabeled data by assigning high-confidence samples with the probability distribution. Nevertheless, this approach is prone to assigning incorrect labels to uncertain data samples. To address this problem, we propose an informative pseudo-labeling framework. This technique initially uses label propagation to obtain initial pseudo-labels. Then, to eliminate the inaccuracies in the initial pseudo-labels, it employs ensemble graph representation and predictive entropy techniques to select the most reliable pseudo-labels from the propagated labels. The selected informative pseudo-labels are used for training, resulting in an improved convergence rate and performance. The proposed framework is evaluated using multiple real-world datasets and is found to outperform existing methods under different levels of label scarcity.

Betatron radiation in a focused plasma channel holds promise as a detection method
for the details of electron beams injected into plasma wakefield acceleration experiments.
The radiation signal is strongly tied to the characteristics of the electron beam injecting
into the backgroud plasma. Research using simulated plasma dynamics and beam lines
of a few-case study points out the potential for the spectroscopy of this radiation to
reveal important details, such as the fact that the electron bunch often experiences
bremsstrahlung during the injection and also undergoes proton injection, though
bremsstrahlung signal might be much stronger than bremsstrahlung one.
Moreover, the spectroscopy of this radiation can measure the beam's longitudinal
profile and influence of the proton injection on the electron bunch. The method could
also detect the beam's transverse size by adding new observation window. The
method could also improve our understanding of how proton bunches interact with
electron bunches by selecting specific patterns in the radiation spectrum.

This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner across multiple devices, operating under various privacy standards. We propose two decentralized protocols that guarantee the protection of individual data, along with their analytical examination. We present two decentralized strategies for privately learning decision trees that meet different privacy requirements, and our results ensure the protection of data even when the distribution of data and query patterns is known by the adversary. One protocol uses a recently introduced differentially private method for private learning of shallow decision trees, and the other employs a novel differentially private approach for private learning of deep decision trees. Despite the known vulnerability of these methods to adversarial attacks, our results show that these protocols remain secure against such attacks. We further investigate how these methods can be modified to provide adversarial privacy by incorporating a type of differentially private noise, and our results demonstrate the relationship between this noise and the accuracy of the learned decision trees. Through an analysis using the concepts of worst-case adversarial noise and noise radius, our results show that these methods can be modified to privately learn decision trees under specified conditions with a certain level of accuracy.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint in the context of exponential families, and introduce an improved moment-matching algorithm, incorporating a bregman divergence and its dual. By leveraging rigorous connections between bregman divergences and Kullback-Leibler divergence, as well as strong duality principles, we establish the algorithm's ability to find exact solutions to the optimization problem. Moreover, we provide computational evidence of the algorithm's efficiency by applying it to the analysis of data generated from the Gaussian distribution under various complex scenarios.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class by introducing the chain event graph (CEG), which retains a compact Bayesian network structure but expands the variable domains to any infinite set. CEGs can model complex, inherently infinite variables, such as time points, intervals, or continuous real values with discrete subvaluations (e.g., clock hours, days, or integer powers). We develop an algorithm to determine CEG potentials from contingency tables and examine the equivalence issue between CEGs and continuous Bayesian networks, which relates to the multitask learning framework. This leads to a finding that a CEG equals a continuous Bayesian network if and only if the CEG parameters satisfy a specific convex optimisation constraint. We show that this continuity condition has practical applications in parameter estimation from contingency tables.

In a Hilbert space, we devise a rapid, dynamic method for addressing a hierarchical minimization issue, where we seek the solution with the minimum norm in a convex optimization problem. This approach involves investigating the convergence properties of the trajectories generated by an inertial dynamic with Tikhonov regularization, and demonstrating its connection to a system with viscoelastic damping. We also present convergence theorems, including one that establishes the limit point's relation to the minimum-norm solution. We then adapt the dynamic model to a time-marching scheme for solving an elastic string equation with damping, and illustrate the convergence properties of the minimization issue. Numerical experiments are performed for verification.

This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and tested with real robots, the results show that these entities can exhibit a wide range of phenomena including wall following, oscillating around walls, meandering, and circular patterns, akin to Haller's grooves. A basic mathematical model is established to depict the robots' behavior and accurately depicts their net movement in various scenarios. Additionally, the model highlights its resilience to minor changes and its ability to generate durable patterns. Importantly, the model's ability to explain the duration of the robots' stays at specific locations and the frequency of their visits at those locations accurately. Several modifications to the model-based algorithm are presented to demonstrate its capability for robustness in modeling stochastic data collected by real robots. A key discovery from this research is that these entities possess contextual, episodic memory but lack spatial memory. Contextual, episodic memory refers to the ability of these entities to recall specific situations that the algorithm has previously encountered, whereas spatial memory allows autonomous entities to recall geographical locations.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, as proposed by P.A. Pfeffer and J.P. Xiong's theory, the
d-oxides cuprate superconductors' complex temperature-dependent microwave conductivity has been analytically expressed and studied.
Conductive response equivalent to an electric field applied parallel to the Cu-O plane and parallel to the layers has been considered.
Results indicate an initial increase in conductivity over the same temperature range that superconductivity emerges, followed by a
subsequent decrease, which aligns with experimental findings, as referenced in J.X. Li et al's study in PRL (2009). Additionally,
the derived conductivity expression enables prediction of an intrinsic a.c. susceptibility that should be verifiable through Archer et al's data.

A modified curvature flow, referred to as crystalline curvature flows, was introduced and has been studied in the literature with limited research on its level set formulation. This paper presents a level set approach for solving flows in any dimension with a specific focus on initial data and existence results. It is worth noting that the standard level set method cannot be directly applied to these flows, as they inherently involve singularities. To overcome this challenge, an augmented level set equation is developed, incorporating an isotropic flow component and a conical motion variable. The variable is handled through a directional integration technique, as found in works by Chelsea Groisman, and Serfaty and Zich. The initial data must be in the CMC class, as proved by Figalli and De Philllis for a previous approach.

Our survival relies heavily on plants, and they're remarkably adept at adapting to changing environments through a process of gradual modification. Plants reacting to external stimuli offer a practical application of reinforcement learning. Our proposed benchmark, GrowSpace, involves simulating plant behavior using a space-colonization algorithm, mimicking real-world plant growth competition for resources. This simulated approach allows us to efficiently study plant movement and growth in a controlled manner, far surpassing physical experiments in terms of speed and efficiency. GrowSpace features an array of challenging tasks that necessitate sophisticated strategies for balancing resource acquisition with space exploration and resource distribution among cells to enhance survival capabilities. Notably, we discovered that plant-inspired policies prove effective not only in simulated contexts but also in artificial life settings, as seen in the underlying framework. The GrowSpace benchmark is accessible at https://github.com/google-research-gdr1/growspace.

It has been established that the SLE loop measure arises as a natural consequence of combining two Liouville quantum gravity disks through conformal welding when the variable $\gamma^2$ equals $\kappa$ in the interval (0,4). To reach this conclusion, we built upon prior work involving conformal welding of LQG disks, utilizing the Gaussian multiplicative chaos technique. When the variable $\kappa$ falls within the interval (4,8), the resulting conformal welding measure bears a resemblance to the SLE$_8/\\gamma^2$ loop measure. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the conformal welding measures corresponding to (8,8) and (0,8) share a common limit as the variable $\kappa$ approaches 8 from the left. This shared limit is believed to be equivalent to the measure associated with the uniformization problem for CFTs involving $(SF,Y)$ with $Y$ following the SLE process. Additional exploration demonstrated that varying Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos has the potential to capture the SLE loop measure. Relevantly, it has been postulated that utilizing conformal welding to combine two copies of the half-plane weighted by $e^{\beta Q_1(LY)}$ and $e^{\beta Q_2(LY)}$ may effectively capture the Gaussian Multiplicative Chaos with the parameter $Q_1(LY)-Q_2(LY)$ equaling $\\gamma^2$.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global partnership that strives for consistency in extracting biomarkers from imaging data, regardless of the application or study. One key goal of IBSI is to standardise the analysis of imaging data to ensure accurate statistical analysis results. Building upon the successes of previous collaborations, IBSI has developed a comprehensive terminology of imaging data analysis, including terms related to biomarkers, image processing, computation, and data analysis, using the Observational Ontology language. This initiative serves as a benchmarking framework, fostering advancements in imaging data analysis and computational imaging. By adopting the terminology, IBSI aims to standardise the language used among researchers, promoting high-quality data analysis and enabling the replication of applications. This partnership's terminology can be accessed via the Ontology-Based Informatics repository.

We have analyzed the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on kaon photoproduction. Two covariant isobar models were employed to simulate this process, with the formalism for high-spin propagators and interaction Lagrangians adopted from existing works. Model parameters were fitted to experimental data on cross sections, observables, and structure functions. Each model incorporated a combination of resonances, including lambda, sigma, rho, kappa*, delta*, and high-spin nucleon and delta resonances up to spin 7/2. With appropriate propagation matrices allowing resonances to contribute continuously to observables, our dual model accurately reproduced existing data within experimental and theoretical uncertainties. Several unique features distinguish our work from previous kaon production calculations. Firstly, our dependence on resonance structure, propagators, and coupling constants is evident. Secondly, resonance contributions to differential cross sections are consistent with their signatures in four-momentum transfer and energy distributions. Thirdly, high-spin nucleon and delta resonances are required to fit differential cross sections, demonstrating their significance in this process.

This research describes the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset comprising 55,134 images. The methodology section delves into the individual steps of the pre-processing sequence, with section two offering a comprehensive overview of these stages. Section three provides detailed descriptions and calculations using OpenCV functionalities to illustrate each step in the pipeline, ultimately concluding with a retrospective evaluation of potential enhancements.

Building upon our previous research \cite{Carr:2019dki}, we delve deeper into the possibility that primordial black holes contribute to dark matter and examine more closely the constraints based on cosmic microwave background observations. Specifically, we analyze the implications of these constraints in the context of a standard model of inflation, where the adiabatic index varies with the number of e-folds. Additionally, considering that primordial black holes' abundance may have fluctuated randomly, we explore the likelihood that some regions of the universe had an optimal conditions for black hole formation, given certain parameters related to the scale of primordial black hole formation and their physical properties. Such variability could potentially allow black holes to evade certain constraints and play a significant role in explaining dark matter, despite initially thought to be ruled out.

University administrators and educational planners are concerned with understanding enrollment patterns at a large scale university system. Students' course enrollment decisions are influenced by multiple factors such as course difficulty, prerequisites, and time constraints. To help planners address the resulting complexity, a pattern mining approach has been developed, enabling the identification of frequent patterns in enrollment rates across university campuses. This method utilizes a data structure called FP-tree to construct concise patterns, thereby reducing OCN^2 space requirements and achieving OCN/ω(CN) time complexity, where N represents the number of students, C denotes course enrollment counts, and ω represents the minimum enrollment threshold. Moreover, a variant of Greedy CSP search algorithm is proposed, incorporating FP-tree patterns to significantly outperform traditional CSP search methods.

Within this investigation, the challenge of vehicle platooning with connected and automated vehicles is resolved by controlling the distance between vehicles in two-defined information networks. One, the 'follow-to-front' system, utilizes the front vehicle's states as reference with each vehicle's controller informed by its preceding vehicle. The other, the 'look-ahead' arrangement, sees each vehicle's controller receive the states of the vehicle two in front of it. Beyond initial conditions, both networks result in the same control inputs and distance between vehicles. To demonstrate this, the 'look-ahead' pre-curvature control method is formally established and expanded to account for curvature. Additionally, the study proves the stability of the system through a Lyapunov function analysis. Simulation trials not only verify the study's outcomes, but also illustrate the significant advantage of using this technique to minimize the distance between vehicles.

One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into a pattern where communication is required only every $s$ iterations, as determined by the $s$ tuning parameter. The efficiency of this technique, which we refer to as Communication-Avoiding SGD (CA-SGD), directly correlates with the frequency of communication occurrence. Consequently, applying Theoretical Analysis via Black-Box Optimizations yields a correlation between $s$ and performance improvements. Moreover, experiments conducted on a large-scale cluster computing system, comprising 128 nodes and a total of 160 processes, demonstrate the benefits of CA-SDG. Specifically, applying the method to real-world datasets reduces communication time, and by adjusting the $s$ parameter, optimizing performance can be achieved with reduced communication times up to 450 times. Furthermore, optimizing the parameter allows processes to complete training $\mathbf{\hat{4}}$ times faster on the same infrastructure.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation through the internet and social media significantly impacts public perception and user behavior, with generative models now making it quicker and cheaper to produce fake content. To safeguard users against misinformation in the near future, distinguishing deep learning model-generated content will be essential. For this purpose, researchers have created an extensive dataset comprising human- and model-generated headlines, which has been successfully applied to develop an effective human-free detection system for identifying content generated by language models.

In polycrystalline or ion-damaged Kitaev materials, a spontaneous breaking of sublattice symmetry occurs, giving rise to a chiral spin liquid with potential applications in fault-tolerant quantum computing. We present a numerical approach that identifies the chiral spin liquid in Kitaev materials suffering partial crystalline symmetry breakdown. This method involves minimizing the closing gap and identifying topological excitations to confirm the chiral spin liquid phase. Using this approach, our simulations of ion-irradiated Kitaev materials confirm the emergence of the chiral spin liquid phase in agreement with previous theoretical predictions. We demonstrate that the gap closing and the emergence of chiral spin liquids can be triggered by even a small number of created/vacancy defects, specifically one, which suggests that the chiral spin liquid phase is resilient against defect-induced disorder.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, where the computational demand increases exponentially with the number of antennas involved. Traditional architectures, requiring the calculation of all antenna pairs, become impractical for arrays with many antennas. The introduction of the FFT-correlator architecture reduces the computational complexity, but its effectiveness is heavily influenced by the coherence interval of distant antenna pairs and the redshift of cosmological signals. This research explores the effectiveness of the FFT-correlator, factoring in the impact of both wide-band and narrow-band data, to establish a scenario in which it offers significant computational advantages. The simulation results show that for wide-band data and moderate redshifts, most pairs remain within the coherence interval, yielding substantial savings in the total computational cost. However, as redshifts increase or band widths narrow, a significant portion of pairs exceeds the coherence interval, leading to similar computational demands between the two architectures. The research suggests that by employing data-chunking and sampling rates tailored to the de Broglie wavelength of cosmological signals, it is possible to optimize the correlation process and maximize the benefits of the FFT-correlator architecture.

For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for portfolio optimization, but it was later enhanced by the Black-Litterman model, which incorporates asset demand. However, the traditional approach relies on historical financial time series, which makes it challenging to adapt to new situations. We investigated the potential of using generative adversarial networks, specifically conditional GANs, to create novel financial time series based on historical data, and to make predictions by conditioning on relevant information. However, the utility of these GANs was limited by their poor performance in generating long-time-step sequences and their failure to accurately model the multi-variate relationships within the data. We resolved these issues by employing a dynamic GAN with time-varying capabilities and a normalizing flow model that could effectively model the inter-asset correlations in the data. By integrating these models with the Black-Litterman model, we developed an innovative method for generating portfolio optimization strategies in novel situations.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$
analytically to three-loop order in QCD for arbitrary values of $N$,
including both single- and double-mass scenarios in the Larin scheme.
Furthermore, the result serves as a crucial transition function for the variable
flavor number scheme at $O(\alpha_s^3)$ and is also expressed in momentum
space for convenient use.

A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of classifying gamma-ray sources. The study focuses on identifying BL Lac objects within the Fermi-LAT catalog, distinguishing between bright, intense sources and faint ones. Analysis reveals a high accuracy rate for identifying bright BL Lac objects as strong as those with State I luminosity. Furthermore, the study develops and applies classification capabilities to Fermi-LAT catalog candidates consisting of BL Lac and FSRQ types. The results show promising outcomes for future work incorporating additional astronomical data, specifically optical spectroscopy, which could significantly improve the classification process by considering complete multi-frequency properties of these sources.

Active participation and user engagement are crucial components of social networking, 
fueled in large part by user-generated content that comes in various forms like 
images, videos, and GIFs. However, this type of content has traditionally been 
overlooked in social media research, which has given us the current understanding 
of online behavior. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining 
multi-modal content in social networking, with a focus on the trends and 
tactics surrounding user-generated video, image, and GIF sharing on Twitter.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensors and demonstrate the equivalence of three hypergraph join formulations. We further establish the validity of two hypergraph projection recipes and show that hypergraphs can be represented using Birkhoff-determinants. This study explores emerging research into hypergraph computation and lays the groundwork for future study on tensor-based hypergraph operations and their potential applications in data analysis.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment and functioning of its initial space observatory, AstroSat, and must leverage this achievement to significantly enhance India's global profile in space-based astronomy and astrophysics research. The Indian Space Research Organisation issued a call for proposals in two phases: first for the concept and design of a new telescope, and subsequently for the detailed design and the telescope itself. In response to this call, we propose the development of a next-generation space telescope, known as INSIST. This telescope, which will be described in more detail below, will feature a semi-active, semi-passive telescope structure and will utilize advanced technologies including superconducting detectors and novel X-ray filters. It will have an extended energy range from 0.5 km to 250 km, and be equipped with an array of 94 X-ray detectors offering high precision and resolution. Specifically, INSIST will comprise of 40 focal plane detectors with an extraordinary resolution and 54 onboard filters providing an exceptional resolution. Furthermore, it will incorporate 54 onboard detectors including 40 superconducting detectors and 14 photodiodes operating in vacuum conditions. INSIST is expected to make a significant contribution to various fields including astronomy, astrophysics, exoplanetary science, and cosmology by observing, mapping, and monitoring celestial sources such as galaxies, galaxie clusters, binary systems, and supernovae. It will particularly aid in locating and characterizing potential habitable planets and identifying novel sources such as

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data over time, the mixed model repeated measures approach often dominates. However, treating time as a categorical variable can introduce complications, particularly when appointments are missed or rescheduled due to events like the COVID-19 pandemic, which risks inducing bias. To address this limitation, a novel method employing natural cubic splines is presented to model time as a continuous variable and utilize treatment effect variations over time.
