The method retains the within-subjects error structure of the original model, making it an ideal alternative for analyzing temporal data in clinical trials.

A novel computational strategy called Action-CSA is introduced, enabling the global exploration of reaction pathways via optimization of the Onsager-Machlup action using conformational space annealing. Action-CSA is capable of sampling multiple reaction pathways without initial guesses and successfully captures both the most dominant and various alternative pathways for reactions of isomerization and association. Furthermore, pathways generated by Action-CSA are in line with those derived from transition path theory and direct-geometry theory, and are accompanied by higher accuracy in calculating associated kinetics and thermodynamics. Action-CSA presents a versatile framework for the analysis of reaction pathways and can be used in the examination of complex biological processes.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates. Moreover, the research expands upon these L-infinity estimates to encompass a broader category of parabolic Hessian equations.

Building on Church encodings in typed lambda-calculi, we plan to develop a
framework for automata theory by transposing a key result from formal
language theory that classifies polyregular functions based on a Hierarchy
Index. This approach will leverage a form of codata induction, similar to
Strathausen's theorem, which will provide the foundation for our encoding
scheme, and subsequently, a Hierarchy Index for polyregular functions. By
this method, we aim to establish a formal correspondence between the
encoding/decoding pair for polyregular languages and the (un)fold/unfold^k
operator pair, as well as relate the Hierarchy Index to the degree of
polyregularity and the number of iterations of the unfold operator.

This concise note clarifies the relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the goal of facilitating exchange of information between the stochastic analysis community based in Paris and that based in Paris-Bicêtre at the Poncelet Laboratory.

Two normal subgroups $N$ and $G$ of a finite group $H$ are termed primitive relative subgroups if the quotient group $G/N$ does not contain any normal subgroups originating from distinct proper subgroups of $H$. This work aims to investigate the characteristics of groups featuring primitive subgroup properties. Firstly, we establish that if a group $H$ possesses primitive subgroup properties, then it exhibits a unique characteristic - namely, no proper divisor of $H$ shares a non-trivial correspondence with $H/$Ch($H$), the smallest normal subgroup of $H$. This characteristic is known as the non-progression property. This property effectively encapsulates group properties such as nilpotency, solubility, and being a $p$-group. Furthermore, we establish that if a group $H$ possesses primitive subgroup properties, then it exhibits non-progression properties for all of its divisors.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating while avoiding potential collisions between robots is a significant challenge, largely due to the unpredictable movements of fellow robots. To tackle this, our method develops a data-driven strategy where each robot resolves a optimization issue to determine the safest navigation route, taking into account the maximum number of collisions that can occur based on the robots' recent speeds and directions. To increase the robustness of navigation in the face of uncertainty, our approach considers various potential scenarios by creating a set of possible robot speed and direction combinations based on historical data, and then uses a measure of data inconsistency to minimize collision risk. By employing a robust optimization technique, the navigation route is planned such that even in the most critical worst-case scenario, collisions are avoided with a certain probability, resulting in a more reliable and robust solution. Through simulation tests using actual robot data collected over two years, our method has demonstrated superior collision avoidance performance and longer navigation time, as well as significant improvements in processing efficiency compared to an optimization method that does not consider various potential scenarios.

Recent data for the Andromeda dwarf spheroidal galaxy And XXV challenges a previous report of negligible dark matter content. Our research significantly reduces uncertainties by doubling the number of member stars, yielding a clearer picture. Andromeda XXV now shows a distinct dark matter component with mass constrained by velocity dispersion measurements within the galaxy's half-light radius. Our findings reveal a stellar mass of approximately $4.26\times10^4$ solar masses, along with a total mass of about $5.79\times10^4$ solar masses, based on kinematic data, including a systemic velocity of $111.52\pm3.25$ km/s. This sheds light on the paradox of sparse, dark matter-rich dwarf spheroidals like And XXV, situated at the edge of the M31 galaxy's halo, which has implications for understanding the galaxy's mass distribution.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), granting numerous users low-latency connections is made possible by non-orthogonal grant-free access with low signaling overhead. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to transform a unitary matrix into a closely-packed, uniform pattern. Subsequently, a second-stage GA is employed to conceal channel state information (CSI) correlation patterns under a specific subsampling strategy. This genetic algorithm-based approach enables the design of unique sequence sets for diverse mMTC scenarios. However, simulated results show that traditional random sequences are sufficient for mMTC uplink systems with high latencies, but performance significantly improves with the proposed GA-designed sequences, especially in systems with low latencies.

A few approaches to model the thermodynamic behavior of moist air rely on approximations that can lead to inconsistencies in accordance with the 1st and 2nd laws of thermodynamics. A new strategy has emerged to accurately describe thermodynamic potentials for a general moist air system while adhering to thermodynamic principles. Investigating the properties of moist air in both saturated and unsaturated states is essential to determine the existence and feasibility of thermodynamic potentials. This research explores the characteristics of moist air in both saturated and unsaturated states, resulting in the identification of thermodynamic potentials for both states. A comprehensive theory for general moist air is developed, including derivation of thermodynamic potentials and their key properties. Additionally, two potential applications of this new theory are presented: one focusing on thermodynamic cycles in saturated systems and another on developing a general Gibbs-free energy function for unsaturated air.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An example of such an element is the symbol ε within the framework of ε-F_1^{\pm} algebra. Furthermore, we discuss the concept of ε-F_1^{\pm} algebra as a generalisation of elliptic modules, and show that specific types of elliptic modules (such as those involving cube roots of unity) cannot be expressed as ε-F_1^{\pm} algebras. Additionally, we explore the properties of ε-F_1^{\pm} algebras in relation to elliptic modules and EllipticIntegers, and outline the possible algebraic structures that ε-F_1^{\pm} algebras can imply.

Research on confusion networks has led to the understanding that they can express more semantic information compared to the top-N ASR hypotheses typically employed in spoken dialogue systems. Although the use of confusion networks is gaining traction for statistical machine translation, its application to ASR is still in its nascent stages. We present a method to efficiently generate confusion networks from top-N ASR hypotheses that can be used in the evaluation of spoken dialogue systems. Our approach also facilitates an analysis of dialogue system performance based on confusion networks. Moreover, we introduce a metric to assess the overall performance of a dialogue system by using confusion networks, thereby enabling the comparison of the output of different systems. We analyze the benefits of the confusion network metric in the context of system comparison and provide guidance on its potential use in the configuration of neural network-based acoustic models.

We have computed Joyce's enumerative invariants for semistable coherent sheaves of specific ranks and degrees on complex projective curves, which are a more extensive application of vector bundle moduli space invariants. This study not only confirms a theorem stating the invariants' non-degeneracy, but also enables determination of the invariants for particular cases through direct enumeration of the involved bundle moduli space. Building upon this, we have successfully proved that the invariants serve as a form of partition for positive integers in a particular cohomology space. Additionally, the invariants' non-degeneracy allows us to apply Joyce's formula to find an explicit formula for the K-theory of the moduli space, which calculates a particular cohomology space for the moduli space.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets. This measure determines the universal access structure, which distinguishes secure and insecure arrangements. All feasible structures with the same minimal count of minimal qualified subsets are considered part of the same class, denoted as $\mathcal{R}_k$. We aim to find the exact number of non-empty classes within $\mathcal{R}_k$ for $1 \leq k \leq 8$ by employing the Burnside numbers of the symmetric groups $S_k$. Through the application of the Burnside p-quasigroups and p-groups method of Miller and Boone, we calculate the Burnside numbers $bs_{S_k}(p)$ for prime $p$ and $k$ up to $8$, thereby contributing to the comprehensive list of Burnside numbers for small $k$. We utilize the results to establish the exact count of non-empty classes in $\mathcal{R}_3$, $\mathcal{R}_4$, $\mathcal{R}_5$, $\mathcal{R}_6$, and $\mathcal{R}_7$. For $\mathcal{R}_8$, we present a conjecture based on an enumeration of the Burnside numbers of the group $S_8$ in relation to prime $p$.

To determine entanglement experimentally in polarization qubit pairs, we utilize quantum estimation theory to develop the most precise estimators possible, which we then apply to achieve optimal measurement accuracy. We conduct a series of experiments focused on measuring the amount of entanglement in various families of two-qubit two-photon states, using visibility measurements of quantum correlations to achieve the highest possible precision. Notably, using optimal estimators does not necessitate full state tomography; in fact, we compare the results to those obtained from tomographic reconstructions using two different sets of projectors, demonstrating the latter's reduced precision. Furthermore, we leverage optimal estimators to assess and compare the performance of different noise models describing decoherence effects that arise during entanglement generation.

The localized clusters within plasma turbulence, denoted as vortices in three-dimensional space or ribbons in two-dimensional space, play a significant role in understanding turbulence's overall impact on macroscopic currents, especially their parallel component. A concept called the 'turbulence control coefficient' quantifies the average magnitude of these structures within turbulence. A study on forceful shear turbulence reveals that this coefficient exhibits geometric consistency, applying equally across various turbulence intensity levels and spanning a wide range of length scales. A pre-existing model describing the formation of vortices helps to explain their observed resilience and uniformity through their direction in three-dimensional space.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various pretraining methods have been proposed for continual learning, aiming to extract transferable features from a sequence of tasks. Contrary to conventional approaches that involve incremental fine-tuning, we examine the effectiveness of "frozen" models, preserving the learned representation from pretraining and adapting it to new tasks without updating the parameters. Through experiments on multiple image classification datasets, we found that a sufficiently trained frozen model can perform well across new tasks when using distillation methods like knowledge dropout or batch feature reduction to update it. Notably, our results indicate that a single pretrained model can learn representations for multiple sequences of tasks, also referred to as various "contingency plans", and even perform competitively on each individual sequence when compared to fine-tuning from scratch.

As social media increasingly influences public perception globally, researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Initially, researchers attempted to address hate speech through semantic text classification using neural networks and various features, but these early efforts were limited by their reliance on supplementary data and their failure to account for the context of hate speech. To build upon these initial efforts, researchers developed more sophisticated methods for hate speech detection that incorporate social and contextual factors. Notably, recent breakthroughs in transformer architecture and graph neural networks have expanded our understanding of hate speech, and future research is likely to build upon these advances.

We investigate the dynamics of closed networks composed of binary neurons using a stochastic relaxation technique to analyze both homogeneous and heterogeneous degree structures. For networks with non-overlapping degrees and binary interactions, we apply the Bethe approximation to examine the systematic deviations resulting from the approximation. These deviations are found to be negligible in networks with paired oscillations and those on the boundary of chaos, but they become significant for other types of oscillations. We extend our analysis to binomial in- and out-degree distributions, discovering that the typical oscillations are suppressed but a new type of oscillation can occur. Furthermore, we examine degree structures derived from a two-neuron model and find evidence supporting approximate pairwise interactions, while also identifying conditions for oscillatory dynamics. Through numerical simulations, we validate the effectiveness of the approximation and examine the influence of spiking neural mechanisms on oscillatory behavior, revealing both similarities and differences with the continuous-time rate-based model.

Recent years have seen increasing interest in Automatic Program Repair (APR) with
numerous approaches being explored. One area of research focuses on search-based
methods, generating potential repairs through syntactic analysis and systematic
exploration of feasible solutions. Conversely, we investigate an innovative
approach inspired by the concept of bugs and repairs from a adversarial
perspective. By utilizing deep learning architectures, specifically Generative
Adversarial Networks (GANs), we are able to produce repairs closely resembling
those generated by humans. Initial evaluations suggest that our approach is
yielding positive outcomes, with a significant proportion of bugs (21.2% out of 500)
 repaired identically to human corrections.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a collection of interconnected rectangles, with specific inner and outer boundaries defined by the individual and combined spectral information rates of the channels. Building upon this framework, we derive the capacity region for specific types of interference channels, with particular emphasis on the 2x2 interference channel with independently and identically distributed input distributions. In the context of the 2x2 interference channel, it is demonstrated that the sum-capacity can be achieved by a unique input distribution, described as the product of two independent probability values, with the lower value determined by the spectral in-mutual information rate of the first user and the higher value set by the spectral mut-inf information rate of the second user.

We aim to broaden the established flow analysis technique to include the quadrupole flow coefficient, $v_2$, in addition to the usual $v_1$. Our focus lies on how the nuclear state equation and transverse asymmetry impact this quadrupole momentum in terms of momentum cutoff and varying pseudorapidity intervals. This investigation will compare the flow behaviour in the most energetic gold-gold collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, using the AMPT and EPOS models. Notably, these calculations indicate that the EPOS model's predictions for $v_2$ are remarkably consistent with experimental data, whereas the AMPT model's predictions are not as congruent.

The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant challenge worldwide, and effectively mitigating the disease relies heavily on early diagnosis and the subsequent management of patient isolation and treatment. Although numerous detection methods have been developed, the difficulties associated with early detection remain significant, particularly in areas with limited access to testing capabilities. To address this issue, the present study employs machine learning algorithms, including long short-term memory networks and decision tree ensemble methods, to analyze patients' digital payment data to identify potential COVID-19 cases. By leveraging a novel data transformation approach, the analysis can establish a link between patients' financial behavior and the onset of the disease, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between financial transactions and health outcomes. Furthermore, the analysis provides practical insights for individuals to identify early warning signs in their financial behavior and, by adopting healthy habits, potentially reduce their risk of contracting the disease.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied in network centrality, link prediction, load ranking, and node classification. However, the extensive applications of GNN are hindered by several challenges, including the difficulty in training due to complex graph patterns and limited data. This study introduces the application of GNN in wireless communication systems and outlines the challenges encountered in adapting the model to this field. We have selected the IEEE 802.11g dataset as the pilot project and proposed a modified GNN architecture to address the challenges. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach overcomes the issues and achieves improved performance in node classification compared to the original GNN model.

The threat of homicide death tolls has raised concerns worldwide and demands attention from researchers and government officials, a trend particularly evident in Brazil where such deaths have increased steadily since 2006, resulting in approximately 43,600 lives lost over the past 14 years.  Although Brazil has witnessed an overall rise in homicide deaths, with some states experiencing sharp increases, as many as 24 states have reported declines in homicide-related deaths since 2016.  Analysis of such deaths by age group shows that homicides affecting individuals between the ages of 15.8 and 34.9 years account for the highest mortality rate, accounting for around 60% of all such deaths, with the primary perpetrators being other individuals.  While the majority of homicides are linked to disputes, the most frequent motivation behind these crimes remains undefined.  This study draws on the Brazilian Homicide Systematized Information System (SISH) to investigate trends in homicide, understand the motivations behind these crimes, and identify factors contributing to such deaths, as well as proposing potential solutions to mitigate them.

Our goal is to modify stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to be adaptable to online optimization scenarios where the objective function and feasibility constraints are uncertain and time-varying. When the objective function is smooth, strongly-convex, and minimizers exist within a bounded domain, we modify SGD with time-varying step-sizes that initially quicken then slow down exponentially. Analytically, we find that the step-size modification allows us to achieve a $O(1/\sqrt{k})$ convergence rate for the objective function value, which is similar to the rate achieved by SGD in static settings when the step-sizes are sufficiently diverse. Moreover, we demonstrate that our modified algorithm is robust to adversarial changes in feasibility constraints under certain conditions. Additionally, we provide theoretical support for applying our step-size control method to stochastic optimization problems, including those involving $\ell_1$-regularization and multi-signal recovery in sparse models. Experimental results confirm our analytical predictions and reveal performance enhancements for the multi-signal recovery problem.

Axions emerge as a logical outcome of the Peccei-Quinn mechanism, the leading solution to the strong-CP issue.  Variants of axions known as axion-like particles (ALPs) also naturally arise within extensions of the standard model.  Both types of particles can be produced in massive numbers and are among the most prominent targets of current and future particle physics experiments, particularly those utilizing proton-proton colliders.  This article provides an in-depth review of the production of axions and ALPs at proton-proton colliders, covering theoretical aspects, detector capabilities, and the associated phenomenology, with a focus on the detailed analyses conducted for LHC experiments.

The occupation number over time is examined for a bosonic oscillator coupled to heat baths with fermionic and bosonic components. This oscillator, having one or two heat baths, does not reach equilibrium and may serve as a means to thwart an opponent's storage strategy. It's also considered how an additional, uninvolved heat bath could influence the occupation number's temporal progression. In cases where this additional, uninvolved heat bath is turned on, it's found that the system may reach a steady non-equilibrium state. Furthermore, the internalised heat bath is seen to function as a thermometer, displaying temperature-dependent behavior. Also explored is how an uninvolved heat bath can alter the internalised system's occupation numbers' temporal progression.

Developing robots with skilled hands that can effectively grasp and manipulate objects is an essential yet complex challenge. In contrast to previous methods focusing on one type of grasping, we introduce a more comprehensive approach called DexGraspNet, enabling robots to grasp and manipulate diverse objects using multiple fingers. By employing a data-driven strategy on an extensive collection of 256,916 grasps from 50,000 objects, DexGraspNet allows robots to successfully apply fingered skills in a variety of real-world scenarios. Unlike existing datasets, our approach integrates complete robotic data, including both object and action components, leveraging a novel set of practical and industrially relevant robotic manipulation tasks. By generating a comprehensive dataset, DexGraspNet demonstrates the correlation between object characteristics and optimal grasp positions, leading to significant improvements in robot dexterity. In experiments, DexGraspNet has successfully applied to two robotic platforms and various tasks such as picking objects with irregular shapes and applying torque-based manipulation techniques. In comparative studies with existing methods, our approach has consistently achieved higher success rates and broader applicability.

A novel approach has been developed to create and restore MRI T2-weighted images of moving abdominal organs in real-time using a 3D MRI T2-weighting technique. This technique employs respiratory motion data and real-time MRI sequences to create stable, periodic images, thereby reconstructing complete organ volumes. A study utilizing data from 40 MRI sessions of two subjects found significant improvements in image quality, specifically in the liver and gallbladder regions, following application of the newly developed algorithm. Moreover, the technique demonstrates potential extension to other MRI applications, such as functional and angiographic studies.

We propose InDistill, a novel model compression approach, InDistill, which leverages knowledge distillation to enhance the training process. The method combines the features of both knowledge distillation and pruning by incorporating a prune-and-train framework where the teacher model undergoes the same training process as student models, and we explore different configurations of when to prune the teacher models. Our experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets reveal that InDistill consistently achieves superior results for compression ratios and accuracy retention, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our findings suggest that teacher models can be trained in a similar manner to student models, and early pruning of teacher models does not necessarily hinder the model's performance.

Two submersion functions from the three-dimensional space to the plane are topologically equivalent if and only if their level set foliations in the sense of Cauchy are regular and internally equivalent.

Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have become increasingly vulnerable due to the rising threat of over-grazing. Unlike traditional approaches, we propose an integrodifference system to better capture the dynamic interactions between vegetation and grazing patterns. Our research reveals that the intensity of grazing in these ecosystems is directly influenced by the spatial distribution of vegetation. Furthermore, we introduce a nonlinear relationship to model the grazing impact, where the resulting nonlinear integrodifference model is shown to possess a unique steady state solution. Our analysis of this model relies heavily on the principles of spectral theory, which enables the determination of the steady state through the properties of eigenvectors and eigenvalues. Specifically, we demonstrate that the steady state is determined by the sign of the leading eigenvalue of the grazing matrix, which in turn depends on the parameters of the model and the spatial distribution of vegetation. Our research provides a theoretical understanding of the possible instability mechanisms within this model, highlighting the significant influence of nonlinear grazing pressure and spatial heterogeneity of vegetation on the dynamics of these ecosystems. Our results indicate that vegetative environments with non-homogeneous distribution tend to exhibit a wider range of values for the grazing parameter, which facilitates the coexistence of multiple equilibrium states including both stable and unstable regimes.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique, CountSketch, employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, specifically the sphere in an orthonormal basis. This "sketching" technique allows for the creation of sublinear-time algorithms that provide approximate answers to various queries. Our analysis shows that the CountSketch projection is capable of preserving the angle between any two vectors in the domain. Furthermore, we present a successful application of this discovery to the problem of suggested optimal transport (SOT) regularization. We derive a solution to the SOT regularization problem involving generalized linear models with polynomial regularizations using the CountSketch technique, thereby achieving improved efficiency and exactness under certain "soft" conditions. Our approach also allows for the creation of an efficient algorithm that determines whether an optimal solution to the SOT regularization exists and retrieves the coefficients of this solution if it exists. This algorithm operates in O(n log(n)) time, representing a significant improvement over the current best algorithm, which has an exponential time complexity. Our problem can be transformed into a type of semidefinite program (SDP), whose efficient solution is known to be computationally challenging even in theory. Our new algorithm makes significant contributions to the SOT regularization problem by providing both a theoretical guarantee of exactness under specific "soft" conditions and a practical method for determining exactness in practice. Additionally, we conduct real-world experiments to validate the theoretical guarantee of exactness, as well as the effectiveness of the SOT regularization.

A python-based program, ipie, has been developed for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, incorporating various innovative performance enhancement strategies. These improvements include parallelization on multiple CPU cores, optimized data storage in NumPy/PySCF formats, and implementation of GPU-accelerated auxiliary-field calculations. The efficacy of these optimizations is demonstrated through benchmarking against the VPSM program. The results show good agreement with the VPSM results for a range of challenging chemical systems, including larger molecules and transition-metal clusters. The ipie program and its accompanying benchmark data are freely accessible online.

High-frequency trading could greatly benefit from first-generation quasi-quantum communication technologies. This text outlines a simplified game-theoretic approach using the two-player game known as Prisoner's Dilemma. It examines how quasi-quantum communication can expedite transactions and benefit traders in the field, leveraging Eisert's protocol on the cloud. Furthermore, as internet connectivity shifts to true quantum capabilities, traders may be able to achieve optimal outcomes in high-frequency trading through cooperative game theory and the process of reinforced learning.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the mechanism or being represented by an intermediary. The focus is on identifying optimal sequential decision-making processes when buying agents have the option to use intermediaries or purchase directly from the seller, and valuations for each buyer are drawn independently from a specified probability distribution.

When buying agents acquire items from the seller directly, the known distribution of valuations, $\mu$, and the number of items, $k$, are available. To address this scenario, we present a novel mechanism that ensures a specific first-best outcome under specific conditions when the distribution of valuations, $\mu$, is uniform and the number of items, $k$, is greater than or equal to $3$. Furthermore, this mechanism produces outcomes that are close to the optimal outcomes achievable through second-best solutions when considering certain classes of suboptimal distributional valuations, $\mu_1$, and the number of items, $k$, is greater than or equal to $3$. 

When buying agents acquire items through intermediaries, the known distribution of valuations, $\mu$, and the number of items, $k$, are not available to the seller. To address this scenario, we present a novel mechanism that ensures a specific first-best outcome under specific conditions when the distribution of valuations, $\mu$, is uniform and the number of items, $k$, is greater than or equal

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism that enables the generation of grounded summaries. This method involves pre-annotating summaries with entity chains, and training transformer models to predict these chains, and subsequently generate summaries conditioned on them. In our experiments, which included pre-training with these plans, we found that: 1) predicting entity chains improved summary fidelity across four datasets, 2) incorporating entity chains into summary generation yielded additional improvements, and 3) integrating our planning method into zero-shot and fine-tuning processes further boosted performance. Notably, our approach outperformed multiple baselines and state-of-the-art models, and saw significant improvements relative to a previously proposed strategy for generating grounded summaries.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversations. To measure this synchronization accurately in two-person dialogues, we developed a dynamic approach that combines convolutional networks and transformer architecture to capture both immediate and long-term conversation contexts. By incorporating attention layers to analyze both internal and external interactions, our model can learn meaningful patterns in social exchanges across various domains. Through classification experiments, we verified the effectiveness of our approach in identifying authentic and inauthentic conversations. Moreover, when testing our model with individuals having Autism Spectrum Disorder, our results indicate a strong statistical link between our entrainment measure and relevant clinical symptoms, regardless of age and gender differences.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building upon this concept, we present a significant subset of typing rules, which formulates a versatile quantum calculus, accompanied by a corresponding categorical interpretation. Specifically, we outline a semantics based on an adjunction between the categories of spaces with linearly combined values and the category of sets with distributed values.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of quasiparticle excitation energies per particle in systems of up to seven electrons within both the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, accounting for the comprehensive jellium potential consisting of electron-electron, electron-background, and background-background interactions. The findings support that the composite fermions wave function outperforms the Laughlin wave function in energy for two quasiparticle configurations, albeit the difference in their energies diminishes with growing system size.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modelling contact-related issues in marine ice sheets, Stokes variational inequalities come into play. This research focuses on devising a weak formulation for this challenging problem, constructing a compatible product space, and establishing its well-posedness. A numerical approach, implemented using the finite element method and the Lagrange multiplier technique, is also developed and analyzed for the Stokes variational inequalities, demonstrating convergence in a unified framework.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles.

Our proposed testbed, SyROF, is designed to facilitate the development and testing of synchronization techniques for robotic swarms. By utilizing high-definition video recording of robotic swarm systems in controlled environments, flaws in synchronization protocols can be quickly identified and rectified. With the aid of two example synchronization protocols utilising LED lights to track timeline progression, SyROF's high-frame-rate video capture enables precise detection and measurement of timing discrepancies. This allows for the efficient evaluation of synchronization techniques under realistic conditions, thereby promoting the development of efficient, scalable, and practical solutions for large robotic swarm systems.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires substantial resources;
however, training on unannotated videos can still provide valuable knowledge through
scene understanding. Yet, typical depth estimation methods based on stereo or
simulated data may not be effective in capturing indoor and outdoor complexities.
We propose that depth estimation from real, unannotated videos can be an efficient
way to acquire discriminative features for semantic segmentation tasks. Although
depth data can be associated with video frames, the corresponding segmentation
labels are often unavailable. We address this challenge by developing an unsupervised
approach to learn a segmentation network using depth information, incorporating
temporal consensus among video frames and using flow as an intermediate feature
for segmentation tasks. Since unsupervised depth estimation can result in ambiguous
depth maps due to motion groups and background separation issues, we propose
utilizing flow information to enhance depth accuracy and robustness. Notably, our
approach achieves state-of-the-art performance when applied to the KITTI dataset.

Let's consider the set of all analytic functions defined within the unit disk in the complex plane and have their absolute value strictly less than one, denoted as the unit disk. The given inequality relates to functions in this set and was initially identified by Bohr in 1947 in the context of Fourier series; it states that certain power series will converge if the following inequalities hold: the sum of the squares of the absolute values of the coefficients is less than or equal to the sum of the squares of the absolute values of the coefficients of a power series that converges everywhere within the unit disk, where the coefficients of the power series are less than or equal to the coefficients of the given function. The given inequality implies that all functions in this set are bounded, and this result has significant implications in understanding the properties of these functions, and this result is equivalent to identifying the set of functions in this category whose 1/2-projective Fourier series converge uniformly, and this category includes functions whose 1/2-Fejér-Fourier series converge uniformly, and this category includes functions whose 1/2-Carleman means converge uniformly, and this category includes functions whose 1/2-Fourier series converge, and this category includes functions whose 2p-type Dirichlet series converge, and this category includes functions whose 2p-type summability means converge uniformly.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces computational time by adapting a standard approach, allowing for quicker calculations when dealing with larger datasets. The modified approach specifically identifies key components in its underlying Hájek projection, leading to a notable runtime improvement for fixed-dimension datasets.

The number of connected devices has seen tremendous growth, creating vast volumes of diverse data that intertwine with our physical world. The Edge Intelligence System has emerged to harness edge computing and AI, facilitating intelligent services through powerful yet balanced distributed infrastructure. With advancements in transportation systems, technology now enables safe and efficient vehicle interactions, data exchange, and analytics to inform informed decisions. We delve into how Edge Intelligence evolves Intelligent Transportation Systems, outlining key strategies, system architectures, and applications with a focus on traffic management, data privacy, autonomous driving, vehicle maintenance, and smart road management. Our objective is to offer a comprehensive overview of the integration of Edge Intelligence and Intelligent Transportation Systems, along with an analysis of the prominent use cases and a glimpse into promising research avenues for years to come.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-variable spaces. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical basis of the Euler characteristic makes it a suitable tool for analyzing complex topological structures in high-dimensional spaces. We demonstrate its practical application through a simulation of points in multi-variable space and an examination of the topological structure of a simulated lunar crater grid.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model based on Holling-Tanner's equations with a Type II predation response, also taking into account a strong Allee effect affecting prey population growth. We build on previous studies by Saez and Gonzalez-Olivares and Arancibia-Ibarra and Gonzalez-Olivares who studied similar Holling-Tanner models with a mild Allee effect. In this modified model, complex dynamics are exhibited, including separations in the phase space, resulting in separate regions of coexistence and extinction. Moreover, we establish the presence of a specific type of homoclinic curve leading to the formation of a stable orbit and we discuss potential transitions such as birth-death, oscillatory instability and a doubling bifurcation types including Hopf, Bogdanov-Takens.

The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it can solve linear programming problems in at most n - d iterations, motivated by Smale's mathematical problem 9, first introduced in the late 90s.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which are Bass nil-groups for general and unitary quadratic groups. Building on a graded version of Quillen-Suslin theory, we establish an analogous concept for graded rings.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent presentations restricts their adoption in high-stakes applications. Effective countermeasures against these deceptive presentations are vital for the safe integration of facial recognition technology. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. In this research, transfer learning is applied from the vision transformer model to tackle the challenge of detecting unknown anti-spoofing attacks. Experimental results conducted on multiple out-of-domain datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly. Our implementation is freely accessible at https://github.com/MVIG-sat/TF-PFT.

One of the primary issues in employing supervised learning for autonomous driving is ensuring that the models developed are reliable across a broad range of scenarios, even in situations encountered during out-of-distribution testing. In this research, we present an alternative approach using self-supervised learning without labeled data. Given a substantial volume of driving images, our method relies solely on driving videos as the input source to derive multiple outcomes, including pixel-level labels for objects of interest. Two primary methods are explored to establish a driving corpus with annotated labels. Firstly, using unsupervised object segmentation, we obtain labels for objects within the videos. Secondly, using a pre-trained model, we obtain semantic labels for objects within the videos. Using these derived labels, we employ self-supervised learning techniques for unsupervised pre-training of the model. Ultimately, our method yields a robust trained model that performs effectively across a range of scenarios, including new and unseen scenarios. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, with significant performance improvements over training the model without any form of pre-training.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in recent years through parallel computing, resulting in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs). However, a major limitation in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs) arises from idling computing nodes after each solution evaluation. As APEAs provide a higher chance of selection to quicker solutions, the evaluation time bias significantly affects search performance, hindering the ability to exploit slower, potentially better solutions. In an effort to address the evaluation time bias, we introduce a parallel parallel parallel (PoPo) paradigm, which runs parallel parallel processing concurrently within the algorithm's iterations and evaluations. The PoPo strategy proves effective in reducing the evaluation time bias and boosts the efficiency of Asynchronous Parallel Parallel Genetic Algorithm (PoPoGA) by maintaining a steady high population size. The results from benchmark problems on multi-core systems demonstrate that PoPoGA consistently outperforms its asynchronous counterpart, showcasing its potential to enhance solution quality. Additionally, an in-depth analysis in the context of hyper-optimization highlights the importance of solution history in understanding the evolution of populations and highlights potential applications of PopoGA in this field.

The recent microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among a group of twelve planets where the planet-star mass ratio exceeded 0.01, situated beyond 2 astronomical units. We have found that the event's point of closest approach was $\bx = (1.17 \pm 0.02) m Jy$, based on the analysis of the Optical Microlensing Experiment. The mass of the lens, consisting of a binary system with components of nearly equal mass, was determined to be $3.26^{+0.15}_{-0.14} M_J$. This is the first instance where the line of sight to a planet has been found to pass closest to the center of the host star, based on the analysis of the point of closest approach. Furthermore, the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 planetary system serves as an example of a group of planets located beyond 2 astronomical units with a star-planet mass ratio situated near the inflection point of the planet-host mass ratio power law. As a result, the OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 planetary system serves to break the current trend established by the mass anomaly and help establish a new one.

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a Markovian master equation of the Lindblad type, poses a significant challenge. In systems with only two energy levels, distinct phases arise where the Floquet generator may be either Markovian or not. Even within the high-frequency regime, numerical analysis often reveals a non-Markovian Floquet Hamiltonian, giving rise to distinct phases even in closed systems. In this work, exact high-frequency expansions for both the Floquet Hamiltonian and Lindblad equation are developed, with the Floquet generator exhibiting phase-like behavior in the high-frequency limit. Notably, in open systems, distinct phases arise due to the complex interplay between system and environment dynamics. These findings are illustrated by examining a periodically driven system with a two-level atom interacting with a single-mode laser field. Our work lays the groundwork for using Floquet engineering to design open quantum systems, even in scenarios where environmental effects cannot be neglected.

Our recent studies of the effects of Rh content in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveal the emergence of magnetic irreversibilities and spin freezing in the vicinity of x ≈ 0.6, accompanied by a suppression of long-range ferromagnetism. To account for these observations, we propose a model in which dynamic fluctuations of local magnetic moments induce the formation of transient neutralizing pairs, concurrent with a spin freezing phenomenon and the loss of long-range ferromagnetic correlations. These findings are consistent with the idea that the Rh series of heavy fermion ferromagnets represent a regime of "f-f hybridization-controlled" magnetic behavior, distinct from the "LS coupling-controlled" behavior exhibited by the Pd series.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope's spectropolarimetric facility, we conducted observations of high-frequency radio continuum emission in two massive star-forming regions, W51 and G035.58-0.33. The regions were scanned with the facility's two polarization modes, resulting in the detection of 11 HI narrow-line self-absorption features and an additional continuum emission module. The detected HI narrow-line self-absorption features exhibited linearly polarized components and were associated with dust polarization patterns, facilitating the estimation of magnetic field strengths and their relationship with kinetic gas pressures. The estimated total mass of the regions studied was approximately $1.23\times10^7 M_\odot$ for W51 and $1.32\times10^7 M_\odot$ for G035.58-0.33.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

This paper presents the results of two experiments, LHCb and CMS, that measured the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from the mixing-induced interference in Bs decays. The experiments analyzed the differential decay rate of Bs to J/Pi Pi, with J equal to 0 or 2, as a function of the squared momentum transfer in the J/Pi system. The results from LHCb and CMS are consistent with each other, in accordance with the standard model predictions. The combined experiments provide the most precise measurements of phi_s to date, with a level of accuracy equivalent to 25 million simulations of data in the presence of instrumental uncertainties. The experiments report phi_s with an uncertainty of 14.1 rad, at a level 1.3 times smaller than previous measurements. The experiments also provide phi_s with a systematic uncertainty 1.2 times smaller than previous measurements. The results were obtained using 2011 data from LHCb, with a total integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb-1, and CMS, with a total integrated luminosity of 3.0 fb-1. The results were obtained using two independent methods, with a systematic uncertainty of 1.4 times smaller than previous measurements. The results are in agreement with previous measurements, with a total integrated uncertainty of 1.0 times smaller than previous measurements. The results provide significant constraints on models of new physics that may be present, with a systematic uncertainty of 1.0 times

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, the concept of domain generalization, which aims to overcome this limitation, is explored. Various domain generalization techniques are examined, with a focus on those utilizing multiple domain-level constraints to facilitate this adaptation. Our experiments confirm the benefits of incorporating additional constraints in promoting adaptability. Consequently, we propose a novel constraint acquisition framework that combines the utilization of domain-level constraints and data-level constraints, thereby significantly enhancing the performance of domain generalization.

In finite fields of dimension 2, an arc is a subset where no 3 points share a line. A particular challenge arises when trying to find arcs covering the entire plane in a specific size, a task closely linked to projective planes of a particular order. By utilizing Steiner systems and specific designs of order $q^2$ and index 3, a lower limit could previously be established for maximum-sized arcs in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$. This paper builds upon that work, offering new evidence for the maximum-sized arcs in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ through the creation of projective planes of order $q^2$ with specific properties.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by illustrating the triangle corresponding to the subset $\{4, 5, 8, 11\}$ when $n$ is $10$.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations for groups of cases (e.g., graphs of the same class). To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel explainer for GNNs, PGExplainer, which parameterizes explanation generation using a deep neural network to explain multiple instances collectively and displays better generalization capabilities and improved applicability in the inductive setting. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets reveal highly competitive explanation generation and prediction performance.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) was proposed as a novel type of recurrent neural network (RNN) capable of being trained end-to-end for tasks such as time-series forecasting, speech recognition, and natural language processing. Building upon the foundational mathematical framework of the Legendre Gauss-Weierstrass kernel, we developed a novel LMU architecture with a specific structure. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this new architecture, with improved performance on RNN tasks and reduced training requirements. In comparison to the original LMU and traditional LSTMs and transformers, the new architecture exhibits superior performance on datasets such as the exchange rate dataset and the Pinterest dataset, with reduced training data needs.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, and the intricacies of the Higgs boson. With significant portions of this puzzle's solution coming from experimental findings outside the realm of direct particle collisions. A newly formed scientific research area, 'light new physics,' is gaining momentum, which focuses on feeble interactions between particles that could significantly impact physics beyond its current boundaries. Preons, which can lead to grand unification, are a key area of study here. With the advancement of detectors and facilities, the exploration of dark matter and new physics has entered a crucial phase, characterized by high precision and sensitivity across a broad spectrum of masses. Two proposed beam dump experiments at Fermilab, the Large Water Cherenkov Neutral Current Beam Monitor and the Silverback Beamline, are ideally positioned to take advantage of this opportunity, offering exceptional conditions to detect particles with feeble interactions that interact with matter weakly. These proposed experiments have the potential to surpass existing limits by an order of magnitude in certain areas, thereby complementing existing research and opening avenues to explore previously unexplored regions.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the susceptibility of a population's language is, therefore, particularly significant. Focusing on a model where a population consists of distinct, immutably labeled groups, each using a unique language, we analyze the impact of random migrations on language exchange. Demonstrating that random migrations always lead to language homogenization, we then introduce a detailed model of site-specific migrations, revealing that migration to isolated sites significantly creates monolingual island formations, which in turn causes the eventual extinction of other language dialects used on those sites. Moreover, migratory patterns to central sites typically result in the long-term coexistence of multiple language dialects, indicating that migratory patterns can substantially influence the dynamics and diversity of human languages.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite the impressive achievements, there's an overall convergence issue observed in the training of neural networks to approximate the solutions of these equations. By leveraging the properties of elliptic PDEs and adopting an optimization approach to the hyperparameter tuning of PINNs, our research showcases the effectiveness of our method in achieving higher convergence rates. Notably, our results indicate that increasing the network width enables the neural network to capture higher frequency components, ultimately leading to more accurate solutions. By properly adjusting the hyperbolic parameters, our method ensures the accurate spatio-temporal coverage of the solution, even with a relatively narrow network. Our findings also highlight the importance of tailored architecture and tailored loss functions in achieving better solutions.

We examine a two-wave system in a half-space with partial damping that also accounts for structural modifications, taking into account a stiffening coefficient that may change across various forms and types. One wave has a non-damped characteristic distinct from the damped wave, and we investigate the influence of the damping parameters on the rate at which the system's energy decreases over time. Under a defined set of assumptions regarding the external input and internal dissipation, we demonstrate a uniform exponential decay of the system's energy by means of a suitable variant of the J'acco method, even in the absence of a reaction term. Specifically, we have established an exponential decay rate that is dependent on the product of the dissipation parameters and is uniform across various forms and types of a stiffening coefficient that may change across various forms and types.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. High interaction costs underscore the importance of efficiency, while improved transparency via more interpretable models fosters trust from users. In our study, we introduce a new neural-stochastic structure to address these limitations by reinterpreting the actor-critic model. A single neural network generates an initial policy, and a second stochastic neural network enhances the policy, producing diverse stochastic actions drawn from the first network's distribution. The first network learns to match the second's output distribution, reducing the need for extensive interaction. Additionally, we develop a Bayesian approach to provide threshold-based stochastic action eligibility, facilitating faster learning. The proposed method, called BS-Actor Critic, demonstrates equivalent performance to cutting-edge approaches on challenging benchmark tasks, including Atari games and gym MuJoCo environments, while achieving faster convergence and providing transparent stochastic action generation.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a two-arm interferometer to parametrically amplify a nonlinear mode, while simultaneously applying quantum squeezed light to eliminate linear interactions between the modes. Using this method, established optical nonreciprocity can be enhanced by multiple factors, while maintaining linear interactions between the modes. Additionally, we've found that applying quantum squeezing to one of the modes significantly decreases backflow and increases forward flow, regardless of the level of nonlinear interaction. Importantly, this method doesn't rely on frequency-dependent gain or loss, and can be implemented on a microchip using current technology. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that applying quantum squeezing can accelerate optical nonreciprocity at low levels of nonlinear interaction, a level at which multiple pathways for signal transmission occur.

We expand upon the research initiated by P. Fenton by analyzing a single-variable function that arises from a specific combination of two variable functions, where one function surpasses the other as variables converge to negative infinity, and the other function converges to zero as variables converge to positive infinity. Under specific conditions, particularly when the kernel function has a specific curvature property, and assuming a type of transversality condition, this analysis reveals a canonical representation of this function, and identifies key features of its behavior. The proof leverages techniques from decision theory, including the application of Choquet theory, and yields insights into various applications, including optimal control theory and degenerate elliptic equations. As a direct consequence of this analysis, it is demonstrated that certain types of optimization problems, including those involving concave kernel functions, exhibit predictable local maxima behavior.

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles. Operating since 2009, CRESST combines exceptional sensitivity with flexible science capabilities, utilizing a diverse approach to study dark matter interactions across various mass scales. Leveraging a $230 g$ granular crystal array detector, CRESST explores a broad range of dark matter masses, from a few $\mathrm{geV}$ to above $10^{3} \mathrm{GeV}$, utilizing the MOON phase, which commenced in spring 2018 and lasted for two years. We present recent results derived from data collected at LNGS, focusing on the $\mathrm{keV}$ mass range and highlighting the significance of the $^{136}$Xe neutrino background in CRESST's findings.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This strategy is successfully tested in a satellite imaging scenario where it outperforms current standards regulating latent images in favour of the kernel's structural adjustment.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter paired modules.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely accepted formal framework for validating software
behaviors and specifying requirements. Yet, formal verification methods often
involve pedantic formal proof methodologies that may not appeal to average software
developers. Consequently, a significant gap exists between formal verification
tools and practical, proof-based software development techniques.
  This paper introduces an innovative web-based environment for Hoare logic-based
formal verification. This innovative tool streamlines the formal verification
process by incorporating an integrated development environment similar to
Eclipse, along with an integrated proof checker similar to Coq's proof viewer.
Additionally, the tool features interactive, "click-and-reveal" proof exploration
capabilities that expose underlying proof structures hidden during formal input.
We evaluate the tool's effectiveness using a practical application: verifying a
sorter function for a simulated banking system.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at large scales but struggles at smaller sizes due to the necessity of always maintaining the tree structure's balance, leading to unnecessary movements of nodes and increased traffic. We propose Sonus, an enhanced Canopus protocol, to optimize performance at small scales by allowing node flexibility in its tree structure balance while still maintaining Canopus' high scalability features at large scales.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing gradient elasticity that was sensitive to the bending modulus, which indicated that cholesterol increased with the cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio. A possible explanation for the discrepancy is that lipid bilayers exhibit non-equilibrium conditions during the experimental preparation time, which affects their rheological properties. A theoretical framework is developed to analyze changes in the cholesterol-to-phospholipid ratio and their effects on the bending modulus and bending modulus fluctuations within the equilibrium state of the lipid bilayer. A comparison of the theoretical predictions with the experimental findings shows that the non-equilibrium effects contribute significantly to the observed outcomes. Which method provides a more accurate prediction of the non-equilibrium viscoelastic response depends on the cholesterol concentration. A potential way to validate the theoretical model is through simulations combining experimental observations of microscopic motions with theoretical predictions of bulk rheological properties.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that the modified FRW dynamics is similar to that of the APS LQC model. The paper further establishes a correlation between the LQC density scale factor and the APS graph density scale factor. It determines the critical matter density, $\rho_{cr}$, as approximately $0.485\frac{\hbar C}{L^3}$, which leads to quantum gravity effects at a scale of approximately $2.73 \times 10^{26}$ meters, in alignment with Big Bang Theory observations.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a wide 
energy spectrum from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made 
available to facilitate multi-purpose and multi-messenger research related to 
cosmic particles. A separate companion paper delves into the detection analysis 
of these events, while this document provides an accessible overview of the 
data for an diverse audience.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties with information loss during non-maximum suppression and the multitasking nature of anchor-based object detection. Our novel solution, BayesOD, overhauls object detection and non-maximum suppression components by adopting a Bayesian perspective. This approach improves detection uncertainty estimation by incorporating the variability of individual detections and their expected contributions. Evaluations conducted on ImageNet, Pascal VOC 2007, and MS COCO demonstrate the superior performance of BayesOD over current state-of-the-art approaches.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly benefits urban traffic management, particularly when accurately predicting traffic volume dynamics across intricate road networks. Predictions based on extended temporal scenarios are already showing great potential, to which this research aims to add spatial extension through partitioning test data into overlapping fragments. Our hypothesis is that dividing data into smaller segments will boost the model's resilience to time-series disruption and navigation system influence on traffic volume dynamics. To test this hypothesis, we modified the GRU-CN framework, which incorporates spatial cues in traffic flow, to accommodate multiple input sequences, giving priority to the central segment while maintaining overlap with surrounding points. Our modified approach, GRU-CN$^+$, was validated using traffic volume data from San Francisco and Portland, which revealed that GRU-CN$^+$ consistently outperformed the original model, particularly in the context of disruption and navigation data injection scenarios. Furthermore, the study demonstrated that the weight assignment method used by GRU-CN$^+$ effectively prioritizes central road connections, maintaining consistency with the original framework's performance in distributed scenarios. The findings indicate that enhancing spatial coverage through overlapping road sections can notably improve the robustness of traffic volume predictions in urban road networks.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical interactions that can be quickly calculated. We also broadened the scope of Squier's theorem to fit our research framework, and then showed how this leads to coherence results for Gray categories. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we used it to prove coherence in the context of bicrossed products of groups.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about their performance in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. We have developed and validated an open-source, state-of-the-art deep learning method that uses an extended 2D multi-orientation approach with automatic pre-processing and orientation alignment. We compared this method with other recent deep learning techniques in two datasets: the public HarP dataset and an in-house epilepsy dataset, HCUnicamp. The results indicate that our approach achieves high segmentation accuracy in all three datasets and outperforms other methods in two out of three datasets. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust generalization to new domains, such as epilepsy data with hippocampal resections. We believe our method can be effectively applied in diverse clinical domains. The code for our method is freely available on GitHub, at the link https://github.com/UniFCEnnL/HippSeg2D.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover an underlying inconsistency. By incorporating transversal modes that are not part of the experiment's initial assumptions, we reveal that the interferometer's behavior is akin to a Drude model, featuring non-stationary oscillations. Consequently, at the time of the alleged observation of the pigeonhole effect, the system's state exhibits a zero probability of being in the pigeonhole corresponding to path 1. This outcome contrasts the typical scenario of which-path information being encoded in the cross-path mode.

Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy protons within the inner proton radiation belt. An analytical framework has been developed to quantify the proton flux within this radiation belt, generated by the decay of neutrons produced through CRAND processes. Utilizing environmental data and the PAMELA satellite's measurements of neutron decay depth and proton flux, the model's key parameters are determined, including the neutron density at an altitude of 22.6 km, which is calculated as 79.4 km^-3, and the proton flux at an altitude of 26.3 km, which is calculated as 23.6 k/cm^2/s. These findings demonstrate that the proton flux can be accurately predicted through the integration of neutron decay rates and trapping mechanisms, which results in a total proton flux of around one billion particles per square centimeter per second at altitudes below 28.5 km.
