The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the constituent
nanoscale objects. Heat units known as phonons exhibit a dual influence on
conductivity: by scattering electrons, they can hinder it but can also enhance it
by facilitating electron propagation through a complex energy terrain. 
In our investigation, we have observed a temperature-dependent, coherent electron
transfer between neighboring nanotubes through measurements of conductivity on
an armchair single-wall carbon nanotube film. Employing atomic modeling to study
electronic states and quantifying both electronic and phonon-assisted linkages, 
we found phonon-assisted conduction to be the major contributing factor behind
high-temperature transport in our samples. These observations reveal the presence
of synchronized, intertube interactions which validate single-chirality, armchair
nanotube films as exceptional macroscopic systems governed by quantum coherence.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The proposed method is called Hierarchical Self-Referential Fuzzy k-means (HSRFk), and it weighs distinct features differently to effectively handle data with multiple perspectives. By applying entropy to measure the uncertainty of each data point at each iteration, HSRFk can identify the most relevant cluster for each point. A comprehensive evaluation of this method against various popular clustering algorithms on diverse datasets reveals that HSRFk consistently achieves superior clustering performance. Furthermore, we analyzed the convergence properties and computational complexity of HSRFk.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of the cross-moment tensor between input data and output responses. While it still necessitates EM-type updates to recover missing mixing weights, the proposed method surpasses all existing alternatives by providing a global convergence guarantee. When applied to both simulated and real-world data sets, this new algorithm consistently outperformed existing approaches, opening up new avenues for learning complex, modular neural networks.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of quantum gravity. A statistical approach by Darabi et al. yields a non-trivial estimate of the proportion of states in gravity that retain global symmetries, albeit one that exhibits power-law divergence with parameters. Utilizing the Generalized Poincare lemma, we re-evaluate the Darabi calculation and reveal that it results in a finite value for the probability of maintaining a global symmetry in the field of gravity. Our analysis yields a deterministic outcome: the proportion converges to zero when the Darabi treatment is applied without further specification. Nevertheless, specifying free fields as in flat spacetime cosmology causes the probability to converge to a non-zero value.

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. These findings were further confirmed by cross-checking the source's cluster membership using data from Gaia Early Data Release 3 and evaluating F435W FUV magnitudes in relation to Gaia's G$_{ Fy2}$ visible magnitudes and F606V color values. Following initial processing, the team applied UV-Gap filtering and source selection criteria to yield a total of 246 cluster members. Subsequently, the team plotted F435W magnitudes against F1275F1305 and F1289F1312 filters, revealing the presence of 246 blue FUV stars, 134 of which were identified as BHB candidates, 64 as BCEPS candidates, 48 as BCEPS/BHB candidates, 8 as variable stars, and 28 as BSS candidates. Notably, these findings were further supported by aligning F435W F1275F1305 diagrams with synthetic HST F255W data for benchmark stars. Our research provides crucial evidence that FUV-FUV color-magnitude diagrams can effectively distinguish between blue horizontal branch, blue cepheid variable, and blue straggler star populations within the cluster, facilitated by precise selection of pure FUV stars.

This paper expands upon the b-principle by establishing that a certain type of oriented colored broken submersions can be equivalently represented by a map that assigns to each point a structured ideal from a specific category, and demonstrates that this ideal-assigning map exhibits a specific characteristic. Additionally, ideal-theoretic homotopy equivalences are identified, leading to a conclusion about the relationship between broken submersions and ideal-assigning maps. As a consequence of this breakdown, a map that assigns to each point a structured set is shown to be a submersion if and only if it satisfies a specific characteristic, and we provide examples of maps that exhibit this characteristic.

The goal of transfer learning with pre-trained deep neural networks (dNNs) is to improve the performance of complex tasks using the knowledge and relationships extracted from smaller tasks. However, the question of what makes some skills more transferable than others remains a mystery. In an effort to shed light on this, our research performs a comprehensive meta-analysis of the transferability of pre-trained dNNs on a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) downstream tasks. Through an empirical study involving over 1000 experiments, our findings reveal that the transferability of pre-trained dNNs on NLP tasks is significantly impacted by various factors, including the type of task, its size, and its relevance to the downstream task in question. Interestingly, our results indicate that the transferability of pre-trained dNNs on NLP tasks tends to decline as the downsteam task becomes larger and less related to the original task, with exceptions being cases where the original task exhibits high degrees of randomness or heterogeneity. Furthermore, our results suggest that the transferability of pre-trained dNNs on NLP tasks can be significantly improved by incorporating more robust original training objectives and architectures, particularly those designed to capture the underlying context of the original data at the sentence and word level.

In complex networks, identifying and measuring key information-spreading dynamics are crucial for numerous applications and theories. Focusing on basic diffusion rules enables researchers to evaluate a network's overall performance. This paper explores the relationship between the efficiency of information dissemination and network modularity in specific scenarios with two fundamental diffusion processes. While previous studies demonstrated that a network's overall speed of information dissemination is maximized when its modules are highly connected, this paper reveals that diffusion efficiency is optimized at a different point, specifically when the average connection between modules is strong compared to within them. This new balance point is derived from understanding the interactions between information-spreading processes on the network's different layers. The results presented here are broadly applicable, as they can explain the optimization of diffusion efficiency in networks that follow a specific community-based structure.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures indicating the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation, and these measurements depend on how close those Lagrangian angles are to being perfectly aligned. Some outcomes resulting from these conditions are a definitive uniqueness proof for special Lagrangians and a detailed criterion describing when a Lagrangian is considered special.

A key assumption underlying the Berezinskii-Zamail classification is the discrete nature of nonlinear interference points, which are used for channel memory estimation based on output statistics. We have developed a method to estimate channel memory without relying on this assumption. Instead, our approach relies on the deviation between observed and expected output distributions, which are compared through a metric based on total variation. We have established conditions for asymptotic channel identifiability and related this method to the previous classification approach based on output statistics. Furthermore, our approach allows for the estimation of channel memory even in the absence of discrete interference points, which was not possible with the original classification method. We have demonstrated the feasibility of our approach using numerical simulations of random discrete-time filters.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android devices, where malicious actors modify APK files directly to evade detection. The study aims to explore this type of attack that often receives insufficient attention due to a lack of knowledge about the Android ecosystem or a focus on general evasion attacks. The study will examine the characteristics, examples, and implementation of problem-space evasion attacks, as well as their challenges.

Service-oriented computing incorporates the ideas of service-oriented architecture and cloud computing, revolving largely around the concept of a service. Traditionally, a service referred to the execution of a business process either fully or partially within the context of distributed heterogeneous systems. However, the definition is lacking clarity, and it's especially ambiguous when describing the nature of service instantiation. Furthermore, the understanding of a service is often perceived solely as a conceptual idea, failing to fully incorporate the aspects of execution. Consequently, the definition of a service needs to be refined, setting it apart from related ideas such as process and program. In this context, we're proposing that a service should be viewed as program instantiation. Notably, this execution can be viewed as either a business process or a simpler computational program. In this revised understanding, the focus on program instantiation opens up new avenues, enabling the explicit identification and examination of service instantiation. It also enables the exploration of the dynamic nature of service instantiation and deactivation. The concept of program instantiation is relatively well-understood within the fields of programming, and it's our belief that applying this understanding to services can provide valuable insights into distributed service execution within the realm of service-oriented computing.

Recent experimental observations supporting the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian topological order are challenged by a reoccurring phase of unusual quantized nature, which is gapped in the thermodynamic limit.  Unlike other known phases such as Pfaffian, anti-Pfaffian, and PH-Pf phases, this new phase emerges at an intermediate mixing of Landau levels.  A proposed wave function accurately represents the unique topological structure of this phase by exhibiting high overlap with the exact ground state and closely reproducing the low-lying entanglement spectra, with topological characteristics that are resistant to flux changes.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., are suitable for describing astrophysical environments. We show that this metric represents a Thakurta black hole, which can emerge in spacetimes with negative anisotropic fluid pressures and temperatures. The Cauchy surface, defining the Thakurta black hole, is formed when the conformal field equation holds true. We establish that the Thakurta metric needs to be rescaled to remove singularities on the conformal Cauchy surface. The rescaled metric corresponds to a globally hyperbolic spacetime, which can be viewed as a locally asymptotically AdS, vacuum state. Notably, our study confirms that the Thakurta metric represents a rescaled AdS space rather than a globally hyperbolic, non-singularity-free spacetime.

The complexity of gaps and ring formations in protoplanetary discs indicates pressure hotspots connected to ongoing planet formation and other factors, with additional mechanisms such as tidal interactions and binarity contributing to the disc's structural intricacies. Using theoretical and numerical models, we investigate how these pressure anomalies affect planet core formation, focusing particularly on the impact of a type of disc feature predicted by planetary tidal interactions, called the co-rotation shock. We find that, in cases where the co-rotation shock is not extremely strong, it facilitates planet core formation by reducing the core growth barrier associated with the pressure gradient near the shock. However, extremely intense shocks can pose a significant obstacle, making it difficult or impossible for planet cores to form. Our study suggests that planet cores may form in areas with moderate pressure anomalies, such as those associated with tidal interactions, and rarely if ever in areas with extremely strong pressure anomalies, such as those associated with stellar binarity.

Extremely large sets of parameters may be beyond what's learnable given the constraints of a problem and the computational capabilities of the learner. Our goal is to investigate whether the need for such large sets is a necessary consequence of having limited computational resources. We're focusing on the basic question: Are there tasks and models that necessitate an exponentially large number of parameters simply due to computational restrictions? The answer is yes. We've identified a specific task - a classification task involving controlled examples - that requires a specific type of model with an exponentially increasing number of parameters to solve. The task involves a pseudo-random selection of inputs. We've proven that there's no alternative simpler model that can solve this task. We've also shown that this task requires at least an exponentially large number of parameters to successfully learn. Furthermore, our results suggest that no algorithm can verify if a given model with a finite - albeit very large - number of parameters is capable of solving this task. The proof involves encoding the model's parameters within the inputs of the classification task.

Two infinite abelian groups are given where one group is discrete and countable, and the other group is compact. A subset is chosen from the countable group such that its image when added with another subset gives a result with no repetition but contains a translation of every element from the subset. It's proven that under specific, less general circumstances, a pattern similar to the selected subset can be found within the result of the subset addition. A simpler situation is examined where selecting subsets based on two-element pairs is possible, and based on this simpler situation, it's proven that a specific pattern can be found within the result of the subset addition. A simpler form of the result is also obtained. A related question is asked.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To effectively compete with these alternatives, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. To achieve this, we explore strategies for selecting pickup and drop-off locations when creating routes, subject to specific service parameters. Initially, we develop a mathematical programming model accounting for service-specific requirements, including a backtracking approach to account for route alterations. Subsequently, we introduce a heuristic location search algorithm, incorporating stochastic backtracking, to efficiently explore a expanded solution space. To validate our approach, extensive computational experiments are conducted and compared with existing solutions in the field.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in the E-commerce sector, a rapidly growing field. One of the primary obstacles in this field is the disparity between distribution and correlation of data, manifesting in scenarios such as missing visual data for items that exist only in text form. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method, known as the Decomposable Modal Pretrainer (DMP), capable of handling and making the most of independent data distributions across individual modalities while effectively combining them into a unified, coherent representation. DMP employs a decomposable model where each modality processes its data in isolation before being fused through a common learning objective, thereby yielding improved empirical results. Our proposed approach also enables modality selection and data sampling to accommodate incomplete data, making it possible to utilize extensive, modality-independent data while effectively combining it into a unified, coherent representation. DMP showcases its superiority over existing methods by achieving notable performance improvements of 21.9% and 11.5% in loss reduction on two key benchmarks, namely the CTR prediction task and the item ranking task.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers considerable potential for examining brain structure adaptability. In this paper, the potential of modified DIM models is compared to conventional supervised networks, such as AlexNet and ResNet, in predicting progression to Alzheimer's disease, using classification between healthy controls, MCI patients with stable or progressive conditions, and Alzheimer's patients as benchmarks. Our experiment utilizes data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and indicates promising results for incorporating DIM in neuroimaging research.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an evaluation metric linking model performance with linguistic semantics in text classification. This score, known as I-score, compares model predictions with actual truth based on linguistic rules. Additionally, the study proposes an architectural modification to LSTM called I-LSTM that incorporates external guidance from I-score, allowing the model to incorporate linguistic semantics and improve performance. Experiments using both English and Arabic languages demonstrate the effectiveness of I-score in evaluating classification models and the beneficial impact of incorporating linguistic semantics in prediction for enhanced accuracy, particularly in rare classes and noisy datasets. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the versatility of I-score across various text classification datasets and the potential of the I-LSTM model to serve as a universal text classifier due to its capability to handle diverse languages with minimal modification.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. As interactions rise in a paramagnetic system, the spin-orbit constant expands, ultimately reaching a point where the ground state transitions to an antiferromagnetic state. In the antiferromagnetic phase, the spin-orbit constant diminishes and varies inversely with the interaction parameter. We investigate the computational time needed to achieve convergence and find that the spin-orbit constant achieves convergence more slowly under heightened interactions. We also analyze the impact of the number of photons and the basis sets on interaction parameters and find that increasing either results in convergence being reached more quickly.

A metastable dark matter candidate emerges as a natural consequence of a
conformal transformation between the Einstein metric, where gravitons are normalised states,
and the Jordan metric governing the coupling between gravity and matter. This
secluded dark matter, isolated from the Standard Model by a large energy scale
above which the Jordan metric diverges from the Einstein metric, interacts mainly
with the Higgs field in the early universe. This interaction enables sufficient
production of dark matter, consistent with observational data. Dark matter with
masses less than approximately one MeV is long-lived due to its seclusion,
yielding a lifetime significantly exceeding the universe's age and existing
experimental bounds. Such a dark matter scenario features distinct, non-relational
features including gravitation affecting the state of dark matter and the universe
exhibiting metric nonrelativity, where the Einstein metric used in quantum
gravity doesn't determine the metric coupling in the low-energy sector. Although
falsifiable, this scenario contrasts earlier proposals involving metric nonrelativity.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and effectively before being used in the general public, it is crucial to assess their performance accurately. Given the limited availability and potential high cost of medical test data, it is necessary to simulate and model real-world scenarios to determine the test performance of these devices when faced with different situations. However, estimating test performance under varying conditions and without sufficient labeled data poses a significant challenge, as it involves making assumptions and using a large amount of unlabeled data. In response to this issue, we propose an innovative framework that uses a unique combination of two models to estimate the test performance of AI-powered devices. This framework utilizes two essential components - a label-prediction model that generates potential distribution shifts from unlabeled data and a simulation model that simulates and predicts test performance based on these distribution shifts and available labeled data. By leveraging these two models, we demonstrate that the performance of the AI-powered device under different conditions can be accurately calculated, even when there are limitations and uncertainties. Notably, the effectiveness and reliability of our proposed framework are substantiated by both theoretical evidence and empirical analysis. Furthermore, the results from our experiments show that the framework can successfully predict the test performance of different models under various scenarios, highlighting its potential value in training and improving AI-powered devices.

High-fidelity simulations involving atomic-level representations are highly beneficial but extremely computationally costly. A compromise has been found, offering a reasonable trade-off between computational expense and the level of detail achieved. This involves the development of a new mapping technique, allowing five out of six rotational degrees of freedom to be simulated accurately while accounting for the remaining one through periodic adjustment. As a result, systems comprising nucleic acids and proteins can be simulated at significantly reduced cost, approximately one-twentieth, while maintaining high precision and detail for all other degrees of freedom. Notably, simulations relying on the optimized potential energy benchmark have shown efficacy in replicating nucleic acid structure and dynamics. Moreover, simulations lasting just one day have been found to match those of much longer, 10 ns simulations, revealing the high fidelity of these optimizations. Overall, this approach represents a significant advancement in the simulation of complex biological systems.

The Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) encoder was originally proposed as an efficient way to compress time-based data in the context of distributed clock offset estimation. However, a compression method can become vulnerable to adversarial attacks that force it to generate overly lengthy outputs, resulting in a loss of efficiency. This issue is studied in a context where the adversary has the capacity to manipulate both the ANS encoder and decoder. Our compression scheme designed to counter these adversaries, referred to as the tabled ANS (tANS), utilizes a predetermined lookup table mapping input symbols to output representations. Despite introducing redundancy, tANS renders the encoder vulnerable to adversarial manipulation no longer. The tANS approach is shown to prevent adversarial tampering by imposing minimum redundancy of at most two, as demonstrated using an existing ANS encoder that employs tANS initialization. Additionally, tANS-based encoders using Duda's initialization incur redundancy of at most three. tANS-based encoders using Duda's initialization incur redundancy of at most three.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials are heavily influenced by the composition and presence of liquid phases. Electrolyte dielectric behavior is influenced in a complex manner by ion-water and ion-ion interactions, and this phenomenon is particularly pronounced in systems where liquid and solid coexist. Pore size and the concentration of the electrolyte have a substantial impact on the dielectric response, largely attributed to modifications in ion-water interactions. Additionally, the dielectric behavior is found to be sensitive to temperature changes, specifically exhibiting two distinct relaxation processes below the freezing point of the electrolyte. One of the relaxations, observed across a broad temperature range, can be associated with the structural reorganization of the ions within the pore. Lastly, the presence of freezing-induced phenomena highlights additional complexities in understanding liquid-clay and porous material dielectric behavior.

We propose a novel spectrum of molecular states, composed of a heavy quark and an heavy antiquark, paired with either a light or a charm light meson. Our predicted molecular spectrum is based on the light-light meson molecular spectrum from the QChromoWebs model. By applying the principles of this model, we obtain numerous molecular states with different quark content, such as $B\bar{D}^*$, $B^*\bar{D}^*$, $B^*_s\bar{D}^*$, $B\bar{D}^{(*)*}$, $B^*_s\bar{D}^{(*)*}$, and others. Some of our predictions for molecular states without a string break up occur at around 6.3 GeV for the $B\bar{D}^*$ system and around 6.8 GeV for the $B^*\bar{D}^*$ system. Additionally, we predict that the $B\bar{D}^{**(*)}$ molecular states string break up begins at around 6.7 GeV and the $B^*_s\bar{D^{**(*)}}$ molecular states at around 6.9 GeV. Lastly, we suggest that the molecular state around 6.15 GeV could explain the X(6251) state discovered by LHCb.

Our analysis encompasses a comprehensive dataset of 544 prominent research papers and 70 online resources related to the development of swarm drones for military purposes. The analysis includes 10 esteemed journals and provides an overview of the evolution of military swarm drones from the inception in 2009 until 2020. The findings reveal that the topic has gained more significance after 2019, with a substantial increase in the number of papers published in 2020. The research provides in-depth evaluations of the practical applications, challenges, and fundamental concepts of military swarm drones. Furthermore, the study highlights the most frequently cited publications in this field and provides insights into potential future areas for further exploration. The research dataset is made accessible through a dedicated online repository, allowing for the review of the included papers and resources.

When performing cosmological inferences based on the Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses usually only consider a specific feature related to baryon acoustic oscillations. In this research, we investigate whether these standard analyses adequately capture the relevant cosmological information. To address this, we directly fitted the 3D Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including their entire shape, to simulate various cosmological models. Our study found that the standard BAO extraction method failed to extract non-baryonic neutrino information, resulting in unnecessary model complexity when trying to fit the correlation functions. We demonstrated that the inclusion of additional features can lead to slightly better $A_\mathrm{z}$ constraints, albeit with very small improvements. Our work suggests that to maximize the cosmological information in Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, the full shape (including its characteristics up to specific certain modes) should be considered for analysis.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight.

Predicting pedestrian trajectories in real-time has significant implications 
for enhancing public safety, security systems, and intelligent surveillance, 
especially in cities and crowded areas. To develop accurate pedestrian 
forecasting models, we introduce the MultiPedia dataset, consisting of a diverse 
set of heterogeneous pedestrian data, categorized into four complexity levels and 
two density conditions. The dataset is divided into a training section with 
distinct starting points and a test section with overlapping starting points, 
enabling researchers to evaluate their models' performance in predicting 
interacting and non-interacting pedestrians at various levels of complexity and 
crowding. The dataset and corresponding code are accessible at (insert link).

Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze intricate systems. This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and relationships. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine model and a recurrent neural network based on incremental Hebbian learning are employed as case studies to illustrate how these measures detect system intricacy. Specifically, the study examines the development of complexity in a system where random connections are repeatedly strengthened in a targeted manner within the context of a target function. This targeted learning process mimics a recurrent neural network in an effort to recognize patterns in time-dependent data. The study evaluates three foundational measures of complexity and a new metric that the researchers have recently developed. The results show that while traditional measures of complexity cannot generalize well, the newly developed metric and another theoretically introduced measure called the Fisher information metric are highly correlated with each other and successfully track system intricacy in both scenarios.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with an advanced deep learning solution for translating hand signals into specific robot commands. This integration enables users to input commands via hand gestures that are translated into acceptable robot instructions. Our test of this technology took place in a simulated environment where users made adjustments to the density of a swarm of red robots through incorporation of IR markers. Our experiments produced effective gesture-based instructions with high accuracy and reliability.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic protocols in driving quantum states involves a supporting, auxiliary gauge field that accelerates a desired state change when coupled with a system. However, when the gauge field exhibits rapid change, it's often challenging to precisely engineer. A new approach overcomes this limitation by using machine learning to design the gauge field, specifically in driving a two-level system via deep neural networks. The developed machine-learning protocol successfully mimics a Butler-VandenWuwer protocol and efficiently achieves rapid state changes.

Color-neutral images are a cornerstone in various image processing applications such as image compression, feature extraction, and printing due to their role in tone mapping. However, valuable image data gets lost when transitioning color images to their grayscale counterparts. In this study, a comprehensive dataset of grayscale images is introduced along with a dataset of color images with accompanying ground truth. A straightforward, non-iterative algorithm is employed for image decompression, yielding satisfactory results. Notably, the proposed approach exhibits superior outcomes to existing techniques. Moreover, the computational costs associated with image decompression using our method are significantly lower. The employed dataset is intended to benefit researchers working with grayscale images.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequent applications of these results enable the computation of certain infinite series connected to Stirling numbers.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, it then becomes conformally equivalent to S^2.

The linear Breit-Wheeler process is a fundamental quantum electrodynamics phenomenon occurring when a photon collides with a free electron, resulting in an excited positron. Researchers previously proposed an experiment utilizing an intense laser to create an electron plasma to demonstrate the Breit-Wheeler process. Our study presents an alternative approach involving an intense laser interacting with an ionization front in a weakly ionized gas, which inhibits photon propagation and consequently reduces electron scattering. By analyzing the balance between photoelectrons and positrons, we determine the conditions under which the Breit-Wheeler process can be observed and estimate required experimental parameters.

In a forthcoming letter, we examine how sensitive the Two Higgs Doublet Model is to a crucial parameter, $m_{12}$, which breaks the symmetry softly and impacts the Higgs boson decays significantly. Although $m_{12}$ often goes to zero in analyses, its variation has substantial effects on the model's outcomes, especially regarding the Higgs boson masses and Higgs-Vachon-Zwieg decays. Consequently, we suggest keeping $m_{12}$ different from zero in studies of the 2HDM.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-covered', a determinable property that ensures specific conditions are satisfied in the resulting RDF data.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing, encompassing recent advancements in applying various nonparametric techniques for productivity and efficiency analysis. This research area is characterized by a broadly defined'shape' and a single observed point per unit. Key recent developments include kernel-free and semiparametric density estimators, as well as an unbiased estimator for a monotone density. This study builds upon these foundational estimators, introducing novel ones for a completely monotone density class, along with asymptotic proofs for their efficiency. Our focus on completely monotone densities is motivated by applications in economics and finance, including stochastic processes and nonparametric distributional models. Notably, the proposed estimators are simple modifications of existing kernel-free density estimators, making them easily implementable. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the introduced estimators exhibit the same strong convergence properties as the underlying kernel-free density estimators while achieving higher rates of convergence. This is facilitated by applying a convex ordering concept to derive tight bounds for the supremum of the estimating functions, thereby allowing the derivation of efficient estimators for completely monotone densities. Some empirical illustrations using economic data in finance and production efficiency contexts are also provided.

This study proposes an innovative mass reconstruction technique for examining the lower mass spectrum resulting from top-quark pairs produced in association with a scalar boson at the LHC. By employing an event reconstruction method that accounts for the presence of a bottom-quark jet, more efficient resolution of the bottom-quark jet mass is achieved. Furthermore, a fit is performed to determine the masses of the bottom-quark jets, thereby adding to the overall resolution. According to simulations, this technique is expected to enhance the mass resolution for identifying the lower mass spectrum by a factor of five when using 300 fb$^{-1}$ of data, collected under the 14 TeV LHC configuration.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which utilise the syntactic knowledge extracted from pre-trained models like BERT. UPOA and UPIO are the first of their kind to apply the self-attention mechanism, widely applied in language models, to unsupervised constituent parsing. UPIO outperforms UPOA through the employment of linear projection matrices for parsing queries and keys associated with self-attention, as well as parsing value matrices for subsequent linear layer transformations. UPIO is proven to be more efficient than UPOA as the dimension of the parsing model increases. UPOA and UPIO achieve parsing results comparable to state-of-the-art unsupervised approaches on the Penn Treebank, and significantly surpass UPOA when combined with UPOS, a parser previously achieving the current best results on the dataset. UPIO also outperforms UPIO on the LAMBADA semantic parsing task. The enhanced parsing model UPIO further exhibits its capacity to apply the self-attention mechanism to unsupervised parsing without reliance on additional training data, as observed in its robust performance under diverse parsing configurations.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), particularly for languages lacking sufficient resources. In this research, various data augmentation methods are applied to a German acoustic model to assess its performance with and without additional training data. A newly created dataset, the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus, is utilized in this study to enhance the modeling of German phonetics. Performance evaluations are conducted with and without the augmented data, and two distinct training approaches are compared: incorporating a pre-trained ThchsRauD feature space into the feature space of the final acoustic model, and incorporating the final acoustic model into the ThchsRauD feature space. In both scenarios, the addition of data significantly improves model performance, as measured by the word error rate (WER). When the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus is integrated into the acoustic model, the WER decreases by 6% and 8% respectively. In the second scenario, the WER decreases by 11% and 13% respectively. When the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus is integrated into the ThchsRauD feature space, the WER decreases by 6% and 11% respectively.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations reveal that their projected rotation speeds cannot all be at critical velocity, instead they range between 320 to 350 km/s. These Be-type stars have slower than expected rotation and there are fewer than expected stars with rotation speeds below 40% of critical velocity. In comparison to normal B-type stars, there are fewer Be-type stars with rapid rotation and even lower rates of being in binary systems with smaller radial amplitudes. These patterns are similar in a sample from the Small Magellanic Cloud and a direct comparison to model predictions prefers a dual evolutionary pathway over a single star one.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization (ITN) is used to convert various spoken forms like numbers, dates, and money amounts into their written equivalents. However, current ITN techniques fail to consider the context in which numbers are spoken, leading to low-quality written forms that can even change the meaning of the surrounding text. To address this limitation, a novel sequence-to-sequence ITN approach featuring a hybrid head is presented, which leverages a "what" head to identify the spoken unit and a "where" head to determine the location of the unit within the spoken sentence. As a result, this model achieves ITN with both local and global context awareness. Furthermore, a dataset with annotated contexts for spoken units is proposed to support the ITN task and evaluate the efficacy of the approach. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method, aided by pre-trained models, achieves superior ITN performance with contextualization, as evidenced by an F-score boost of 5.86% over baseline ITN methods without contextualization.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical real-world applications such as medical imaging. A promising approach to gaining insight into these models involves generating natural-looking examples that highlight the connections between input and output variables. Despite some methods producing examples that are visually plausible and relevant, others fall short in these aspects. To address the problem of evolving these methods in a way that facilitates learning from these examples, we developed an innovative technique called ReAct. By allowing the model to discover new examples based on the ones it's previously been shown, we're able to unlock its full potential for using these examples to identify key features, adjust parameters, and even transfer knowledge to similar models. Our results, encompassing natural images, text, and summaries, show that our approach significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art methods.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations have no impact on the topological classification of non-Hermitian systems, as long as the local interaction Hamiltonian commutes with the system's non-Hermitian part. However, correlations do alter the edge states of non-Hermitian topological systems, causing them to transition from being non-Hermitian Dirac points to ordinary Hermitian points. Moreover, correlations have no influence on the topological edge states of systems with vortical non-Hermitian profiles, as long as the local interaction Hamiltonian does not commute with the system's non-Hermitian part. The characteristics of vortical topological states in correlated systems are marked by complex and multifaceted behaviors, including singular points where non-Hermitianality is broken, a connection between non-Hermitianality and Hermitianality, and periodic oscillations in energy gaps.

Our current speech synthesis approach produces speech with a wider range of emotional expressions, and we utilised subjective evaluations to determine which acoustic elements enable warm synthetic speech to be distinguishable. We found that incorporating F0 standard deviation and higher pitch peaks contributed to warm speech, whereas negative F0 deviations had the opposite effect. Additionally, we discovered that including the 10th order D4C statistic enhanced warm speech. By incorporating these essential features, we were able to design a metric that accurately measures the warmth of synthetic speech and we have made the associated code available for future reference.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop radiative processes, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the 1-500 GeV mass range. Dark matter production in the early universe is addressed, particularly focusing on the freeze-in mechanism for bosonic dark matter within the framework of this model. Stability and cosmological feasibility of bosonic dark matter are ensured by the selection rules and cosmological requirements. By analyzing the mass spectrum of this model, we identify a region satisfying stability and cosmological compatibility, corresponding to a 200-460 GeV mass range for the dark matter boson.

Building on the geometrical collective Bohr-Mottelson model, we develop a novel method to determine the minimum length associated with nuclear structure, employing the fission of heavy and superheavy nuclei as a testing ground to explore its implications. Applying the minimization technique, we find that the minimum length predicted by this approach aligns well with experimental confirmation of nuclear deformation.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are inherent in groups structured by direct sums of rings with identity. Furthermore, in the context of GCM quadruples, it is observed that GCA pairs are naturally derived from rings with identity. Relevant examples are provided to illustrate these findings.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features from hierarchical and shallow levels. By utilizing different feature fusion strategies, we evaluate the effectiveness of shallow fusion and hierarchical fusion on the ISBI 2013 dataset, finding that the latter significantly outperforms the former by 4.7 dB in terms of objective change detection quality measures.

A comprehensive study examines the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an extensive, high-accuracy dataset. The concept was first introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977; this research demonstrates that scaling leads to a nearly linear correlation between residual entropy and reduced viscosity across a broad range of substances (argon, methane, CO2, and several others), including different model potentials. The initial "universal" correlation of the Rosenfeld relation was found to be limited, yet correcting for density and temperature fluctuations yields a straightforward expression for the log of the entropy change. The obtained viscosity entropy coupling, approximately equal to 3.0, does not depend on the type of interaction or state point, remaining stable across different molecular fluids. Additionally, this research applies dimensionless entropy and density, and initially entertains the idea that these choices might underlie the "universality" observed in the entropy viscosity coupling.

The possibility that our Universe undergoes a periodic cycle of expansion, driven by ρ(Ω), a relationship between matter density and curvature, is investigated. This hypothesis implies a periodic pattern in the Hubble parameter's graph, leading to a predicted 'turnaround' point where the graph peaks. Assuming the law of gravitation by Newton and an effective dark energy law governing the universe's expansion, the periodicity condition yields two potential candidates for ρ(Ω) out of a vast set of possible functions. These candidates are compared to data on the cosmic expansion history, revealing a reasonable correlation between the predicted and actual rates of expansion for one candidate, but not the other. This analogy is similar to the conventional 'ΛCDM' model, attributing the universe's expansion to a combination of dark energy and cold matter. Additionally, the periodic cosmology offers distinct characteristics, including an initial period of slow expansion, lengthier periods of acceleration, and a present expansion rate significantly lower than the maximum. This variant of the periodic cosmology shares similarities with the 'ΛCDM' model of the universe, leading to a similar prediction for its current expansion rate.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into the study of quantum foundations. Despite this potential, developing a clear hidden-variable model for it has been lacking. In this work, an hidden-variable model for the theory is developed which illustrates its key features. A hidden-variable model for the theory is being proposed with a high level of precision. The Invariant-set theory is being compared to other superdeterministic theories and nonlocal theories, and an analysis is being conducted to determine how close it is to quantum mechanics. According to this analysis, achieving precision comparable to current quantum standards would require incredibly fine-tuned initial conditions, resulting in a violation of Bell correlations.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage.

In the case where lattice spacing vanishes, the analysis focuses on the dimer model on isoradial graphs in the presence of $SL(N,\mathbb{C})$ gauge fields with zero curvature. It is demonstrated that the two-dimensional Dirac partition function is equivalent to the partition function of the $Z_n$ percolation model on isoradial graphs with the same gauge fields in place. When the gauge fields are trivial, the results conform with established findings, particularly those regarding the equivalence between the two-dimensional Dirac and Tutte polynomials. Owing to the complex nature of the gauge fields involved, the results presented expands upon previous research. Further to this investigation, we also examine the asymptotic characteristics of the two-dimensional Dirac partition function on the torus and derive an interpretation of its logarithm as a critical value is approached. This interpretation is linked to the behavior of conformal field theory, with specific components related to the $Z_n$ percolation model on the torus, involving the dilaton and the $Z_n$ conformal field.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires engineers and analysts to assess variables one by one, posing a computational problem. Our solution develops an efficient and straightforward statistical method to learn numerous variables and reduce dimensions without relying on any additional assumptions. The proposed method employs multivariate cluster analysis to create groups of variables, which are then used in a straightforward regression model. The method's effectiveness in dealing with large datasets, sparse problems and different data types is illustrated through experiments using electronic data.

In recent years, the needs of embedded systems have grown more complex.  These systems not only require reliable, hard real-time capabilities but also diverse computational demands that can encompass scientific calculations or data analysis.  These unique requirements present challenges for current virtualization solutions, which often compromise efficiency.  Our research introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor designed specifically for the distinct needs of mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Unlike other hypervisors that cause significant overhead, T-Visor achieves efficient co-existence of hard real-time and non-real-time guest operating systems.  The supervisor's streamlined functionality and hardware resource allocation strategy in T-Visor enable the efficient management of shared resources.  Additionally, our testing indicates that T-Visor's performance loss is minimal in comparison to other hypervisors.  Successful practical applications of T-Visor have been demonstrated on an ARM-based platform, showcasing its potential to provide embedded real-time systems with advanced security features, including memory isolation and trusted boot, while maintaining high performance and efficiency.

When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned with gravity, thus reducing the complexity of panoramic stitching. Our study explores the impact of aligning cameras to the vertical axis on the accuracy of panoramic images captured from a single camera. We found that camera alignment has a significant influence on stitching accuracy. Our results demonstrate that when cameras are aligned vertically, the stitching process becomes simpler and more precise. We further show that the stitching process can be reduced to two dimensions and efficiently replicated using existing one-dimensional panoramic stitching techniques. This insight provides valuable knowledge for both researchers and practitioners working in visual computing. Inspired by the success of vertical alignment, the concept of horizontal alignment is also investigated in this study.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We've analyzed chimeras in systems where phase states depend on multiple variables, investigating the effect of different types of coupling behavior, as exemplified by two specific types of coupled oscillator systems. Our research involves numerical analyses and stability assessments of chimeras in these contexts, highlighting the distinct influences of different coupling mechanisms on the emergence and stability of chimeric states.

We aim to eliminate the need for exploration in reinforcement learning by introducing environment dynamics into the learning process. Building upon PPO with integrated Policy Gradient methods, we develop a model-based algorithm that estimates future states through complex neural network calculations. By incorporating TD error optimization, we frame the problem as a mean-squared error minimization, allowing the incorporation of the Bellman equation into the loss function. By leveraging policy networks that output continuous state distributions, we enable the utilization of sample mean estimates for the Bellman error. Leveraging the advantages of model-based algorithms and policy gradient methods, we achieve superior performance with minimal sample complexity. Our results show that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing state-of-the-art model-based and model-free reinforcement learning techniques.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can create a finite-dimensional slice algebra with a specific mutation behavior and with a higher mathematical complexity, indicating its higher non-deterministic properties.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between reflected entropy and entanglement wedge cross-sectional area.  Building upon this concept, we applied it to random tensor networks, first developing reflected entropy across coplanar slices in two-dimensional space and then extending it to arbitrary dimensions.  We discovered that our results from holographic theories, specifically the Page paradox, can be achieved in random tensor networks by accounting for all possible network configurations.  We found that an entanglement wedge divergence arises from short-term density matrix corrections, with reflected entropy returning to an ER=EFT value once in the long-term limit.  We found that the short-term effects impact networks with duals and decrease as network size increases.  We discovered that non-local correlations can produce reflected entropy discrepancies, yet in most cases, the impact will be minimal.  However, we hypothesize that short-term effects may be masked by other short-term effects in networks with low density matrices.  We found that our short-term limit approximation aligns with all other approximations, including the entanglement wedge and island duality.  We discovered that our approximation preserves duality and Poincar\'e symmetry.  We found that our model generates a non-linear Page curve.  We discovered that island size effects can be determined by computing entanglement entropy within an island.  We found that our model produces an entanglement wedge divergence. Earth's life is defined by dynamic processes that transform and change over time. Nature's patterns, patterns of society, and patterns of thought are all exemplified through the physical sciences' concept of patterns. Although patterns are initially resisted by the energy gradients and entropy increase in the environment, they thrive by stabilizing internal energy gradients and reducing entropy within them. In this study, we investigate how long-lived patterns can emerge and persist even on an irreversible thermal scale. To do this, we consider a simplified model of a thermosculptor, a thermal device that creates ordered three-dimensional lattices of crystals representing artistic ideas. To simulate irreversibility, we introduce random perturbations to the energy gradients. In our model, we find that pattern longevity is directly influenced by the frequency of entropy production and the energy provided to maintain the patterns. When the rate of entropy production surpasses the rate at which the patterns can be replenished, the patterns dissolve, an event that can be observed in the decline of artistic ideas due to cultural entropy increase in the environment. In contrast, patterns that are constantly resupplied by external sources will eventually dissolve if the rate of entropy production inside the patterns surpasses the rate at which the external sources can replenish them. In both cases, the patterns will gradually disappear even if the external sources of energy remain uninterrupted.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. A thorough analysis of bifurcations in this system reveals that the emergence of periodic orbits, especially at specific resonant points, leads to distinct patterns in the parameter space. The system also exhibits complex attractors such as invariant circles and chaotic motion, identifiable through rotation numbers and Lyapunov exponents. The chaotic motion includes patterns similar to those of H\'{e}non and Lorenz systems, arising either from a period-doubling sequence or from the disruption of stable circles near the unstable trajectory of a fixed point.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that links black hole mass to electric charge and photon momentum. This relationship is expressed as $M = q^2/\sqrt{2}$ for black holes and $M = \frac{p^2}{\sqrt{2}}$ for graviton amplitudes. This study confirms that both BH and graviton mass equations remain unchanged in the high temperature and high energy limits. It also demonstrates that when the temperature and energy laws for BH's are applied to graviton amplitudes, their corresponding scattering amplitudes exhibit identical behavior. This study further explores the connection between BH's mass equations and their scattering amplitudes in the high temperature and high energy limits. Utilizing BH's mass equations in the high temperature and high energy limits reveals that when the temperature and energy laws are applied to graviton amplitudes, their scattering amplitudes exhibit random behavior, indicating that when the high temperature and high energy limits are applied to graviton amplitudes, its scattering amplitudes revert to their respective BH values, indicating recovery of BH's properties.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining how
the number of hook lengths divisible by $t$ in the partitions of $n$ varies.
The support of the resulting distribution, $Y_t(n)$, grows with $n$. The
lower bound of its support, given by $cn^a$, where $a \geq 1$ and $c > 0$, is
established for both $t$. The value of $a$ is fixed at $2$ for $t = 2$ and at
$3$ for $t = 3$. Additionally, the asymptotic growth rates for the expectations and
standard deviations of $Y_t(n)$ are determined. The findings for $Y_2(n)$ extend
previous results by Rouzé and for $Y_3(n)$ were previously established by the
authors. The findings for $Y_2(n)$ demonstrate that hook lengths mod $4$ follow
a mixed Poisson distribution while those mod $3$ follow a Poisson distribution.
The analyses make use of combinatorial methods, the concept of "rubbing hooks," and
the generating function for partitions with hook lengths divisible by $t$.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times: the actual time through the barrier and the time measured from the classical point of view. For particles approaching a square potential barrier in one-dimensional space, both tunneling times are calculable. Calculations show that the difference between these times is a constant, equal to half the period of a classically forbidden oscillation. This result is applicable regardless of the barrier's strength or the particle's state. When considering coherent states, which cover the full range of possible energies, the tunneling times correspond to early and late arrival scenarios. Coherent states produce a broader range of tunneling times compared to classical particles in the quantum-mechanical scenario of a free particle passing through a square potential barrier.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons, demonstrating that at a leading order approximation, these amplitudes can be represented by a single, universal function applicable across all relevant types of mesons. Utilizing QCD light-cone sum rules, we examine the leading and next-leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave mesons, derive their respective moments, and calculate their average magnitudes, Annie. These calculations are conducted for mesons composed of different quark combinations (u, d, s, c and b fundamental representations), as well as for charmonium-like mesons.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry and information processing in Bose-Einstein condensates. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory or nonlinear differential equations. These descriptions sometimes conflict with key principles in interferometry and information processing. Nevertheless, a possibility of compatibility remains, and we provide a solid foundation for quantum operations, derived from solving evolution equations, and build upon this base with control techniques and efficient state sampling methods to develop practical nonlinear gates, especially a nonlinear Hadamard gate. Furthermore, our work in BEC interferometry and quantum computing redefines the paradigm by incorporating principles from nonlinear quantum mechanics.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is predicted to be the symmetry algebra of the quantum gravity S-matrix. However, determining the algebra of quantized extended BMS charges has proven challenging. Recent advancements in celestial holography indicate a closed symmetry algebra without a central extension or anomaly, whereas other research suggests that quantizing these charges results in a deformation when combined. This paper reexamines this problem considering updated understanding of superrotation charges and finds that quantization of eBMS charges within a new phase space, which includes spin and boost charges, results in an deformation with a 6-dimensional cocycle.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges, especially when training models can only occur once for each example. Our research focuses on solving this problem by developing an algorithm that learns new categories without retraining existing ones. We enhance this process by integrating contrastive learning techniques, which improve the model's ability to distinguish between categories after each training episode. Our proposed algorithm, Echo, utilizes a unique two-step training protocol: initially, it enhances inter-category distinctions and subsequently, it focuses on the internal structure of each category, facilitating more effective recognition and differentiation. Through various experiments, we found that Echo yields better results compared to multiple baseline models, and its effectiveness is especially evident in large-scale scenarios.

In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized Cauchy surface conditions have been introduced. These conditions lead to a 2nd-order elliptic differential equation, and we demonstrate that a metric with these conditions can be described as a conformal rescaling of a unique underlying Einstein metric. This characterization has a geometric implication in a ball model, essentially stating that if an Einstein metric with these conditions is complete, then it must be compact.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The prevalence of these parasites in remote areas and following
natural disasters often leads to infection. Consequently, intestinal parasite
infections lead to various health issues, including malnutrition and anemia.
An online survey was conducted among healthcare professionals in Bangladesh to
gather information on the treatment approaches and outcomes for intestinal
parasite infections. The survey provided valuable insights into the treatment
methods used in the country and highlighted the necessity of establishing a
system for monitoring parasitic infections in the country's healthcare system.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation method is used to simplify the nongame-like portions of the model. A clear approximation error estimate is derived and convergence to the Nash equilibrium is proven. Additionally, the model's parameter convergence is also demonstrated.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively captures the nonlinear dynamics of quadcopter motion. The integration of a derivative filter enhances the stability of the PIDA controller without compromising stability or causing oscillations. The proposed PIDA control strategy is evaluated using theoretical stability analysis and an optimal control theory approach. The results show that PIDA control can ensure the asymptotic stability of a specific optimal solution for quadcopter motion. The efficacy of the PIDA control strategy is demonstrated through simulations of attitude and position control. The outcomes highlight the superiority of the PIDA control strategy over conventional PID control, resulting in reduced error trajectories and faster convergence to optimal solutions with robust stability.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key concepts and tools, such as chiral effective field theory and
dispersive unitary elliptic functions, are introduced in detail, with particular emphasis
on their practical applications and implications. Additionally, discussions of outstanding
issues, such as the long-standing pion-nucleon sigma term enigma, are included.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot pilots for enhanced data transmission. Nevertheless, it exhibited difficulties with predicted phase transitions, necessitating the development of a replacement solution. In response, the silicon pixel prototype was reconstituted with modified pilot modules featuring increased radiation resilience, fan-out front-end design, and an amplified signal-to-noity ratio. In this capacity, the modified pilot modules demonstrated resilience against the LHC's high levels of noise and expected levels of ionizing radiation, while also showcasing improved functionality in accordance with requirements for future LHC phases.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to accurately identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the first billion years of the universe's existence. To do this, we employed two cutting-edge datasets from the DESiMAL and CANDELS observational programs, which provided us with approximately 800 images of diverse galaxies spanning different time periods in cosmic history. We trained four artificial neural networks, each specialized in classifying Hubble Space Telescope images based on established morphological markers, to recognize early-type galaxies characterized by a single or multiple bulge structure, as well as galaxies with prominent disks. Through a comprehensive evaluation process, our system demonstrated exceptional performance, successfully classifying approximately 500 DESial host galaxies into either early-type Hubble Sequence types or not, while achieving similar results with a separate dataset of more than 300 galaxies from the CANDELS program. Notably, our system accurately detected the influence of a central black hole on the host galaxy's overall morphology. The successful application of our machine learning framework in identifying AGN host galaxies paves the way for its potential utilization in large-scale imaging surveys, such as the LSST, to better comprehend the relationship between massive black holes and galaxy evolution.

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations. In order to understand how these correlations affect the nucleus's bulk properties, it's necessary to study their spatial distribution, denoted by the correlation function $D(r)$, and its relationship to the kinetic energy, denoted by $E_{kin}$. Nuclear density function $\rho(r)$, as well as $E_{kin}$, are influenced by short-range correlations, characterized by $D(r)$ and manifested in fluctuations around the point of minimum interaction, denoted by $x$. The relationship between $E_{kin}$'s spectral function $A_{E_{kin}}(\epsilon)$, the single-particle energy level density $\rho_{Sp}(\epsilon)$, and $x$ was studied. Analyzing $E_{kin}$'s spectral function, characterized by $A_{E_{kin}}(\epsilon)$, allowed for the identification of its main features, associated with the single-particle energy spectrum, $x$, and high-momentum components. The single-particle energy spectrum $\rho_{Sp}(\epsilon)$ was found to be dominated by the kinetic energy spectrum $\epsilon_{Sp}$. We are studying complex scaling as an inherent component in neural networks, one that is often overlooked despite its potential to streamline network design. Our previous findings revealed that complex scaling was naturally present in Neural Arithmetic Units. This led us to investigate its general applicability to standard convolutional neural networks. By introducing complex-valued scaling as a distinct layer type, we have developed an innovative deep complex network architecture. Our models, which incorporate this new concept, exhibit improved performance on various datasets, notably the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN. Interestingly, we observed that such designs could even surpass ResNets with batch normalization after extensively searching their configurations. This novel approach offers a new paradigm for feature engineering, one that holds promise to further differentiate complex-valued deep learning from its real-valued counterpart in the future.

Our study centers around determining the amount of variability in the abundance ratios of metal-poor stars, as indicated by the [X/Fe] values, using a sample of 229 metal-poor stars with measured abundances of Fe, Ca, Si, Ti, and Na, derived from very large spectrograph emissions. By analyzing the mean abundance ratios and their standard deviations, we found that there's some level of variation among the stars with the highest [X/Fe] values, but the extent of variation can be controlled by the number of stars analyzed and the sensitivity of the lines used, until we reach Fe abundances around -2.5. However, this mean variation could be as high as 0.2 dex for Si and Na, as well as 0.15 dex for Ca and Ti, which provides some constraints on various models that explain the formation of these stars, suggesting that local variations could be significant and responsible for some, but possibly not all, of this variability. Furthermore, we found that stellar internal variety can also result in some, but possibly not all, of this abundance ratio variability. By analyzing how these elements were gathered and transported and then analyzing the abundance ratios, we found that local variations could be significant and responsible for some, but possibly not all, of this variability.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm extends the capabilities of machine learning, enabling not only predictive tasks but also robust inference and sensitivity analysis.
