Research on Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems has intensified due to their potential for controlling the communication environment and combating multi-path interference effectively. Nonetheless, the precision of channel estimation in such systems is significantly compromised by the increased risk of underutilized cyclic prefix resulting from additional cascaded RIS channels, especially at high data rates. Therefore, we propose an efficient algorithm called the Iterative Sparse Bayesian Estimation (ISBE) approach to enhance the accuracy of channel estimation in OFDM systems enhanced by RIS. By incorporating a data-driven method, ISBE effectively increases the effectiveness of underutilized cyclic prefix and achieves better performance than existing state-of-the-art techniques, such as Hybrid Deep-Sparse Bayesian Approach (HD-SBA), in various testing environments.

We are investigating a type of equality related to the work exerted on a system being observed with unsharp, non-projective measurement methods. We establish work definitions for both continuous energy measurements and those with discrete, granular energy increments. Our research demonstrates that quantum systems undergoing observations of this nature cannot be treated as a single, well-defined path in the system's history. Rather, the outcome depends on a complex interplay of factors, including the observables being measured, the uncertainty in those measurements, the energy meter's resolution, and the fluctuations in the number of energy increments considered. Notably, the greater the resolution of the energy measurement device and the smaller the energy increments being considered, the closer the system's trajectory approaches a well-defined path, albeit one with inherent randomness. Our research also reveals conditions under which an increase in system energy can be achieved by observing quantum systems, even when those observations have relatively minimal effects on the system itself.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of small deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of the elliptic operator, which results from the application of the spinor-bilinear Dirac operator to the two Killing spinors associated with the instanton.

The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and approximately 430 million reported cases worldwide. Following the initial surge in the pandemic, many nations introduced contact tracing apps to contain its spread, but raised concerns about the vast data collection that could potentially compromise users' anonymity. With the ongoing battle against the ongoing Omicron wave by the global community, which was first reported in December 2020, the issue of contact tracing also arose. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of contact tracing apps is uncertain, especially in preventing hospitalizations, a key aspect of many government policies. Furthermore, the widespread adoption of contact tracing apps has also led to a significant increase in data breaches, enabling hackers to access users' personal data. In order to gauge contact tracing app effectiveness and protect user data from cyber threats, this study aims to evaluate the security of a select few contact tracing apps in terms of data encryption, vulnerabilities, tampering, reverse engineering, malware, adware, ransomware, spyware, and phishing. The study will subsequently provide an overall safety rating based on the results. Specifically, this study will employ the latest version of Android malware analysis tools to conduct in-depth security testing of Aarogya Seva, CoCoGa, Delhi Covid, hema, Iowa Contact Tracer, PANDEMIC, PanDemiA, PanDemic, PanDemic COVID-19 Contact Tracing, Care, Tr

The central nervous system's underlying physiological processes drive a constant series of spontaneous quantum vibrations in brain neurons, which we treat as quasiparticles exhibiting nonlinear, interdependent behavior. These quasiparticles can generate correlated quasiparticle pairs that, when measured, exhibit significant interdependence only upon interacting: the more they interact, the more correlated they become. This interaction can be thought of as a form of cognitive processing. We propose that a measurable sign of cognitive interdependence - a fundamental mental phenomenon with a specific set of physical manifestations - can be detected through studies of quasiparticle correlations in brain activity. By modeling how these quasiparticle pairs behave when they're apart and when they're interacting, as well as analyzing the experimental results, our findings support the existence of a cognitive "wave function" that changes depending on whether the quasiparticles are correlated or not. This discovery suggests that the effective nonlinearity of brain behavior may arise from a fundamental nonlinearity in how the quasiparticles interact, rather than solely from the known nonlinearity in brain activity.

This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems.

A cluster of young compact asteroids connected to 39991 Iochroma undergoes a dynamics analysis in this study. Our findings show the Iochroma family's location within two adjacent three-body resonance zones - specifically 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2. This paper establishes the precise positioning of the Iochroma family within the 3J-1M-3 resonance and explores the computational challenges encountered in identifying the 5J 3S-2 resonance, which is harder to define due to the insular and dispersed nature of its members. Our research provides key insights by demonstrating that proper motion universality applies to asteroids within these resonance zones, facilitated through the accurate matching of proper motion curves between the Iochroma family and its two distinct resonance zones. To achieve this alignment, the Iochroma family's proper motion is adjusted by factors equivalent to precession rates of the resonance curves. Once the adjustment is made, the family's members are found to fit the proper motion of their respective zones. This study offers a new understanding of proper motion in outer planetary systems by establishing the connection between resonance precession and proper motion. By identifying the Iochroma family as a member of two adjacent three-body resonance zones - 3J-1M-3 and 5J 3S-2, this research contributes to the knowledge of asteroid clustering in planetary systems.

Building upon Ramanujan's well-known formula for odd zeta values, we establish a related expression using the Hurwitz zeta function. We introduce a novel integral kernel that relates to the Hurwitz zeta function and serves as an extension of the integral kernel linked to Ramanujan's identity. Additionally, we deduce various infinite families of identities comparable to Ramanujan's formula.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Recent uses of machine learning in algebraic geometry and physics are explored,  
revealing how problems in this field can be easily translated into tensor mapping,  
a concept suitable for supervised learning, as well as offering a chance to use unsupervised  
methods to analyze geometrical data. A primary aspect of this project involves understanding  
how to use geometry within machine learning, as well as how artificial intelligence can be applied  
to advance mathematical research. This discussion is featured as a chapter within the book,  
Machine learning and Algebraic Geometry, edited by A. Kasprzyk.

This paper provides a comprehensive, next-to-leading-order examination of the angular distributions in $J/\psi$ production through $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ ($J=0,1,2$) using the nonrelativistic QCD factorization method (NRQCD). The study derived numerical results for total cross sections, polarization implications, and angular distribution characteristics in $J/\psi$ production, which were then compared against experimental findings. The analysis revealed that the NRQCD results can explain the observed $\chi_{c1}$ polarization and, subsequently, the $J/\psi$ double longitudinal polarization as resulting from the convolution of spin-amplitude functions and parton distribution functions. However, this approach failed to account for certain production properties of $\chi_{c0}$.

Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 54% of users knew what PINs were used for in Signal. Enthusiast users predominantly utilized complex PINs (over 20 digits) and frequently changed them, whereas casual users used shorter PINs and changed them less often. Notably, 75% of casual users stored their PINS in the same place as their primary phone number, indicating a lack of understanding of PIN security best practices.

This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently compute the solar irradiance integral, which is used to determine the energy generated by a photovoltaic panel under varying atmospheric conditions and distinct solar spectral profiles. By adapting standard formulas, we derived quadrature rules suitable for the total solar irradiance. We applied the "discrete" approach to construct these rules, which we then tested using synthetic and real-world data. Our findings, obtained using Python and Fortran programs, demonstrated the methods' reliability and convergence, resulting in accurate results and minimal error rates for common solar spectral models when applied to real-world datasets.

The curvature formed by the Hessian matrix or its generalized Gauss-Newton approximation with regard to the loss function of a deep network holds crucial significance in understanding the training process of such networks. However, the matrix itself is impractically vast in scale, rendering it infeasible for direct computation or utilization. This work presents an innovative method of diagonalizing the curvature matrix without undergoing the O(n^3) complexity, at a reduced complexity of O(n log n). This method employs randomized algorithms.

Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects sharing the same gender draw closer together in word representations, we observe this distinct categorization in these languages. However, conventional debiasing techniques have not proven successful in eradicating this distinction. To rectify this, we discovered that selectively eliminating grammatical gender influences during the process of creating word representations is an effective strategy. As demonstrated, this deliberate removal has positive consequences for the overall quality of these representations, both within a single language and across multiple languages. While neutralizing these signals is feasible, accomplishing it in an automated manner poses significant challenges, thereby underscoring the necessity of further research in this area.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which is a more comprehensive interpretation of Furstenberg's earlier work concerning patterns on the torus. Additionally, under the assumption that the group has a certain higher-level structure, we prove that the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, and have a certain complexity structure, exhibit rigidity as well.

This study tackles the complex problem of pose estimation, particularly when the system encounters new objects. To address this challenge, we utilised recent developments in self-supervised learning techniques. Initially, we developed an approach to create a universal object model, which serves as a foundation for our method. Through our work, we found that, similar to zero-shot learning, our approach can successfully identify novel object categories without category-specific training. Moreover, we optimised our model to increase robustness by minimising reliance on specific object parts. To further evaluate our model's performance, we conducted comprehensive experiments on two publicly available datasets, utilising metrics that measure both alignment and accuracy to gauge the pose estimation's accuracy. Notably, our results demonstrate that our technique achieves comparable results to existing state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in categorising objects. To facilitate comparison and replication of our results, we will make our code and model available to the public.

Predicting short-term traffic is crucial for navigation and planning. While advanced machine learning methods, such as graph neural networks and autoencoders, effectively capture the complexities of this problem, they often overlook essential factors like location, time of day, and road structure. To address these limitations, a new approach called the Gated Attention Graph model has been developed, combining the strengths of spatial and temporal attention with a more flexible graph structure. This innovation allows the model to dynamically prioritize its inputs, focusing on the most relevant ones. Experimental results on a large-scale dataset indicate that GAG consistently outperforms other methods in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness, while also providing valuable insights into its performance.

This study presents VACA, a new family of variational graph autoencoders developed specifically for causal inference tasks where there are no hidden confounding factors, using solely observational data and causal graphs. VACA models key aspects of a Structural Causal Model (SCM) without requiring any assumptions about its underlying parameters. By leveraging these properties, it provides a versatile framework for predicting interventional outcomes and determining causal relationships between variables, which was successfully demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, showcasing improved performance for predicting intervention results and identifying causal relationships.

State-of-the-art radio interferometers such as the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) are now capable of producing massive data at speeds of hundreds of gigabits to terabits per second. This significant data rate complicates observations, especially those lasting multiple nights, by introducing varying conditions and radio frequency interference (RFI). To address these challenges, we have created the LOFAR Time Domain System (LoTDS), a comprehensive data flow system designed to automatically analyze and flag LoFAR data for contamination. Incorporating advanced flagging tools, LoTDS aims to minimize processing time and streamline science observations, including real-time observations and long-duration experiments like blind searches for fast radio bursts and gravitational wave counterparts. Additionally, we have developed multiple advanced analytical tools within LoTDS, including automated RFI detection and spectral polarization analysis. By utilizing these technologies, scientists can efficiently access and analyze various radio phenomena, such as fast radio bursts, pulsar radiation, and transient radio sources related to gamma-ray bursts and cosmic neutrino emissions.

In recent years, advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence have driven significant growth in photonics research, leading to cutting-edge photonic systems including traditional waveguides, nanoantennas, and metasurfaces. The innovative application of AI-driven methodologies empowers the design of complex photonic elements that can be fabricated with increasing precision and efficiency. This review provides an overview of AI algorithms applied to photonic design, underscoring the diverse set of problems they seek to solve, before highlighting various photonic scenarios where AI-driven methodologies excel. Furthermore, the review presents an assessment of the current limitations of AI methods in these contexts, along with future prospects for their integration in photonic research and development.

The high-risk, high-reward nature of filmmaking means predicting which movies will be profitable at the box office has become a daunting task. In an effort to minimize financial losses, major film producers and studios constantly seek a more reliable and accurate method for assessing movie potential before investing. Researchers attempting to address this issue can either analyze raw data or rely on questionnaires to gather information about the movie, its genre, demographics, length, rating, and other key factors. By analyzing data from 858 films released between 2008 and 2019, this study aims to establish which attributes have the greatest impact on a movie's revenue. Furthermore, this research will compare several machine learning models to forecast a movie's revenue based on its characteristics, and ultimately, develop a proposed framework for assessing movie potential based on their attributes. The analysis reveals that genre, age demographics, and quality of acting are significantly more important than other attributes, such as marketing expenses and movie duration. The proposed framework utilizes a combination of machine learning models, including decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting, KNN, SVM, and linear regression, to forecast a movie's revenue. The results demonstrate that gradient boosting and KNN models perform significantly better than the others, and a proposed ensemble model, which combines the predictions from these two models and linear regression, achieves an R-squared score of 0.65, representing an improvement of 0.06 in comparison to the top-performing individual model.

The energy shift poses a threat to the stability of the power grid's operation, 
which necessitates maintaining both voltage amplitude and frequency within 
safe limits. Research has primarily concentrated on the stability and 
frequency dynamics but largely overlooked voltage stability. This work aims to 
investigate the stability of simple networks through both linear stability and 
bulk analysis, specifically evaluating how the secondary control for frequency 
responds to incidents affecting voltage and reveals an unexpected effect on 
voltage dynamics while failing to address the incidents directly.

Cyber Physical Systems are transforming into cohesive units, allowing multiple systems to collaborate, giving rise to novel properties and behaviors. The automotive sector, in particular, is seeking to capitalize on this systems of systems approach, utilizing advanced technologies to create smart, interconnected vehicles. Conversely, the focus within the utility sector is on Smart Grids, with a focus on effectively managing the flow of energy across grid, network, and transport layers. Both domains, when brought together, can inform one another about the development of systems of systems. By merging these two paradigms, we can unlock new potential for urban mobility and energy management. Our approach to systems of systems in energy and road mobility (ESOR) aims to bridge the gap between automotive and smart grid technologies, providing a comprehensive overview of the dual perspective. Our objective is to reveal previously hidden interconnections between urban mobility and energy management, enabling the creation of innovative solutions that address these challenges. Through the development of ESOR, we can leverage these two complex domains to design and deploy cutting-edge solutions that merge energy and road systems.

Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in certain blazars. Predictions are made about the polarization characteristics that polarimetry missions should detect for two specific blazars: AO 0235+164 and 3C 279.

In various fields, researchers study complex landscapes representing functions from multiple fields. To distinguish between actual and spurious stability, a metric is developed to pinpoint Stokes regions, which serve as boundaries for distinguishing stable stationary points. This innovative approach is applied to recognize critical transitions characterized by abrupt changes in dynamics and morphology across identical landscapes. This framework has far-reaching implications for analyzing diverse applications in science and technology.

To develop optimal methods for identifying identical pure states with perfect accuracy using limited resources, we investigate effective strategies for analyzing multiple state copies in real-time.  These optimized methods utilize specific measurements, may be adaptive and only use each copy's local properties, resulting in the potential for quantifiable advantages over previously proposed techniques.  By examining real-time methods against optimal post-processing strategies, we reveal the advantages of timely analysis.  Our analysis also extends to the scenario where identification accuracy is compromised, allowing us to identify parameters yielding a predefined probability of error.  Additionally, we explore the trade-offs between measurement probability, state discrimination accuracy, and processing speed in real-time methods.

Baryon creation is investigated using a quantized fragmentation model based on QCD strings. Following initial QCD principles, baryons are formed through the breakup of QCD strings. A quantized fragmentation model is employed, where partons and baryons form by linking and unlinking strings. With the quantities involved being numerically well-defined, this approach allows for a clear understanding of QCD's underlying mechanism for baryon production. Using data on proton and lambda particle spectra from RHIC's STAR and PHENIX collaborations, we analyze various key aspects. These include fragmentation functions, baryon yields, rapidity distributions, transverse momenta, polarizations, and spin-isospin properties. Our results show significant agreement with experimental data.
