As smart cities expand, they generate an increased need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, human errors inevitably occur during this process.  To address these issues, we introduce CitySpec, an innovative AI-powered system for demand classification and error detection, and for automatically generating high-quality, precise specifications in a standard format.  CitySpec consists of three main components: a demand classification module that utilizes pre-trained models to quickly identify demand types; a error detection module that leverages multiple, sophisticated NLP techniques to pinpoint mistakes; and a specification generation module that is grounded in organizational knowledge guidelines.  To evaluate CitySpec's performance, we conducted an experiment comparing its performance to that of humans and existing AI systems, demonstrating its capabilities to enhance quality and speed without requiring human input.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By incorporating inverse gate implementations, noise levels are diminished and the robustness of quantum states is improved, particularly for quantum computers with limited coherence times. Applying this noise mitigation strategy, we successfully eliminate the need for classical post-processing to achieve precise expectation values, and as such, it serves as an error prevention measure rather than a correction mechanism. Our study examines the application of this approach to basic quantum algorithms such as quantum gradient measurements and imaginary-time evolution. Furthermore, we analyze its practical implementation on realistic quantum hardware. Experimental results, conducted on a superconducting quantum processor, demonstrate the substantial error reduction achieved by incorporating the noise-mitigation strategy, resulting in a substantial acceleration in simulation speed. This advancement holds promise to enhance the performance of complex quantum algorithms like quantum Monte Carlo and quantum natural language processing.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not preserve the order, but in the case of regular categories this property holds true. The sum of partial orders in a regular category is preserved when the category's operations satisfy regularity conditions, leading to the definition of the suprema of partial orders in such categories, which are the limits of suprema of partial orders in subcategories. In the case of the suprema of partial orders in subcategories being discrete (containing only single elements), the category itself becomes a discrete category. Conversely, a category is discrete if and only if it satisfies a specific condition of preserving discrete objects. In the case of presheaves in $\mathbb E$, the suprema of partial orders in subcategories are preserved when the suprema of partial orders in subcategories are discrete (containing only single elements), which leads to the definition of the discrete suprema of partial orders in such categories, which are the limits of discrete suprema of partial orders in subcategories. In the case of the suprema of partial orders in subcategories being discrete (containing only single elements), the suprema of discrete partial orders in such categories are discrete (containing only single elements), which leads to the definition of the suprema of discrete partial orders in such categories, which are discrete (containing only single elements).

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is employed to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. By pre-training with randomly sampled image-text pairs, CLIP fails to pinpoint the optimal visual and textual features necessary for matching. As a result, it compromises the quality of visual-text alignment, particularly in low-frequency features, resulting in diminished performance in downstream tasks. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel approach called Focal Contrastive Pre-training (FCPT). To encourage the model to focus on distinguishing variable frequency visual-text features, we employ different dimensionality sizes for image and text embeddings. Our findings indicate that FCPT yields better performance compared to the baseline CLIP model in image classification, object detection, and visual recognition tasks. Notably, our model achieves a Top-1 accuracy of 69.9% on the ImageNet dataset while utilizing significantly fewer parameters compared to the original CLIP.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting framework, we extend it to nonsymmetric matrices, pioneering this approach for general matrix classes. This innovation has the potential to accelerate error reduction in computational models across various fields, including chemistry, physics, and other areas of science, philosophy, and engineering. Through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the shifted matrix method yields a minimum error lower limit. While the method doesn't guarantee an error decrease at each shift, our findings reveal that certain data scenarios facilitate sustained error reduction. One such scenario involves iterative shift calculations, fueled by matrix multiplication or factorization, including the application of iterative sparse matrix multiplication. To validate the theoretical predictions, we perform numerical experiments, showcasing the method's ability to make progress in systems challenging to tackle via the underlying Monte Carlo method.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. In the process, we compute the Mackey functors for $\underline{\pi}_{k\rho} H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's construction, we derive a generalization of a previously established theorem regarding the rationality of Hilbert functions in equidimensional excellent local rings. Furthermore, we analyze the connection between the $F$-splitting ratio and the $F$-rationality of monomial ideals in specific local rings, also examining instances where these ratios do not dictate $F$-rationality.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is gaining significant attention. 3D medical volume analysis requires image data with standardized formats, which DICOM provides.  The standardization of training machine learning algorithms using DICOM enables better communication and promotes open data policies, which is essential for training these algorithms.  The paper discusses model training, validation, and evaluation methods for medical image analysis tasks, highlighting tools and their advantages, especially for training and evaluating deep learning-based models.  It includes code examples to facilitate task implementation and emphasizes the importance of reproducibility in medical image analysis.  The paper also provides directions for future research in this area.  The paper and its accompanying repository are at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolbox.  The repository contains code at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxCode.  A community discussion is at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxDiscuss.  An animated tutorial is at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxAnimated.  A paper summarizing animated content is at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxPaperAnimated.  A GitHub version of this text is at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxVersioned.  A GitHub version of the author list is at https://tinyurl.com/mrlToolboxVersionedAuthors.

We present a derivation of Noether's first theorem from the inside out, starting with a Hamiltonian action on a codimension-one slice in spacetime and continuing to the asymptotic region, where we establish a relationship between charge and Noether current in relation to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. We explore the implications of this approach for black holes and consider a simple example based on the Schwarzschild black hole. Next, we investigate a more complex case involving diffeomorphism-invariant theories of gravity and a simple soliton solution. Finally, we apply our method to a soliton solution of Einstein-Hilbert action, demonstrating that the charge associated with surface gravity matches the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy.

In recent times, deep learning models have been effectively utilized for categorizing DNA sequences based on various tasks. A major challenge often arises due to the lengthy and variable nature of these DNA sequences. In our current research, a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder model is applied in an unsupervised manner to derive a standardized, fixed-dimensional latent representation for long and variable DNA sequences. The resulting latent representation achieved notable success in enhancing the classification of similar DNA sequences with low similarity scores, while also improving the detection of distant sequence relationships. The improved quality of the latent representation is attributed to its ability to retain standard sequence alignment information. Furthermore, we observed that the intermediate representations extracted along the latent representation pathway demonstrate diverse expertise in different tasks. Building upon this, we developed a hybrid model that combines the standard sequence identity information with high-level sequence features to optimize the classification of distant sequence pairs, yielding superior results compared to the baseline models. The proposed model's effectiveness is substantiated by successful application in three DNA classification tasks, namely distant sequence similarity and homology assessment, and functional sequence classification, thereby showcasing its potential as a general-purpose DNA representation learning framework.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep understanding of the effects of surface termination, essential for accurately diagnosing phase transitions and properly characterizing film properties.  Our research involved conducting density functional theory calculations on (001) and (111) surface terminations of V$_2$O$_3$ to analyze metal-insulator transition phenomena.  Results indicated that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films is influenced by surface termination, with double layer-like sp-bandings near the Fermi level observed in (001) surface terminations but not in (111) surface terminations.  Also, (111) surface terminations exhibited an insulating state with localized t$_{2g}$ orbitals and a sp-band, whereas (001) surface terminations displayed an insulating state with a sp-band formed from the surface state.  Our research suggests that the presence of sp-band reveals a 2D character in (001) surface terminations but a 2D character is absent in (111) surface terminations.  Moreover, (111) surface terminations displayed an insulating state with a sp-band, illustrating a quasi-two-dimensional characteristic.  Our research implies that surface termination significantly affects the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter providing a reason why Clebsch canonization is called that. Moreover, we established that any dynamically equivalent dual momentum maps arise from this canonization process. Finally, we discuss two key implications of our results: (a) any Lie-Poisson system with a dual momentum map can be re-expressed as an integrable Hamiltonian system when it possesses two level sets of Casimirs; and (b) such systems are also integrable when they have a dual momentum map and possess an $SU(2)$ invariant coadjoint orbit.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet AnomalyFinder in 2018-2019, resulting in 9 newly identified and 8 previously known planets, bringing the total to 17 planets during this two-year period. Out of these 17 planets, 8 have a known mass ratio, along with their own mass. This new information enhances our understanding of the exoplanet mass-ratio distribution, particularly in the medium and high mass ratios. Following a detailed statistical examination, the researchers found that the distribution of planets with a mass ratio greater than 0.1 is significantly non-uniform, indicating a deficiency in planets with a mass ratio between 0.1 and 0.3. Furthermore, the researchers found that the distribution of binary stellar companions within the lens is consistent in the mass range where the Galactic distribution of the conjugate field is typically sampled. However, the researchers noticed an imbalance in the lens mass range where the Galactic distribution of the conjugate field is typically sampled, and the mass ratio distribution of planets with a mass ratio greater than 0.1 is significantly non-uniform, indicating a deficiency in planets with a mass ratio between 0.1 and 0.3.

To address the challenges posed by the inherent nonlinearity and structure of hyperbolic conservation laws, a method is developed for deriving first-order conditions for optimal control, using the example of the canonical case of quintic scalar conservation laws. This derivation leverages an entropy-entropy production framework, similar to those employed for optimal transport and variational assimilation. Next, the method is extended to the more prevalent situation of systems of conservation laws, for which first-order conditions are identified under a perturbative approximation. It is demonstrated that the conditions for the scalar case are retrievable from these for the system. These first-order conditions are incorporated into a perturbative perturbation recovery method. This method, similar to those used for inverse problems, employs the first-order conditions to mitigate the effects of perturbations in both the solution and control. This approach is showcased on a quintic scalar example and a Lorenz system-based example, both subject to perturbations.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit losses and align their lending policies, thereby contributing to sustainable financial growth. Given the new loans disbursed every month, banks are in constant need of updated information to make informed decisions, specifically to determine NPLs and evaluate clients' creditworthiness. This research focuses on predicting NPLs for new loans in the context of retail lending, with an emphasis on insights rather than outcomes. We introduce a novel regression framework, 'Credit Risk Evaluation through Loan Analysis,' designed to disentangle time-varying factors influencing NPLs predictions. By applying this model to retail NPL data in India, we uncover key insights on factors like loan amount, client characteristics, product type, and NPL status, revealing that factors such as client age, employment, and loan amount hold more significance than collateral or loan purpose. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that time-varying fluctuations in loan defaults are linked to macroeconomic conditions, with significant NPL variations observed during economic downturns, including the demonetization and COVID-19 shocks. However, our results show an unexpected increase in NPLs during the demonetization period, with initial increases in NPLs in December 2016, contrasting the anticipated effect. Similarly, our NPLs predictions failed to reflect the anticipated impact of the COVID-19 shock in April 2020, with an initially elevated NPL rate, although it later declined

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analogue, are crucial in the field of Hodge theory. In a separate context, Macdonald posed conjectures in the realm of $q$-analogues, which were later solidified by Andersén-Winckler. Our purpose is to prove, in a more general setting, the combinatorial interpretations provided by Guay-Paquet, in terms of $q$-Hukuhara-Sugiura sums, specifically for Dyck paths that adhere to particular criteria. This broader interpretation also applies to related concepts such as non-attacking rooks, providing an alternative proof to Guay-Paquet's findings for this subject.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), which incorporates a orientation-aware mechanism to learn representation extraction. By utilizing a consistent set of filters across different orientations, OCNs can achieve superior performance on image recognition tasks while maintaining efficiency and training complexity similar to that of standard DCNNs. Our results demonstrate improved performance over state-of-the-art methods containing rotation networks on various benchmark datasets, and highlight the effectiveness of our model in achieving orientation invariance and learning meaningful image features.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the spectral isolation technique pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we derive comparisons of the elliptic aspects of the involved relative trace formulas, ultimately yielding novel outcomes that extend Waldspurger's theorem to the scenario where n is not equal to 1.

We develop a systematic method to study the impact of mass on the pole mass in comparison to short-distance masses like the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ mass for a heavy quark, using QCD with a flavor dependent kernel. Our method involves an iterative process where each step directly applies renormalization group techniques to remove mass dependence from the remaining scale, thus enabling the use of scale choices beyond traditional $n$- and $\bar{n}$ values. By integrating our method with methods like the extended renormalization group technique and soft-collimation technique, we derive a method to compute the relationship between pole mass and short-distance masses with a flavor number of two. Furthermore, we use this relation to study the pole mass ambiguity for a single flavor in detail. For a flavor number of two, we compute the pole mass of the $b$ and $c$ quarks and an approximate value of the pole mass of the $t$ quark with $\alpha_s(M_Z) = 0.118$.

Consider a graph $G$ and let's denote the set of its edges as $E$. A specific edge coloring called the $R$-sequential $t$-coloring occurs when each edge $e = \{v, w\}$ in $E$ is assigned a color $\sigma(e)$ based on the rotation order of the vertices $v$ and $w$ around the rooted subtree $T$ of $G$. A particular challenge arises in proving the existence of $R$-sequential $t$-colorings for certain graph structures.

We have developed a new approach for proving the existence of $R$-sequential $t$-colorings in highly connected graph structures. By using this method, we have successfully demonstrated the existence of $R$-sequential $t$-colorings in the Cayley trees $T_{n}$ for any $n \geq 4p-3$.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome is founded on a broader comparison principle for the growth of solutions to a type of differential equation without terms, and a model operator approach.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces inaccurate results. Computed Tomography
scans can provide valuable assistance with COVID-19 diagnosis, although they expose
patients to a significant amount of radiation, which can be detrimental to those
requiring multiple scans. To address this issue, we studied low-dose and ultra-low-
dose scan protocols, which minimize radiation levels while maintaining image
quality suitable for diagnostic purposes. Nevertheless, these scans pose a challenge
for COVID-19 diagnosis, particularly in areas with limited data availability. To
overcome this limitation, we employed a unsupervised anomaly detection technique
that can produce reliable results with limited data. The method involves using
self-supervised techniques like Contrastive Learning and transfer learning based on
homogeneous classification models to classify lung lesions in low-quality and
low-dose CT scans. The proposed method's performance was evaluated using five
datasets, including Chexpert, COVID-Chest, CoronaNet, RSNA-Pneumonia, and
Zhang et al., which are commonly used in diagnostic image applications. The
results indicate that the method's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art
unsupervised diagnostic techniques, making it a reliable option for COVID-19
diagnosis in patients with normal chest anatomy.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupancy pattern to minimize interference while maximizing service capabilities and service availability is critical. This study introduces a novel space occupancy model called "S" and utilizes the maximum packing problem for circles to derive a solution framework. By transforming the problem into a two-player game, where one player arranges satellites in the most space-efficient manner and the second player arrains them in a power-least fashion, the proposed model identifies the optimal combination of these two patterns. Furthermore, the study introduces a new algorithm, the "S" pattern, in addition to existing ones, such as the Martin's and Sugimoto's patterns. Consequently, this research is a initial step towards developing an optimization method for the given problem.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created, which allows for intricate quad configurations due to its unstructured layout. Subsequently, we build upon this foundation with a flexible T-mesh structure, which can be manipulated to optimize the mesh topology by assigning varying lengths to its arcs. Utilizing advanced optimization techniques in the form of integer linear programming, we efficiently resolve the mesh simplification process while adhering to intricate quad configurations. Ultimately, we derive high-order quadrilateral meshes that prioritize geometric complexity and compatibility while exhibiting exceptional alignment with curved boundaries, resulting in robust and accurate analytical results in various applications, including numerical weather prediction, as demonstrated by our tests with the CHARACTERS framework and the Weather Research Forecast code.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation is often evaluated using a hypothesis test, resulting in a p-value. Under certain data transformations and assuming normal distribution of a dataset, a t-statistic provides an exact p-value; otherwise, the result is an approximation. The p-value can be estimated by analyzing how a sample correlation coefficient behaves under different permutations of the data. Although such estimates may rely on approximations of distribution moments, an inductive approach in this paper offers a formula to compute exact moments under specific data assumptions, facilitating improved estimates of p-values and correlation coefficients. The formula relies on a decomposition of the sample correlation metric into components that can be computed via sum operations, along with accounting for edge covariation effects. The researchers conducted a small experiment to assess the effectiveness of this method.

We outline the framework for a quantum S-matrix framework aimed at tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. This approach draws inspiration from the findings of \cite{Vallejo:2020qer}, which demonstrated that constructing an operable quantum S-matrix in $\lambda\Phi^3$ relies on the method of expansion by elimination. Our proposal suggests that employing this technique to address two-body scattering in general relativity will involve employing methods reminiscent of soft-collinear perturbation theory.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) in three dimensions. This research contributes new findings by showing that under specific conditions, a combination of two novel approaches - a non-local internal observer-based control in two dimensions and a non-local hybrid strategy in three dimensions - can establish the exponential stability of the model. Furthermore, our study provides an alternative proof of exponential stability for the simplified system without external influence in three dimensions that has been previously demonstrated by other authors. This simplified system without external influence in three dimensions that has been previously demonstrated by other authors. This research contributes new findings by showing that the finite dimensional feedback control is effective when the dimension is greater than or equal to three. This research contributes new findings by showing that the finite dimensional feedback control is effective when the dimension is greater than or equal to three.

Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by providing 
word definitions. Conventional dictionaries have a structured format with 
existing word lists and definitions. In contrast, a new generative dictionary 
is proposed, which is equipped with a generative model that dynamically 
generates definitions based on the words being learned. A key advantage of 
this generative dictionary is its ability to expand its word list and definition 
collections as more words are encountered. The dictionary's generative model is 
trained using existing large corpora of written text available online. The 
generative dictionary's efficacy in enhancing vocabulary growth was validated 
through experiments with learners who used this dictionary in conjunction with 
existing definitions to learn new words.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, thus falling short in guaranteeing the accuracy of generated explanations.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be produced more efficiently by replacing traditional lead materials with a novel alternative, specifically using InAs quantum wells as the superconducting channel material. However, the implementation of InAs quantum wells is hindered by reduced electron mobility caused by irregular surface patterns. In this study, the surface irregularities are investigated and the electron mobility is measured in relation to these irregularities. Furthermore, the surface irregularities are linked to the formation of an insulating layer that forms at room temperature. Interestingly, a similar layer does not contribute to the weakening of superconductivity in the InAs quantum wells, as demonstrated by the preservation of supercurrent even at temperatures as low as 1 K.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are necessary for the reliable development of learning algorithms, although such assumptions might not accurately represent real-world conditions. To address this challenge, we investigate the capabilities of non-parametric learning methods that rely on local membership queries (LMQs) to classify complex datasets. Our study introduces robust theories for LMQ-based learning that extend beyond independent and identically distributed data sets, encompassing more general applications, including those involving ergodic processes. Additionally, we develop an almost optimal test to verify when a dataset generated by a stochastic process meets the required condition of being robust. Our analysis further highlights key differences between LMQs and other examination methods. Lastly, we outline potential avenues for expanding our findings to cover more complex scenarios.

Our previous research demonstrated that L/U-CoLT matrices possess key characteristics of permutation matrices, enabling efficient division and multiplication operations in linear time complexity. This study builds upon those findings, applying L/U-CoLT to solve certain sparse matrix problems, such as solving tridiagonal systems, inversion of certain sparse matrices, and evaluating Toeplitz-based circulant matrices. In the process, it proves that L/U-CoLT can perform additional sparse matrix operations in linear time.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk and a nearby protoplanetary disk, presents an opportunity to explore variability in the photoegodic process and potential exoplanet habitability. AU Mic, and especially its tidal regions, exhibit significant X-ray activity, which research has recently studied using multiple observations from XMM-Newton. These observations revealed 16 distinct X-ray bursts, 6 of which were accompanied by super-ELODAs (Extended Large Project -- Exo-Disk) data, yielding a total of 42 hours of UV and X-ray emission monitoring. The analysis of these data allowed for a thorough examination of AU Mic's corona and its ultraviolet and X-ray emission mechanisms. The presence of these high-energy forms of radiation can impact exoplanets in the system, including those within its debris disk and tidal regions, and may lead to significant atmospheric loss in certain scenarios. Notably, the total integrated X-ray energy delivered to AU Mic's exoplanets is expected to be much higher than what has been observed so far, indicating a potential for increased photoegodic effects and potential habitability constraints on these exoplanets.

We develop an approximation for the frictional effect on radiation loss experienced by charged particles moving through a medium with mechanical friction. Introducing the medium's friction affects the electric field of the particle in such a way that it is proportional to the transverse component of the velocity, enabling comparison with existing microtron theory. According to our findings, the rate of radiation loss can be expressed in terms of the Larmor radius, velocity, and friction coefficient, indicating that the frictional effect on radiation loss increases as the particle's velocity approaches the speed of light. Furthermore, the radiation loss in the narrowest part of the acceleration cycle is determined by the frictional effect and, at high particle velocities, the frictional effect on radiation loss is similar to that predicted by energy loss due to electric field damping.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, operating under conditions of disparate group sizes. This new framework develops asymptotic theory and relevant test statistics for assessing the effectiveness of the nearest neighbor classification method when encountering significantly uneven group sizes. This theory validates a generalized statistic that performs well even when faced with extreme uneven group sizes, and it suggests a relevant modification that handles the nearest neighbor classification method specifically. This relevant modification is shown to be a "majority rule" method when the nearest neighbor classification method performs poorly in uneven group sizes scenarios. This theory also addresses the Bayesian perspective on nearest neighbor classification, a topic that has been largely neglected in the field to date.

We employ photometric methods to derive the luminosity function of a quasar population observed by the Panoramic Survey Digital Sky Explorer, which specifically targets luminous quasars defined as having a bolometric luminosity greater than 40 billion solar units. This population is present in a three-dimensional space with specifications up to a redshift of 4.5. At the heart of our analysis lies the assumption that the distribution of a quasar's intrinsic luminosity follows a power-law model. In doing so, we have calculated the total density of these quasars and have used our results to estimate the overall density at different redshift values. Our results match those of other studies in terms of quasar density, indicating that the density pattern remains consistent at various redshift values. Additionally, we have calculated the relationship between the number of quasars and their luminosity at different redshift values. In particular, we have established the one-eighth magnitude luminosity values at different redshift values as $4.25\pm0.15$, $3.83\pm0.19$, $3.28\pm0.24$, $2.98\pm0.27$, and $2.74\pm0.32$ with one standard deviation respectively.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional current conductance measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy levels. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of Majorana modes or other unconventional quasiparticles.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in conservation laws. We demonstrate, under certain conditions, that such shockwaves will not diverge when initial distances become vanishingly small. This study reinforces and expands previous findings by Majda and McDonough. Our work promotes the inclusion of relevant examples in textbooks to better illustrate conservation law behavior.

We explore novel view generation for outdoor view synthesis, a challenging problem due to its inherently extrapolative nature - generating novel perspectives from few reference images of complex scenes. Notably, traditional unsupervised generative adversarial networks struggle with this task, producing significant discrepancies between the generated data and real images. In response to this limitation, researchers have resorted to more complex probabilistic networks. In contrast, we adapt and implement \textit{image-conditioned diffusion models}, a relatively simple yet robust approach established for more straightforward view-synthesis applications. When applied to the more demanding long-range scene extrapolation task, the results demonstrate a notable improvement over established \textit{diffusion models} and \textit{GAN-based methods}. Furthermore, the data-free nature of \textit{image-conditioned diffusion models} facilitates their adaptability to various datasets without necessitating multiple training sessions. Our dataset, realmix, comprising a diverse set of datasets, enables a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art view-synthesis techniques in the context of long-range scene extrapolation. The corresponding code and dataset have been made publicly available.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, discovering similar relationships at a larger scale is more challenging. We've made a significant discovery, revealing that specific patterns in complex networks where agents interact with multiple neighbors do indeed exist and can be widespread in various networks. These patterns, which describe how agents transition between states over time, can be used to create predictive models for those systems and to guide control and policy-making approaches. We've also found that the relationships between network structure and dynamic patterns, while not easily readable, can be understood at a more detailed level, providing insights into the workings of these complex systems.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated around a fiber with a periodic annular groove. The model reveals that slip leads to increased rates of perturbation growth in any imbalanced film segment. Furthermore, it is found that slight differences in film thickness can result in significant nonlinear effects, and the model provides explicit calculations of these nonlinear terms. The findings suggest that the impact of liquid-solid slip on perturbation growth could lead to a reduction in stability in film segments with minimal thickness. The model's predictions are such that the maximum stability threshold is expected to decrease as slip coefficients increase.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics in the group of diffeomorphisms via $\alpha$-pre-Lipschitz conditions. We establish a criterion for and provide an example of differential equations where solutions with bounded Lipschitz stability are not weakly monotone.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled movement to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. Two human evaluators measured and compared the coronal image deformity angles acquired from both robotic and manual scans. The results showed that robotic scanning yielded comparable deformity angle estimates to manual scanning, with values averaging 26.8 degrees for both methods. Furthermore, the difference in angles between robotic and manual scans was minimal, averaging only 1.4 degrees. This method demonstrates potential as a reliable alternative to traditional scoliosis assessments, particularly for individuals unable to stand upright or who require continuous monitoring.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team examined the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks, as well as those employing transfer learning with BERT models, all of which utilized a shared task dataset. Key findings revealed that BERT-based models excelled in tasks related to hate speech detection and offensive language identification, whereas tasks requiring more precise categorization of hate speech subtypes proved challenging for all models.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption on constrained devices such as smartphones and AR/VR devices. This study suggests that a key issue with current MIMO frameworks lies in how they allow subnetworks to learn and share features. In response, we introduce an innovative 'unmixing' procedure for MIMO networks to facilitate shared feature learning among subnetworks. Our preliminary results demonstrate the efficacy of this modification, yielding feature sharing and better performance in smaller network configurations.

This analysis examines the key challenges and opportunities within Document Image Analysis, a subfield of pattern recognition and computer vision that focuses on extracting information from documents. The main tasks encompass text detection, segmentation, and recognition, in addition to semantic segmentation, identification, and other analytical tasks. The primary objectives of these tasks involve accurately generating masks or boxes to describe visual objects and assigning categories or extracting data from visual content. The primary methods for achieving these objectives include supervised learning approaches, such as classic pattern recognition systems, and unsupervised learning techniques. The central challenge involves efficiently extracting relevant information from complex visual content, and solving this problem requires significant datasets, advanced models, and high-quality annotations. The main technological hurdles include overcoming issues in low-quality images and developing scalable design frameworks. The main applications, including document design, information extraction, and search, involve diverse objectives such as identifying and filtering visual content, and extracting data from it. The central challenge involves striking a balance between capturing content and filtering it, and solving this problem requires a deeper understanding of the goals and objectives of IAD. The key challenges and opportunities vary widely depending on the specific task at hand, and the most pressing issues and opportunities are identified and summarized.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are ill-suited for tasks such as drilling and grinding, with positional inaccuracies often totaling several millimeters. Even after equipping these robots with precision improvement tools like calibration and feed-forward filtering, positions are generally determined to within a margin of a few hundred microns. Consequently, a need exists to tackle the sources of inaccuracy mentioned above by proposing a novel method of dynamics modeling. The proposed method, based on the rigid-body model, utilizes measurements from a six-axis force-torque sensor, and is accompanied by an accompanying experimental study that evaluates its performance in practical settings. Results indicate that the proposed model is able to mitigate the inaccuracy issues mentioned earlier, and enable robots to meet the required accuracy for machining tasks based on their physical dimensions and the data from the force-torque sensor. Specifically, a significant 75% reduction in the radius of uncertainty associated with the end-effector's position was observed when using the proposed dynamics model as opposed to a static model. Moreover, it was found that the proposed method consistently provides more precise estimates than other comparable methods of dynamics modeling.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily focused on later-life influences, overlooking the importance of early-life experiences and societal and economic factors. This research employs a sophisticated modeling approach in a semi-parametric framework to examine how the interaction between early-life health issues, socioeconomic status, and other societal and economic factors impact a person's future health trajectory. The analysis reveals significant connections between early-life health problems, lower income, and education levels, as well as other societal and economic factors, and a person's future health trajectory. The results indicate that certain individual, societal, and economic factors can anticipate future health problems, as shown by the substantial evidence supporting the relationship between early-life experiences and later-life chronic disease risks, as well as the correlation between economic status, education levels, and lags of these factors with future health problems, as demonstrated in various tests of time. The research highlights the importance of early-life experiences and long-term, widespread societal and economic dynamics in shaping a person's future health trajectory, and this future is often determined before they reach middle age. The findings also demonstrate that both macroeconomic and societal dynamics as well as individual socioeconomic factors can influence a person's future health, as indicated by the significant lag structures in the coefficient patterns in these situations.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decrease rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at multiple points to estimate integrals, which has been adapted and optimized for the specific needs of electronic structure calculations involving molecules with multiple atoms. Key aspects of this method include determining the optimal number and location of grids, developing a partitioning scheme that accurately accounts for atomic shapes, and implementing efficient algorithms to evaluate the associated integrals. By applying these principles, it is possible to achieve high accuracy and performance while evaluating the electronic properties of large complex molecules.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertex pair, there exists a set member that is closest to one of the vertices over all other set members. The problem of finding a minimum-sized resolving set of a graph, known as the metric dimension problem, has been a well-studied challenge. The problem has been explored for chordal graphs, specifically for a subclass known as loop-free chordal graphs. A new upper bound was established for the metric dimension of loop-free chordal graphs, based on a related property of their clique-cut-set partitions. Such partitions describe the minimal subsets needed to cover all cliques in a graph. The bound expresses the metric dimension as at most one plus the size of the smallest such partition. The proof relies on analyzing a related hypergraph, known as the rank hypergraph, whose rank represents the size of the smallest clique-cut-set partition. A new algorithm was also introduced to find these smallest partitions in a reasonable amount of computational time, as tested on a collection of 70301 chordal graphs with up to 50 vertices. The analysis showed that the algorithm's time complexity grows exponentially with the size of the graph, but can consistently identify small metric dimensions in these graphs. The results suggest that loop-free chordal graphs with a large number of vertices tend to have consistent and small metric dimensions. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm "hothouse" environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, distinguishing them from modern and future expected climates characterized by increased precipitation and potential water loss through evaporation and condensation processes. The investigation of atmospheric water cycles in these warm climates is necessary for understanding their dynamics and responding to future climate changes. The analysis of atmospheric water flow in steady and time-varying conditions was conducted by solving the mass transport equation with sources and sinks in two-dimensional Cartesian space using standard methods.
Results from two models with integrated water vapor and temperature profiles indicate that, in a stable and unstable atmosphere with vertical heat absorption, temperature-dependent water loss results in altered atmospheric water distribution and water supply to the ground, leading to increased precipitation in advanced regimes. The findings also show that, in a stable and unstable atmosphere with external heat absorption, increased evaporation results in altered atmospheric water distribution and water supply to the ground, leading to decreased precipitation in all significant "hothouse" scenarios.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a large, clean dataset of properly annotated images. Unfortunately, the annotation process is often marred by noise, which negatively impacts classification outcomes. To address this issue, we propose an innovative approach utilizing knowledge-driven information to correct the errors in image labels. Initially, we identify high-error instances based on their deviation from expected outcomes and the consistency of surrounding labels. Subsequently, we employ a sequence of shallow models to generate predictive results from these images. Finally, we adjust the image labels using adversarial training techniques to minimize instance errors. Through experimental evaluation on two diverse medical image datasets, we demonstrate that our method achieves error correction while maintaining model interpretability. Moreover, the corrected image labels produce a notable increase in model performance.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function $f$ defined within this cube as part of the set of continuous functions in $C(Q_n)$. The norm of the function can be calculated as the maximum absolute value it achieves within the cube. The problem seeks to establish whether there exists a function $g$ within $C(Q_n)$ and an integer $k$ such that $g(x)$ equals $k$ throughout the cube $Q_n$, with the function's norm measured in a specified manner. This function $g$ can be seen as analogous to a quantized function in digital signal processing. The main results derive an upper bound on the norm of the function $g$ in terms of a real constant and the dimension $n$. The function's construction that leads to this bound involves an auxiliary cube $Q_{n-1}$ within $Q_n$ and a function $g'$ in $C(Q_{n-1})$ that varies continuously between two values. This function $g'$ is in turn constructed from two further functions $g''$ and $g'''$, with $g''$ taking the constant value $1/2$ in $Q_n$, and $g'$ in turn depending on a saw-tooth function $g$$$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover matrix, the evolution matrix of the Grover walk on a graph G, and the heat kernel, the transition matrix for random walks on G. Since the Grover matrix and heat kernel are generally not invertible, we reformulate the CRW in terms of the Grover matrix alone for an arbitrary graph G. This approach is exemplified in the cases of cycle graphs and hypercubes.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a specified evaluation depth. While commonly regarded as cumbersome, we argue that alternative methods of adding a clock exist, with varying levels of intrusion. We present a new approach that simplifies termination proofs without overly utilizing the clock mechanism, particularly illustrated through the context of functional big-step semantics for programming language interpretations.

The accuracy of models predicting the spatial arrangement of turbulent motions in turbulent flows is analyzed by comparing against direct numerical simulations of a specific type of flow. This investigation focuses on a particular type of flow, which is the most challenging to accurately simulate using turbulent flow simulations, and it examines two different methods of calculating drag in turbulent flows. The models evaluated included those based on simple drag predictions and those based on a more complex drag prediction method. The results showed a significant discrepancy between the accuracy of models when considering only the surface of the flow, and those accuracy rates increased when adjusting the model to match the characteristics of the flow. The analysis found that a significant portion of discrepancies in simulations of turbulent flows could be attributed to assumptions regarding the characteristics of turbulent motions in realistic turbulent flow conditions. The results also indicated that certain key factors, such as the characteristics of turbulent motions and how they are accounted for in simulations, play a significant role in determining the accuracy rates of models. The investigation further found a significant correlation existing between the characteristics of turbulent motions and how they are simulated, which in turn affects the accuracy rates of models. The results suggest that further research is needed to refine the models, which rely on inaccurate estimates of turbulent motion characteristics in realistic turbulent flow conditions.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual equations whose solutions manifest as the limiting solitons that achieve this bound. The lower bound on energy, known as the Bogomol'nyi bound, exhibits proportionality to the topological charge of the Skyrme field, thereby being quantized. Conversely, the overall magnetic flux is unrelated to any derivative of the Skyrme field, thus exhibiting gauge invariance.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model with a fixed point at the origin and an orbital magnetic field, we analyze the drift motion of monopoles in the three-dimensional Euclidean space based on the winding numbers around a point. The motion is described using the adjoint representation of the Euclidean SL(3,ℝ) group. Upon transforming to a new coordinate system, the drift motion is found to follow specific quadratic equations of state, thereby classifying monopole configurations in the magnetic field into four distinct bands. These configurations can exhibit symmetry either of 2-fold rotation or inversion, but not necessarily both. Consequently, they may display distinct band structures, with band touching occurring in certain configurations and preventing it in others. As a result, an orbital magnetic field can transform a Weyl semimetal with an odd number of monopoles into a chiral topological insulator, whereas a magnetic field with a specific orientation can convert a chiral topological insulator into a Weyl semimetal. Additionally, we found that an orbital magnetic field can transform a Weyl semimetal with an odd number of monopoles (all of the same chirality) into a chiral topological insulator coexisting with an electric field.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design, consisting of a hybrid silicon nanoring coupled with a localised assembly of quantum dots, which together constitute an efficient source of unidirectional photons when subjected to optical stimulation. The structure features a narrow, ring-shaped silicon component, 200 nm in diameter and 40 nm thick, supported by a silicon-on-insulator substrate, beneath which there's an array of three groups of three self-assembled InAs quantum dots arranged in a triangular formation. Our comprehensive simulation study utilises the finite-different time-domain method to evaluate the interaction between a dotted surface plasmon polariton mode and emitted light from the quantum dots in response to left-hand circularly polarised resonance. By strategically positioning the quantum dots directly beneath the nanoantenna, we've discovered a resonance mode that enhances the absorption of constituting materials by eight times, leading to the efficient emission of photons with a directed propagation direction. The achieved output power exceeds the spontaneous emission limitation by silicon nanophotonics, showcasing the effectiveness of this novel design in transforming absorbed light into directed photons.

Numerical simulations of strongly nonlinear mechanical properties of glassy solids, including polymeric amorphous materials, provide empirical evidence for a plasticity model based on mesoscopic deformations. The results reveal that a particular threshold of strain triggers profound microscopic rearrangements within these materials, resulting in two distinct types of screening and the emergence of a particular type of dynamics. The existence of these mechanisms leads to the development of a framework describing plastic flow in terms of underlying structural changes, where the material's microframesets undergo continuous recrystallization, ultimately producing a characteristic plastic flow pattern.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top/cavity and decoration at the hole positions for manganese-decorated hexagonal boron nitride systems. Manganese decoration at the hole position results in a substantially increased Hubbard parameter of around 1.75 eV, which is closely aligned with the value observed in manganese-doped silicene systems. This suggests that hexagonal boron nitride provides an alternative to metallic substrates, or other manganese monolayers, with weaker interactions.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the GC at J2000 coordinates 17: 44: 24.78,  - 2:  25.1, appears to be a symmetrical circle of 18.55" in diameter, with an estimated age of 10,000 to 20,000 years.  A total of 3w, 4f, and 8f frequency combinations were used to continuum map Sgr A East at 4.5, 8, 10, and 8 GHz, as well as 6 GHz (unpublished), with the results of 4.5 and 8 GHz previously published in 2017.  This present research combines previously published data with new maps at 10 GHz and 8 GHz (collected in 2017) to produce a comprehensive study of Sgr A East.  A unique set of luminosity and spectral index distributions at 4.5, 8, and 10 GHz, and new spectral index maps at these frequencies have been developed, with the results indicating a possible non-thermal emission origin.  A comparison of radio and mid-infrared data suggests that Sgr A East may be interacting with nearby molecular clouds, specifically at 8 GHz and mid-infrared wavelengths, where the cloud at [MPY2009] 89 is being affected.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using 61 datasets from the UCI machine learning repository. The outcomes reveal that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy and stability of classification models compared to the majority vote, particularly in undersampled systems and datasets with extreme minority class examples. The findings also indicate variations in the performance of different oversampling methods across datasets, suggesting the importance of exploring diverse oversampling techniques to improve multi-class text classification accuracy.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a month-long snapshot of the system's output, we observed notable patterns. Firstly, we found that areas with higher national death rates received more attention from local news, and this correlation strengthened over time. Additionally, we discovered that local news outlets tend to prioritize coverage of nearby regions experiencing low COVID activity if those areas have larger populations. Our results also show that local news often focuses on nearby regions with fewer restrictions and better economic conditions, even if other areas have lower case or death rates. This pattern is particularly evident if local news outlets have larger audiences and are less reliant on national advertisers.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels for total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the conservation of quadratic invariants (e.g., angular momentum) remains feasible with second-order accuracy, this conservation is lost at third-order and higher, due to issues with quadratic invariant preservation in SPH. Our research presents multiple approaches to rectify this issue: a novel smoothing kernel engineered to safeguard angular momentum conservation and two methodologies (adjusting particle positions or velocities) to restore quadratic invariant preservation after time integration. These methods require no significant increase in computational complexity and can be seamlessly integrated into existing frameworks. Furthermore, our approaches result in minimal alterations to mass transport, while also maintaining physical stability and preventing unphysical mass movement. Notably, our methods guarantee conservation of angular momentum and the preservation of quadratic invariants, while also upholding fundamental SPH principles.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs electric to magnetic form factors in the ep $\rightarrow$ np $\rightarrow$ np scattering process. The study found that measurements of a specific polarization transfer compartment and form factor ratio are correlated but independent of $Q^2$ when form factors are assumed to follow a Stein-Stein-Coleman dependence. However, assuming a Hohler dependence for form factors, the $G_E/G_M$ form factor ratio influences the $A_y$ cross-sectional ratio at low $Q^2$ values but differences diminish as $Q^2$ rises. Furthermore, when comparing JLab kinematics to theoretical predictions from form factor models, including the hyperfine form factor model and the Regge model, the study showed that the study's assumptions lead to agreement between the study's cross-sectional ratios and these form factor models at low $Q^2$ values. However, the study's cross-sectional ratios differ from these form factor models at higher $Q^2$ values.

We develop a novel, yet efficient, method for augmenting existing data to enhance learning efficiency, which is applicable to both reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning. The proposed method, known as synthetic experiences, generates virtual transitions created from the existing ones through a two-step approach: first, it determines relevant similarities between states and then imagines how the environment would respond to these similar states as if a real transition had occurred. Specifically, it uses a pre-trained neural network to identify analogous states and then generates virtual transitions by applying the identified similarities to a knowledge-sharing mechanism. The generated virtual transitions are integrated with the existing data and used for both RL and imitation learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced training time. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces training time by at least 43% while also improving performance, which is particularly evident for large complex problems.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons, independent of each other's charge states, has been conducted utilizing the full dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions captured by the CMS detector at the LHC between 2016 and 2018, operating at a 13 TeV energy. The investigation examines the Higgs bosons' separate and paired production in events featuring two photons, one of which is a pseudorapidity displacement from the other, with a combined transverse momentum exceeding 350 GeV. The analysis is executed while accounting for background influences from top-quark pairs and other non-Higgs-related phenomena. The occurrence of this Higgs pair production, not facilitated by resonance, is constrained to not exceed 3.8 times the Standard Model's predicted rate, based on the 95% confidence level, while observing no instances of charged Higgs pair production, not facilitated by resonance, and establishing an upper limit of 81.1 times the Standard Model's predicted rate, also at the 95% confidence level.

Atomic magnetometers that employ self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in use for over a decade, has significant potential in various healthcare applications, including MRI system replacements and lung disease diagnosis tools.
Despite its value, self-oscillating atomic magnetometers face major drawbacks: limited field-of-view and severe environmental sensitivity risks, which severely impede their practical applications in real-world settings.
A recent study presents a new self-oscillating atomic magnetometer, designed with a broad field-of-view and minimal environmental sensitivity.
The system relies on an unshielded laser and advanced detection techniques, allowing it to identify a 1 mT magnetic field change from background noise.
The development marks a significant breakthrough in atomic magnetometry, particularly in real-world application suitability improvement.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation demonstrates that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The study sets benchmark lists for direct detection, lifetime, and collider constraints, as well as reexamines long-lived neutralino dark matter in the context of EDMs and related processes.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (EPTAS) to solve the critical node detection problem and design a simple heuristic for finding an exact solution, both applied to general graphs with the possibility of having negative edge weights. Furthermore, we introduce a similar EPTAS for finding the minimum spanning tree with specified degree constraints and apply these methods to previously unapplicable instances, specifically, multicommodity flow optimization problems depending on node subset values. To address the complexity of finding an optimal multicommodity flow, we prove that a restricted version of this problem is in the NP-hard class. We also introduce a new approximation method for finding the minimum spanning tree with specified degree constraints for general graphs with the possibility of having negative edge weights. Furthermore, we extend the EPTAS to high-dimensional scenarios and provide theoretical evidence supporting the feasibility and effectiveness of these methods. We test the proposed methods on various synthetic and real-world datasets and evaluate their performance in terms of execution speed and accuracy. The results show that the proposed methods achieve high approximation ratios across different parameter settings and test scenarios, with significant speed improvements for high-dimensional cases and accurate results for most test datasets.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks involves utilizing the second-order information of individual modules to create a shared update tensor. Each module's update is based on local data and a partially instantiated optimization subproblem. The main innovation is a communication strategy where data and optimization parameters are exchanged via average aggregation as needed. We investigate a comprehensive set of theoretical and experimental issues, including convergence and rate of growth, utilizing a dual decomposition approach. The proposed $NSNA$ is compared against state-of-the-art algorithms in experimental contexts, specifically quantum chemistry-based optimization problems. The analysis demonstrates Newton's optimality, the efficiency of a single communication event, and a single data batch processing capability. It's worth noting that some findings are dependent on a specific assumption, indicating a potential improvement for future studies. The accompanying code can be found on the EPrintServer platform at a specified URL.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages with limited knowledge. Finally, our findings are made publicly available in an open-source format, allowing for easy verification and fostering a discussion that promotes accountability around language-based technologies, especially in contexts where resources are scarce.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, opens up a wider range of scientific possibilities for dark matter and neutrino research, as well as penetrating deeper into Earth with double monolithic detectors. The precision and sensitivity required for directional dark matter detection are particularly challenging, whereas in neutrino research, the difficulty lies in distinguishing between nuclear and electron recoils. This report will explore the progress made so far in understanding and controlling these processes, as well as achieving directional detection, with a focus on relevant single-crystal technologies.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting commercial driving behavior and designed an questionnaire to capture experts' opinions on their significance. Our analysis of the questionnaire results revealed that most experts consider contextual factors when evaluating driver behavior, underscoring the necessity of incorporating environmental conditions into the driver assessment process. Additionally, our findings indicate that different experts have distinct perspectives on behavior and contextual factors, likely influenced by their individual roles and experiences.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,844,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
