The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset and framework are now available for further research at http://visual.ai.cimel.sorapure.net/oov2022/.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving the calculation of space-varying mean curvature and associated first-order differential equations. By applying this approach to a theoretical model, it was demonstrated that a system with interacting random variables exhibits a transition from orderly to chaotic states, illustrating the intersection of random field theories and system biology. The findings also imply that random field theories provide implicit spatial models, offering new avenues to explore complex systems' states and the intricate relationships between their random and random-like characteristics.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function $L(s,F,\chi,St)$ and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of Boecherer. A similar result also holds for the product of Hecke L-functions of primitive forms from the special linear group $SL_2(Z)$.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The findings show that connecting full graphene nanoribbons to ferromagnetic contacts results in low spin polarization due to minimal magnetization within the ribbons. Conversely, spin polarization reaches nearly total saturation (100%) in nanoribbons with significantly wide bands, achievable by increasing the width of the ribbons or shortening the barrier width between them and the gate electrodes. The proposed electric control of the barrier height using a ferromagnetic gate resolves issues of contact disorder and interface defects, allowing fine-tuned electronic properties within the ribbons. The band structure of these ribbons can be optimized by adjusting the barrier width and the gate voltage, facilitating room temperature electrical conductivity through graphene nanoribbons.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a pancyclic structure.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of unevenness in the collision and how it affects the direction of which these particles travel. It found that the unevenness of the collision can explain which way these particles move, how much they move, and what patterns they move in. This study considered not only particles with a certain charge but also particles in general, as well as several other particles, such as mesons, baryons, and anti-baryons. The research showed that the origin of the collision's unevenness does not affect the direction of which way these particles travel it does however affect how much these particles move and what patterns they move in, and that the amount of matter that participates in the collision influences the direction of which way these particles travel.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method (ASK) is an algorithm for approximating multi-dimensional dynamical systems by elevating their state space to a higher dimension. ASK utilizes spectral methods to approximate functions representing the initial conditions' distribution and associated expectations. By employing Gaussian quadrature in one spatial dimension, ASK can significantly minimize computational requirements. Our investigations demonstrate that ASK achieves substantial reductions in computational costs in higher dimensional systems compared to time-evolving methods incorporating adaptive mesh refinement. Furthermore, ASK yields highly accurate estimates of expectations compared to other quadrature-based approaches. Notably, ASK's accuracy and efficiency improvements are particularly pronounced in systems with a moderate number of dimensions (three to five) and outperform traditional methods, while remaining competitive even in systems with more than five degrees of freedom.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored, leading to the development of resonance parameters. RES-pot, a new program, is presented as a tool for systematically calculating resonance parameters in one-electron atoms and ions, based on the exterior complex amplitude method. A thorough examination of the program's underlying assumptions and physical meanings of its variables and parameters is conducted. The program's effectiveness is demonstrated through the calculation of resonance parameters for hydrogen-like ions with nuclear charges between 0.5 and 3, and how it can be utilized to determine coupling potentials between bound and continuum states, and calculate various physical properties. The program's ability to handle highly autoionizing states, influenced by non-hermitian effects, is also explored. The derived resonance parameters can be utilized in various applications, such as calculating photoionization cross sections and autoionization rates.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a dominant method for solving the Schrödinger problem in diverse fields. Notably, as the complex values approached absolute unity, the problem undergoes a degenerate transformation where the solution tends towards zero, rendering the Sinkhorn algorithm ineffective. This work presents an alternative algorithm in the complex plane, and demonstrates that it remains consistent even when one of the complex values equals zero. Moreover, when the problem becomes degenerate, the proposed algorithm resorts to solving a linear equation, thereby avoiding the issues encountered by the Sinkhorn algorithm.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (syst. error) ± 1.1 pb (lumi.) ± 0.9 pb (beam). This outcome is consistent with theoretical predictions formulated using next-to-leading order perturbative QCD and amounts to 66.9 pb. This measurement represents the first t¯t cross-section determination in 5.02 TeV collisions and involves the smallest integrated luminosity recorded at the LHC so far.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this phenomenon in the context of systems involving multiple interacting particles coupled with a central qubit or cavity, both in both non-local and local contexts. There's some evidence suggesting that these core elements might display protective characteristics against decoherence. However, there are opposing results, with conflicting results, particularly for systems consisting of multiple particles, leaving the matter uncertain.

We've explored the behavior of a central element - the central degree of freedom - when connected to the disordered lattice model of a system consisting of interacting fermions under high density conditions. This central element is represented as a multiple of the local gap excitations' average - the local gap is the energy difference between the highest and lowest occupied states at high density - which varies depending on the core's excitation level. We've discovered the emergence of two distinct phenomena, where the behavior of the core is barely influenced by the surrounding system for small core excitations and the core's characteristic relaxation time increases significantly with the core's excitation level despite the surrounding system's inherent characteristic of not supporting long-term current flow. We've explained these phenomena by suggesting that the core's characteristic - the core's characteristic scaling with core excitations - acts as an effective current blockade rule, preventing the core's characteristic relaxation when the core's characteristic effectively blocks the surrounding system and the core's characteristic scales with the surrounding system's

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, and $v$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,v}(z)$ satisfies the subordination relationship $u_{p,v}(z) < Az+B$, where $A$, $B$ are real numbers, $p$ and $v$ are parameters.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related restrictions isolated individuals and impacted urban confidence, resulting in a global decline in well-being. In response, technology has been used to create virtual environments for interaction and support emotional stability. Yet, the impact of these digital interventions is difficult to assess due to a shortage of data and standard evaluation methods.

This research investigates how technology can be utilized to enhance urban well-being in intelligent cities by identifying key factors influencing emotional stability in urban areas. A fuzzy logic-based framework is proposed, which incorporates well-being as the adaptive variable, influenced by a diverse array of inputs including physical and social urban encounters. Moreover, remote sensing and IoT data are combined with digital mental health analytics to determine urban well-being with high accuracy and rapid processing. Additionally, the proposed approach utilizes machine learning algorithms to classify well-being states as healthy, at-risk, or unhealthy.

A realistic scenario involving a well-being aware smart city for residents affected by mental health issues is presented, followed by the introduction of an algorithm grounded in fuzzy logic and machine learning for classifying well-being states. We discuss how this method may be adapted and expanded upon in other urban scenarios, while emphasizing the need for further research on the application of AI in addressing urban well-being crises triggered by COVID-19 and similar pandemics.

This research project focuses on developing an innovative, step-by-step nonlinear field division method for solving complex two-phase fluid dynamics and transport issues at the pore level, which are modeled by partial differential equations. Some essential features of the proposed method include utilization of pressure-based models, integration with flux-based models, compliance with free boundary conditions, and the application of a two-split algorithm that breaks down complex nonlinear problems into simpler, more manageable two-part equations. This method can be applied in conjunction with versatile, field-adaptive numerical methods. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the practical implementation of the two-step nonlinear field division method by integrating it with the finite volume framework of an existing finite volume-based poromechanics code. This integration involves replacing its standard nonlinear solver with the new algorithm. The study also evaluates the practical efficiency of the proposed method through numerous test cases, which are primarily chosen from the domain decomposition field for their simplicity and ease of numerical analysis. Two-phase flow and transport issues are employed as study cases to verify the practical applicability and efficiency of the proposed method.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic molecules to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter, in response to chiral light with the right or left-handed polarization orientation, undergoes specific interactions, whereas non-chiral matter does not. This interaction potential can be utilized to differentiate between the two forms of chirality present within a mixture, effectively allowing for a selective activation/deactivation process. Notably, the concept has been explored for controlling stereo-selective reactions of chiral molecules by employing chiral light to interact with the mixture. Specifically, researchers have demonstrated that chiral light can be utilized to induce interactions between chiral molecules and a particular surface by interacting with the molecules prior to reflection onto the surface. This interaction potential, which depends on both the chirality of the light and the orientation of the molecules' rotation symmetry, can be harnessed for future applications in controlling chemical reactions on surfaces at the nanoscale.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model, including the Witten effect. This similarity extends to the perturbative amplitudes in the context of two-dimensional string theory, which align with those derived in recent studies. Nonetheless, in the context of two-dimensional string theory, an odd power term appears in the expansion of the free energy, influenced by the Witten effect, with a coefficient proportional to 1/(4 constant term in the beta function), whereas for JT gravity, this coefficient is simply 1/4.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, including a specific special case derived from the Einstein-Feldman equations with a vanishing cosmological constant, which simplifies to the perfect fluid source alone. Due to difficulties in solving the Einstein equations with a non-zero cosmological constant analyically, we instead present a numerical solution for a warp drive metric induced by a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant. We then analyze the key features of these spacetimes, focusing particularly on the gradient of the warp function, and discuss their potential implications for achieving warp speeds.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas, sewage), hindering construction projects that necessitate knowing the locations and relationships between above-ground and below-ground infrastructure. The rise of Building Information Modelling (BIM) enables the effective management of above-ground structures, but a comparable system for underground infrastructure is lacking. To address this, this research proposes developing digital twins for underground infrastructure to mitigate the associated risks. A proposed solution involves utilizing a dedicated platform to connect various service providers, enabling the creation of digital twins. Key services include data fusion to blend geographical and structural data, and spatial analysis tools to facilitate efficient maintenance coordination and issue detection. The feasibility of this platform was validated through a pilot test involving real-world problems during the development phase.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized both experimental and simulated approaches. Excluding noise from external influences, our findings suggest that the limitations on motion arise from the discrete nature of the Wigner crystal's vortex states and self-trapping effects. This restriction on motion within the crystal is predictable and independent of the system's size. However, this limitation on motion can potentially be overcome by manipulating the Vortices within the crystal, enabling the simulation of superconductivity by mimicking Bose-Einstein Condensation.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, a comprehensive theoretical explanation for its signal amplification has not been developed. Our research offers a detailed model incorporating the effects of electromagnetic field enhancement near metallic tips and electron tunneling transport. This model enabled the creation of an equation quantifying TERS intensity that aligns with experimental frequency measurements. Our findings suggest that the primary factors contributing to TERS signal amplification are the electromagnetic field and electron tunneling, with the latter significantly boosting the TERS frequency spectrum. Our study sets the stage for optimizing TERS' exceptional resolution by increasing its sensitivity.

Research has shown that Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) observed at radio wavelengths could originate from grains containing highly ionized substances, though the grains' size and charge distribution are uncertain. Electromagnetic theory predicts that AME-producing grains would also emit Anomalous Sunlight Emission (ASE), a counterpart visible in optical spectra, but no such signal has been detected so far. We examined data from the Gaia mission for evidence of AME-producing grains by searching for grains that emit preferentially at their polar ends, as grains of this type would be efficient emitters of AME and ASE. We identified and analyzed 14,845 grains of this type, then calculated their effective emissivity using the Gaia instrument's sensitivity limits. While our search was limited by poor signal-to-noise ratios, we were unable to detect ASE for any of the grains due to the constraints of our data. We concluded that future observations using higher signal-to-noise ratio missions such as Euclid or LSST would likely be able to detect ASE before the grains' emission peaks at radio frequencies.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the substantial entropy change, which has now been resolved through an extensive experimental and theoretical study. The findings indicate that the large entropy variation stems from changes in ammonium sulfate's lattice, rather than from the ammonoium ion's disintegration into hydrogen and nitrogen gases as previously speculated. Instead, the significant entropy change arises from the ion's gradual loss of crystalline structure and mobility within the lattice, and further research has revealed that this process is linked to ferroelectricity and high functional capabilities. Additionally, the study has identified an earlier phase transition, previously thought to be non-existent, which exhibits both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties along with ferroelectric, antiferroelectric, and ferrielectric states.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a conservative approach, which involves choosing options with a certain probability, whereas the optimal strategy would have them pick those options with certainty.  I've found that a dynamic quantum-system model can effectively illustrate this phenomenon, where the conservation of resources doesn't necessarily mean maximizing the reward.  This model, based on lossy quantum circuits, demonstrates that organisms might sometimes prefer a mixed strategy over the optimal one, which requires eliminating noise from the system.  Using a relevant performance measure, our analysis shows that this mixed strategy has its own benefits and can be viewed as an adaptive response to the system's environmental changes.  Specifically, this model can be seen as an equivalent version of a well-known theory about animal decision-making, which suggests that a mixed strategy might serve as an indicator for adaptive behavior.

A proposed approach for constructing a tetrahedron using a unit octagon in four-dimensional space is presented, which could provide an innovative geometric representation of the E8 root system. Each tetrahedron edge's length could be set to one unit, offering a possible new framework for visualizing this complex Lie algebra structure. If successful, this model could facilitate the development of tools for geometrically studying and working with unit octagons in four-dimensional space, potentially leading to advancements in geometry and physics.

The Fréchet distance is a significant metric in the field of computational geometry, used for measuring the similarity between curved paths in the plane. It's particularly valuable when analyzing the similarity between polygonal curves, especially when defining a maximal perfect match. We've developed an algorithm to compute this match in linear time, even when dealing with loops and complex polygonal curves. Unlike previous approaches, our method employs an entirely discrete procedure, free from randomization or approximation. Instead, it identifies whether a perfect match exists; if it does, the algorithm finds this match. Otherwise, it provides an approximate match with a specified proximity to the actual one, also found by the algorithm. We've demonstrated that our discrete problem is equivalent to a version of the well-studied TSP with neighborhoods at a specific edge length. Using this connection, we've proven that a perfect match's existence is indeed decidable. Furthermore, we've discovered that a perfect match's existence can also be determined using a volume argument. However, the algorithm we've devised is fundamentally different from the TSP variants it's connected to, as it handles more general types of curves, allowing for example, the inclusion of paths with copper measurements.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose the use of Bayesian inference as a potential MEM approach, evaluating its effectiveness on both realistic noise-controlled and extreme noise-scenarios, specifically on the IBM Q network. Our study demonstrates that a Pinheiro-Budagov model serves as an optimal prior distribution for Bayesian scaling, while showcasing the resilience of this scaling method even under the most severe noise conditions. Furthermore, we produce distributions that meet specific experimental requirements, and discuss the possibilities of extrapolating to broader applications, such as quantum algorithms.

When humans operate robot arms, there's often a misunderstanding about how to correctly hold the handle, leading to confusion and lost knowledge among users. To address this issue, our research focuses on assisting teleoperation tasks while informing users about the most effective way to control the robot and adapt its movement. By combining assistive and educational modes in a 'competition' framework, our system can quickly and efficiently transfer knowledge to users, even within tasks, and still meet assistive goals. Moreover, our findings indicate that incorporating educational aspects doesn't hinder productivity and that learning the optimal handling technique doesn't interfere with mastering other holding techniques. This study is based on a simulation environment known as BimSim.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on specialized sensors, such as 2D LiDARs, which are often used in research settings but not practical for consumer-grade robots. This study aims to develop a mapping solution that works with RGBD cameras, a more commonly deployed sensor on household robots. An online probabilistic mapping algorithm is presented that uses a 3D occupancy grid representation to build a map, incorporating camera-based SLAM for local map construction. An additional step is taken to assemble a global map from multiple local maps, leveraging the depth data in a Monte Carlo-based triangulation method. The proposed mapping approach demonstrates its efficacy in simulated environments and real-world scenarios involving a robotic tank. The findings indicate that the algorithm is effective at building useful maps, although it is not as accurate as 2D LiDAR-based SLAM methods when it comes to point cloud accuracy. Nonetheless, the method shows significant potential for building a useful map and navigating in unknown environments using consumer-grade RGBD cameras.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D synchronization, and phased array antennas. This paper presents a novel method to directly construct two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets by utilizing multivariable functions. To achieve this, an inter-group complementary code set is first developed using multivariable functions and subsequently utilized to produce the desired two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets. Utilizing multivariable functions not only allows for the determination of two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sets with considerable sizes, but also facilitates the analysis of their key characteristics.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. A proposed three-step algorithm combines sparse representation, total variation penalty, and the Anti-Osborne Algorithm, which is specifically designed to address polyenergetic X-ray noise and is tested on simulated and actual CT images.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas separated by a very narrow gap. We compare the results of a simple local response model and a more advanced nonlocal model that incorporates Hirschberger et al.'s approach. We examine both models under various gap widths and electron densities, with the latter being modelled using two different methods. The local model sometimes produces unrealistic results such as divergence, but the nonlocal model provides a consistent description of the propagating mode's properties. We also analyze how the electron spillover parameter influences the mode's effective refractive index and discuss its implications.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative significance of those terms. Although CNER bears some resemblance to related concepts such as List Question answering and Entity disambiguation, its primary goal is to gather a set of entity instances based on a given text input and pre-existing knowledge, without necessarily identifying the corresponding entities. We introduce a novel interface and gather a large dataset known as WebData, comprising over 5000 entity instances annotated by users in relation to various search terms and contexts. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for CNER and conduct a comprehensive set of experiments involving baseline algorithms and the developed dataset, showcasing the efficacy of user-provided cues in improving results. The code and datasets are made publicly available to foster future CNER investigations.

Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, with both intra- and inter-subject correlations present. While analyzing time series and longitudinal data differs in certain aspects, they frequently employ similar visual display methods. Our approach to creating data visualization tools and algorithms for these types of data involves identifying, evaluating, and addressing the unique characteristics of each domain using a uniform methodology. This research document outlines this methodology and applies it to create customized visualization solutions for time-based and longitudinal data. The proposal aims to develop an adaptive framework that allows for an in-depth analysis and tailored approach to visualizations, depending on the domain's specifications, requirements, and predefined criteria.

The quality of healthcare can significantly improve with the assistance of machine learning models analyzing Electronic Health Records. However, due to the contained sensitive information, access to public datasets is restricted, necessitating the development of techniques to protect patient privacy while maintaining data utility. Our solution employs Differential Privacy to safeguard privacy through the application of a metric called $\mathcal{H}$-Differential Privacy. We propose a method to quantify the application of DP, utilizing a defined template for a privacy metric that considers a DP mechanism's impact on a specific dataset. The template involves a privacy parameter $ε$ and a sensitivity metric $Δ$, both of which must be known to guarantee a dataset is protected consistently. We develop a proposal to determine $ε$ and $Δ$ automatically, enabling the creation of a public health dataset, along with an evaluation of its utility, specifically its classification effectiveness in the context of a public EHR classification challenge using machine learning methods.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions in the boundary using self-consistent field theory. We apply our model to a specific case, modeling the charged surface as a weakly coupled flexible sheet with periodic boundary conditions. We analyze our results, comparing them to Poisson-Boltzmann based models that account for non-uniform particle sizes. We also discuss how our method can be extended to study more complex systems, such as charged nanoscale pillars and charged inhomogeneous surfaces in the presence of specific ion properties.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE with two larger, more varied datasets. We evaluated the models' performance using a range of metrics and observed that fine-tuning a model with a small, high-quality dataset can be more effective than training the model on larger, more varied datasets.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between two users is established, and a multi-relay diversity network connects them. Each relay uses an inordinate amount of energy, and is activated only when it's close to the receiving user, and the signal from the primary link is extremely weak. A mix of the relay nodes' energy consumption and the signals they transmit, is taken into account when determining the power each relay uses. A specific set of parameters is identified, and the energy efficiency is calculated for this scenario, as well as one without network coding. A comparison between these two cases is presented, and the impact of some key parameters on the energy efficiency is examined.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and employs the scattering matrix formalism to calculate the impact of multiple impurities on the superconducting properties. Our research involves a detailed examination of the local density of states (LDOS) near the impurities in relation to their position, separation, and interaction with a nearby interface between different superconducting materials. One notable application of this model discusses the competitive and cooperative effects of multiple magnetic impurities on the Andreev bound states formed at the interface of Nb/Ta/Nb trilayers, which demonstrates the model's agreement with experimental observations.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To address these issues, our paper introduces an approach that incorporates both a deep learning-based alignment module and a graph-based propagation module.  The learning model learns key features of distributions while the graph-based model transfers knowledge from the initial scan to the next without relying on deep learning-based maps.  The combined algorithm allows the distribution shape to guide the graph-based propagation module, which preserves the integrity of the deep learning-based map.  When tested using data with significant changes, our method significantly improves registration accuracy compared to other methods.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure and a considerable amount of labeled data.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering a rapid transformation in the material's electronic structure. The resulting modifications significantly impact the material's absorption of X-ray energy, particularly in the vicinity of the target's core electrons. By intensely focusing X-ray flux onto a target, researchers can precisely analyze the abrupt changes that occur in the X-ray absorption process, using this information to construct three-dimensional, time-resolving images of the excited core regions. Due to its high spatial and temporal resolution, this approach is highly effective for in-depth analysis of the core regions of solids. However, the intense X-ray flux also gives rise to non-linear, fluence-dependent changes in the material's X-ray absorption cross-section. In this work, researchers demonstrate that by controlling the intensity of the X-ray pulse and selecting an optimal detector distance, the fluence-dependent changes in nickel oxide can be minimized, allowing for clear, time-resolving measurements of valence core excitations with high precision and detail. The study showcases the potential for spatially integrated examination of valence core excitations with high temporal resolution, even under extreme conditions induced by intense X-ray pulses.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to mitigate the effects of such attacks by removing malicious interference before feeding data into a DNN-based classifier. The proposed approach specifically protects AMC systems from attacks that generate noise based on pre-defined templates. The method's effectiveness against three types of templated adversarial attacks is demonstrated through simulations, showing significant improvements in DNN-based AMC accuracy and robustness against these attacks. Additionally, a comparative assessment of the DNN classifier's performance is conducted under adversarial conditions, with or without the adversarial attack generator (AADG), in the context of different attack template matching methods. The results showcase the efficacy of the proposed framework in enhancing the resilience of DNN-based AMC systems against templated adversarial attacks.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is crucial for assessing disease progression and disability scores but is difficult to automate due to non-specific imaging features and diverse lesion types. A fully-supervised deep learning approach is impractical because manual annotation is too time-consuming and costly for the majority of patients. Semi-supervised segmentation is hindered by the scarcity of complete segmentation labels, while pseudo-labeling methods produce low-quality fake labels that can impede performance. In response to these limitations, we propose a novel algorithm that leverages the advantages of active learning and pseudo-labeling in an adaptive and iterative process. By selectively relying on a limited subset of difficult cases from an ever-growing unlabeled dataset, the method iteratively refines its pseudo-labels and segmentation model. As a result, the approach requires fewer queries compared to alternative active learning strategies, achieving high performance on par with fully-supervised models when trained on a relatively small subset of labeled images. The process is iterative, allowing the model to progressively adapt to changing conditions with increasing sophistication.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

To evaluate the performance of reinforcement learning agent models using time-series data, we develop an asymptotic analysis for a broad class of continuous-time systems with generalized reinforcement learning. Our research indicates that the generalized reinforcement learning algorithm achieves a generalized Bellman principle approximation with adjusted bias, and we establish specific relationships between the algorithm's parameters, the sampling interval, and the approximation errors. Our findings reveal that the rate of convergence is influenced by the time-interval T, which affects the generalized error in a polynomial manner. A CT-Value Iteration method is proposed to estimate value functions and demonstrates a rate of convergence that scales with T. By combining these results, we establish a link between the performance of RL agent models and their training sample sizes, which corresponds to the value of T. Our research also presents a direct assessment of existing RL methods, revealing their limitations in learning continuous-time systems.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this mass enhancement of protostellar cores as a sign of mass accretion triggered by outflow dynamics, with support drawn from the findings of numerical simulations.  Conversely, far-infrared to 1.3 mm spectral analysis suggests that both protostellar and starless cores share comparable physical properties, including velocity, distance, temperature, and column density.  Ultimately, our research suggests that outflow-accelerated mass accretion dominates the dynamics of the outflowing cores, with mass gain likely occurring at an accelerated rate.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be detected by looking at the gamma rays they would emit due to the annihilation of particles produced through Hawking radiation. The restriction on the mass of such black holes based on variations of X-ray and gamma-ray data is explored in this study, focusing specifically on the potential influence of black holes with masses greater than $10^{14}~\mathrm{g}$ since these are out of range for stellar formation. The study examines Hawking radiation-produced axion and scalar particles, as well as semi- and fully-annihilating dark matter particles, and considers both the direct emission from black holes and the secondary gamma rays created when Hawking radiation particles interact with matter. Theoretical limits on PBHs have been imposed across various densities of matter, with the study demonstrating that gamma-ray data from the Major Atmospheric Gamma Imaging Cherenkov Experiment rules out most of the lighter PBHs with masses ranging from $3 \times 10^{14}~\mathrm{g}$ to $10^{16}~\mathrm{g}$. A broader range of masses, ranging from $10^{14}~\mathrm{g}$ to $10^{16}~\mathrm{g}$, has been excluded based on constraints on the matter density of the universe. These findings reinforce existing bounds from variations of X-ray and

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, confined to a narrow range of shapes. Our study explored systems in three dimensions with up to 512 molecules, modelled using the potential energy function developed by Shaw and McGrother et al. This potential accurately mimics the interactions found in real systems, however due to calculations limitations, we were unable to study smectic phases, instead focusing on nematic and isotropic liquid crystals. Our results revealed that systems with packing densities below 0.5 exhibit liquid crystals with isotropic and nematic structures, whereas systems with higher densities exhibit sol-gel transitions, featuring both nematic and isotropic structures, as well as hydrodynamic nematic and columnar structures. We also discovered that the nematic and columnar nematic phases exist in systems with specific density and temperature relationships and examined the transition dynamics between these phases.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial importance of special tokens in pre-trained language models.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning to rank documents in search outcomes, our findings indicate that the latter framework yields superior performance and greater interpretability. To achieve this, we developed an attention-based approach within the Siamese network framework, where the added item is maximally represented in the new collection, thus facilitating more accurate comparisons.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental data from Caruthers and Medvedev. This relationship enables us to reframe the generalized entropy theory for glass formation, combining the lattice cluster theory and Adam-Gibbs model, based on any of these properties to simplify the analysis. By utilizing thermodynamic scaling to assess correlations between properties and dynamics, we discovered that dynamic property scaling exponents are consistent regardless of which properties are used. This universality facilitates a direct link between static and dynamic characteristics, offering a valuable tool for predicting dynamics from static information and vice versa. Additionally, this approach allows us to refine the interpretation of dynamic scaling in complex fluids and minimize unnecessary variability in their dynamic behavior.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology that haven't been extensively tested. We utilize a decoder-only Transformer to assess children's understanding of these concepts, which involves reordering a sentence to make sense of it. Our findings indicate that the Transformer excel in reasoning about exclusion and inhibition but fall short in dealing with denial.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. Key concepts, such as globalization, are defined and distinguished from 'localization with insertion procedures', as seen in Witten's deformation $\mathcal{G}$-moduli spaces. Relevant insights come from a simplified model - the complex line bundle and its associated curvature on a one-dimensional complex projective space. In this example, the weights can be calculated directly, and this result serves as a reference point for the full, formal calculation within any symplectic manifold. Moreover, the example demonstrates how connection and curvature weights share a common structure, being rooted in a single type of graph known as an 'alternating wave'. Consequently, the full connection and curvature weights can be expressed through a combination of these alternating waves, which simplifies the calculation in the one-dimensional complex projective space case.

This research involves calculating entropy and the logarithm of the minimum eigenvalue of the square of the Hessian for the O(N) sigma model on a sphere topologically equivalent to S^{d-2} for dimensions of odd numbers and all non-negative integer values, using the dimensional regularization method. It demonstrates that in the large N limit, the entropy remains finite for any odd dimension. The findings show that the ratio of the entropy to the logarithm of the minimum eigenvalue exhibits order-dependent behavior, contradicting a previously proposed universal relationship.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on continuous-time Markov chains. This article builds upon their work, presenting a simplified method for calculating the transition matrix of the reversed Markov chain in partially asymmetric red Brownian motion with drift. The implementation of this method demonstrates that the reversed Markov chain can be computed directly from the transition matrix of the original Brownian motion. Consequently, the transition matrix of the reversed Markov chain for partially asymmetric red Brownian motion with drift can be derived by extrapolation from the known results for the Brownian motion without drift. Furthermore, the article derives explicit formulas for calculating the transition probability of partially asymmetric red Brownian motion with drift at any positive time and illustrates the applicability of this result in pricing Asian options.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated how cosmic rays interact within galactic clusters using cosmological magnetohydrodynamical models. Their analysis, which included a database of 10,000 clusters, yielded some key predictions: a uniform gamma-ray spectrum at energies ranging from a few hundred GeV to around one hundred TeV, a pattern that matches the diffuse gamma-ray background, and a strong connection between high-energy gamma-rays and the electron-rich plasma within these clusters.

Cosmological inflationary models that closely match the characteristics needed to explain the universe's homogeneous expansion, also enable the study of highly excited classical oscillators. This scenario includes the potential for these oscillators to produce particles when they decay, leading to a rapid expansion of the universe - an outcome that agrees with observations of a flat, non-expanding universe. However, if such oscillators remain highly excited during the universe's expansion, their behavior becomes akin to that of free massive scalars. This similarity raises concerns about potential discrepancies in the universe's model, given that highly excited oscillators typically release energy as they decrease in amplitude, resulting in a violation of the null energy condition for the scalar field. This paper explores the possibility of this excess energy's impact on cosmological inflation and the transition to a radiation-dominated era. The analysis reveals that there are limited window periods during the universe's early stages in which highly excited oscillators can generate the necessary particles without disrupting the universe's model via mode mixing.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called $L_{f}\cdot x$ is introduced that enables the analysis of whether and to what extent aspects of an image contribute to a model's output. By utilizing this framework in conjunction with existing visualization methods, the connections between these techniques and the model's decision-making process can be more accurately identified. Moreover, a new image manipulation algorithm is proposed that involves replacing image regions with synthetic patterns, thereby enhancing the accuracy of region importance analysis. The proposed techniques have been successfully applied to demonstrate the specific image regions that influence the model's classification in specific cases.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates, capable of capturing key characteristics of their complex behavior, remains an unresolved challenge in physics. This paper demonstrates how incorporating long-distance interactions between electrons and phonons into a microscopic model can lead to novel interactions competitive with traditional superexchange. In a simplified representation of cuprate materials, our model indicates that this coupling leads to a strong forward scattering effect, causing electrons to exhibit more correlation and potentially giving rise to additional interactions. This enhanced interaction strength facilitates both superexchange and a weaker, more distant interaction, creating an environment where magnetism and charge can become intertwined, leading to various complex phenomena observed in cuprate materials, such as long-distance ordering, different types of pairing, and underlying parallel ordering patterns. This basic theoretical framework thus offers a new perspective on the underlying physics of cuprate superconductivity and other related effects, such as long-distance ordering, pairing, and underlying parallel effects. This basic theoretical framework thus offers a new perspective on the underlying physics of cuprate superconductivity and other related effects, such as long-distance ordering, pairing, and underlying parallel effects.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. This study proposes a novel causal learning approach to identify crucial indicators and causal links related to the 90-90-90 targets. This method employs machine learning techniques to create causal models, incorporating important variables and connections while dismissing irrelevant ones. When tested on five African nations, the approach demonstrated its effectiveness in pinpointing key indicators and causal relationships linked to HIV awareness and treatment. For example, the study found that female awareness of HIV was associated with primary school attendance, while male awareness was linked to migration to urban areas. Notably, the approach worked better for men than women, likely due to social biases and differences in men's and women's behavior.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state, when triggered by magnetic fields, goes through a phase characterized by partial topological charge reversal. Utilizing Lorentz transmission electron microscopy, the magnetization patterns within this material were directly visualized while decreasing the magnetic field's strength. Due to skyrmion stability, the transition directly into the helical phase is ruled out and an equilibrium skyrmion lattice is ruled out as well as the existence of a fraction of disorder-induced skyrmions. An alternative explanation, based on the competition between the energy expenses for skyrmion lattice creation and helical phase creation and the increasing disorder within the lattice as the field decreases, proposes that the observed phase transition occurs into an intermediate state containing antivortex solitons.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation
of such models, encompassing both dynamic factor models of large systems and
factor augmented models of expanded systems, are examined in depth.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field, albeit accompanied by an insufficient understanding of its foundational principles. Building on the successes of deep neural networks, Bayesian deep learning makes an effort to rectify this by quantifying uncertainty. However, there remains controversy surrounding its implementation in deep learning models. Drawing inspiration from classical Bayesian statistics, BD integrates uncertainty estimation into predictive models by treating data and parameters as interconnected nodes in a Bayesian network. This allows for the separation of data and model uncertainties, facilitating the allocation of uncertainty to disparate components of the model. This tutorial will concentrate on advancing understanding of BD, fostering collaboration among various research groups, and showcasing cutting-edge research in the application of BD to deep learning. We will commence with an introduction to key concepts in Bayesian statistics and their practical utilization. This will be followed by an in-depth exploration of BD, encompassing its approaches, challenges, and current trends. Subsequently, we will present numerous applications of BD, encompassing computer vision, machine learning, medicine, self-driving vehicles, and quantum computing. Finally, we will outline future research directions, including emerging topics and promising avenues for further investigation.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global convective dynamo simulations to investigate turbulent properties in the models. The study focuses on the turbulent advection of magnetic fields in the interior of rapidly rotating stars with different internal structures and surface magnetic activity levels. The study evaluates and compares the application of various numerical methods to calculate turbulent parameters, such as the turbulent diffusion coefficient and the alpha-effect. The study further explores how these turbulent properties vary across various regions within the models and under distinct magnetic states. The study concludes by examining the implications of these findings on the explanatory power of the mean-field theory with respect to solar and late-type star phenomena.

A study has revealed molecular outflows in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 using the ALMA. At a high resolution of ~0.3", the ALMA detected outflows of molecular gas emitting CO emission with high velocities of up to 6400 km per second. Since this galaxy has a high rate of star formation and intense starburst activities, it's expected to have outflows of gas that can be seen across the entire spectrum, from radio to optically. However, there's no clear relation between the molecular and ionized gas outflows despite both emitting certain wavelengths of light. It's suggested that the molecular gas outflows in this galaxy have no direct connection to the energy produced by the starburst activities. Instead, it's proposed the gas outflows have been compressed and heated by the starburst activities, causing the gas to form in clumps that can be seen in certain wavelengths of light. Another possibility suggests that the gas outflows have no clear relation between the molecular and ionized gas outflows. It's suggested the gas outflows have no clear relation between the molecular and ionized gas outflows.

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations for magnetized plasmas is provided by quasilinear theory, describing how particles interact with waves through resonant processes. The reduced model in a turbulent regime shows that the distribution of particles changes over time due to a kinetic diffusion effect. The model's analytical solution reveals a universal scaling of the particle distribution, which depends on the momentum's distribution in the initial condition and the time $t \propto t_0 (\kappa p_0)^{-4}$, where $\kappa$ is the wave number, $p_0$ is the average momentum, and $t_0$ is the initial time. The scaling of the interaction effect is independent of the type of particle and wave involved, indicating a universal kinetic effect in the interaction between particles and waves in magnetized plasmas.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper presents a comprehensive review of the theoretical aspects of dimuonium, a bound state composed of an antiparticle and a particle, formed from different muons. It examines the interactions of dimuonium within atomic systems and nuclear forces, focusing on the structural and spectral properties of dimuonium atoms in various environments. The review also discusses methods for observing and measuring bound dimuonium, including experimental techniques. The examination of antimatter-based bound states like dimuonium expands our understanding of atomic physics and potentially enables new muon experiments, contributing to our knowledge of the atomic behavior of two muons and the interaction between dimuonium and matter.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our proposed model encompasses both absolute and relative wealth in a comprehensive utility function. The utility functions, derived from power law equations, allow for flexibility with varying exponents to suit individual benchmarks or market scenarios. The outcome provides an explicit solution and is compared to the original Merton problem outcome, with implications for the Capital Asset Pricing Model framework.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This is due in part to the limited star formation occurring within these galaxies, ultimately resulting in the preservation of pristine conditions and the presence of pristine interstellar mediums (ISM). This makes them ideal subjects for studying the evolution of the cosmic ISM. This paper outlines findings from the study of a pristine ISM in dwarf galaxies, which was accomplished by analyzing data from the Local Irregulars View of Survey Anatomy (LIRAS) and the Nine-Sigma Survey. This research demonstrates that the ISM in dwarf galaxies contains both neutral and molecular gas, which can be observed in the $^{12}CO(1-0)$ and $^{12}CO(3-2)$ emission. A correlation between dust and CO emission in these galaxies was noted but found not to be particularly strong. Data from the GALEX survey indicated the presence of low levels of star formation in these galaxies, ultimately resulting in the classification as pristine based on the ratio of star formation rate to ISM mass density. This low ratio in these galaxies can be explained by the constraints imposed by the mass density of the ISM and by the limited dynamic range of the star formation process. This research further suggests that the mass of the ISM in these galaxies can be accurately predicted based on their stellar mass and by the mass of gas, which can be observed in the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological

We examine the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle is resistant to collapse. The insulating behavior of fermions is attributed to an immense gap forming between the fermion and fermion-like states. This stability is exceptional due to the absence of fermion-fermion interactions and is characterized by the ferromagnetic peptide structure of the bosonic excitation. Consequently, a substantial increase in bosonic excitation levels results in enhanced stabilization of the fermionic quasiparticle. Moreover, the relationship between the bosonic excitation's energy and the number of lattice sites reveals that the fermionic quasiparticle achieves a heightened level of stability when the energy per bosonic excitation follows a logarithmic increase with the number of lattice sites.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to broader classes of these groups. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a linear divergence function. Furthermore, our study encompasses the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $BV$. Alongside existing results in \cite{Kodama:2020to}, our findings confirm that these braided groups display linear divergence as well.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. An improved RAG variant, called full-rag, is developed by incorporating span-based retrieval and generation components within a single neural framework. The efficacy of full-rag is assessed through practical applications, including natural language inference and question answering tasks, where it outperforms the results achieved by the original RAG model. Furthermore, the performance of full-rag is compared to RAG-based automatic text compression methods, showing that it significantly outdoes its precursor in terms of accuracy and efficiency. all-rag implementations are accessible via publicly hosted GitHub repositories, located at https://github.com/ashishbakulchandani/end-to-end-rag.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we verify a long-standing conjecture of A. Magnus regarding these coefficients, making use of the Riemann-Hilbert and Tornheim problems in conjunction with some unique Askey-Romaniuc polynomials properties.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as annotation quality, reliability, and cost efficiency. Specifically, obtaining accurate annotations of complex tasks like software code summaries can be particularly challenging. To combat these issues, we propose a novel multi-stage approach, referred to as QCS, aimed at accurately annotating software code summaries while simultaneously monitoring and adjusting the mechanism to mitigate the concurrent problems of annotation quality and labor expense. Our solution entails (a) initially utilizing expert-provided examples and high-quality annotations derived from them to train models that can accurately predict code summary accuracy; (assistant}(b) leveraging these models to assign tasks to the best MTurk workers, thereby improving annotation quality; and (c) employing a partially self-supervised learning mechanism, where a subset of annotated summaries serves as training data for a CS-based automatic annotation tool, and subsequently unfreezing the CS encoder to predict code summaries for unseen programs. Our results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances annotation accuracy (from 71% to 84%), as well as the efficiency of the system, with the automatic annotation tool achieving an impressive overall performance of 80% accuracy.

Text-based image rectification involves shifting text characters to a common reference point while preserving their original orientation, unlike common delinking approaches that ignore text displacement. A novel neural network, named TS2-Net, is developed to automatically perform this text-based image rectification task. Distinguishing it from other delinking methods, TS2-Net's token shift module captures the relationship between rotated text characters, enabling it to predict a common reference point for various text shifts. Additionally, the neural network's token embedding module encodes text images into embedded forms suitable for processing by downstream delinking models. Furthermore, the attention-based token selection module facilitates a direct connection between the text image embedding module and the token shift module, ensuring that the delinking process focuses on text information. A synthetic text dataset is created to evaluate the performance of TS2-Net and other delinking methods, with experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this neural network in correcting text-based images while producing high-quality delinked outputs.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, can appear naturally in new physics scenarios, especially in composite Higgs models. It's been shown that existing experiments provide little restriction on these interactions, but they can potentially be detected at the Large Hadron Collider by looking at rare top decays and in other processes involving top particles, specifically through further research at the LHC, specifically in searches for top partners that exhibit enhanced interactions with top particles.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested that blends rules for preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  A key innovation is the introduction of a balance parameter, referred to as $\mathcal{B}$, to regulate the extent of these processes.  It's noted that this type of network falls within the scope of the general triangle inequality model established by Barabasi and Albert's preferential attachment model, making it analytically tractable.  A key outcome from this analysis is the derivation of a distribution for the in-degree sequence that is capable of capturing diverse degree distributions.  It's argued that this type of hybrid network offers a more nuanced representation of real-world networks, whose degree distribution often falls between the results of pure preferential attachment and uniform attachment.  A range of numerical experiments are presented to examine the characteristics of this hybrid network, including its clustering coefficient, which is found to be relatively low compared to other similar network models.  Ultimately, it's suggested that this type of hybrid network could serve as a useful platform for analyzing and drawing insights from real-world networks where a single attachment rule is insufficient to explain the observed behavior.

The expanding utilization of unlicensed frequency bands necessitates dependable interference management systems and hence reliable identification of wireless interference (WII). Our research proposes a novel WII approach that leverages a deep convolutional neural network to accurately identify multiple co-channel interferers for diverse signal types, such as Wi-Fi, LTE-FDD, LTE-FDD, and Wi-Fi 6, using a single receiver. The proposed method employs a deep neural network to analyze the distorted signal at a receiver and pinpoint the source of interference, which has been successfully tested and validated for various scenarios and architectures. The results show that the proposed approach achieves an average detection accuracy of nearly 100% for 2-Tier scenarios and up to 99% in 3-Tier scenarios.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary systems, we must rely on accurate quantum mechanics theories. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in previous quantum mechanics interpretations, eliminating false assumptions that have led to misunderstandings of gravitational effects. A valid method for calculating energy levels of particles influenced by gravity involves deriving them from the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. This requires considering the complex nature of quantum systems, reflecting both potential energy influences and momentum influences. When a free particle moves under gravity without any restrictions on its motion, its energy evolution can be directly inferred from solving the Schrödinger equation with a gravitational potential, taking into account that the Hamiltonian in this case combines kinetic energy operators with gravitational potential energy operators. If the gravitational field is static, the Schrödinger equation can be adapted by expressing the Hamiltonian as the sum of kinetic and potential energies. For quantum systems not experiencing freedom of movement, their energy influences can be calculated by solving the Schrödinger equation with a Hamiltonian representing the interplay of kinetic and potential energies. Despite its validity, the Schrödinger approach has limitations when dealing with macroscopic objects due to its minuscule size constraints. In contrast, a new quantum formalism offers a different perspective that seeks to avoid these limitations and may provide alternative solutions to them.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value equal to or exceeding 1.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be constrained by exclusive processes. Researchers have proposed a method to analyze generalized parton distributions with a nucleon using electro-excitation form factors. This method applies to both spin-1/2 and spin-3/2 particles and yields 15 independent distribution parameters for particles with a non-zero spin.
